docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Django] Web Framework

created by Anthropic’s AI Claude at the request of Serge Tahé - September 2026

This document is a translation of the original French version, generated using an automated tool. Some expressions or technical terms may not fully reflect the original meaning.

This course shows, step by step, how to build an MVC web application with the Django 6.1 framework and Python. The HTML pages are generated by the server with Django templates (the DTL language), with no JavaScript framework in the browser, and data access goes through the Django ORM.

It has two parts. First come 28 small examples, each focused on a single concept: routes (urls.py, path, include), views, responses, redirects and middleware; request parameters, data classes and forms used as validators; DTL templates, parent template, tags and filters, Django forms, the Post / Redirect / Get pattern, messages and CSRF protection; internationalization with gettext; data scopes (request, session, cache, signed cookies); the request life cycle with middleware and signals; JWT authentication in a cookie, roles, captcha and rate limiting; and finally a layered web / business / DAO architecture with the Django ORM and MySQL, with transactions and optimistic locking.

Then comes a complete case study, RdvMedecins: an appointment-booking application for a medical practice, with three roles (administrator, doctors, patients), available in French and English, in which every file is commented.

Prerequisites: the basics of web programming (HTTP, HTML) and of the Python language (variables, lists, dictionaries, functions, classes, modules). The tools used are Python 3.12 or later, MySQL or MariaDB, Visual Studio Code and curl.

This course belongs to a series that covers the same 28 examples, number by number, with other frameworks: NestJS, ASP.NET Core MVC, Spring MVC, Flask, Laravel and Symfony. The frameworks can thus be compared example by example, but this course can be read on its own.

All courses by Serge Tahé

docs.title: 13.1. Installing Python
docs.text:
The examples and case study require [Python] 3.12 or later ([Django] 6.1 requires it). They have been tested with version 3.13.

Under [Windows], download the installer from the python.org/downloads page (the "Download Python 3.13.x" button, or a more recent version). On the first screen of the installer, check the "Add python.exe to PATH" box, which allows you to type [python] in any console, then click "Install Now." The installer also installs [pip], the [venv] module, and the [py] launcher ([py -3.13] launches a specific version when multiple versions are installed). In [Windows] 10 and 11, typing [python] without having it installed opens the Microsoft Store: this is a system shortcut that can be disabled (Settings / Apps / Advanced app settings / App launch aliases).

On [macOS], use the python.org installer or the [Homebrew] package manager: [brew install python@3.13]. Under [Linux], [Python] is already present, but the modules [venv] and [pip] are often separate packages. Under [Ubuntu] 24.04 (where the version of [Python] is 3.12):

sudo apt install python3 python3-venv python3-pip

Under [macOS] and [Linux], the commands are named [python3] and [pip3]; in an activated virtual environment, [python] and [pip] are sufficient. Verify the installation in a new console:

python --version
python -m pip --version

The first command should display a version number equal to or greater than 3.12 (for example, [Python 3.13.7]).

docs.title: 13.2. pip and virtual environments
docs.text:
[pip] is the library manager for [Python]. It downloads libraries from the [PyPI] (pypi.org) repository: an Internet connection is required during installation. If you are behind a corporate proxy, specify the proxy using the environment variables [HTTP_PROXY] and [HTTPS_PROXY], or using the [--proxy] option of [pip].

A virtual environment is a folder containing a lightweight copy of the [Python] interpreter and its own libraries: each project has its own, in the versions it requires, without affecting the [Python] installation or other projects. Useful commands in a project folder (the one containing [requirements.txt]):

python -m venv .venv                 # create the virtual environment (.venv folder)
.venv\Scripts\activate               # Activate it (Windows)
source .venv/bin/activate            # activate it (Linux, macOS)
pip install -r requirements.txt      # Install the project libraries
pip list                             # the installed libraries
pip freeze                           # the same list, in requirements.txt format
deactivate                           # exit the environment

Under [Windows], [PowerShell] sometimes refuses to run the activation script (“script execution is disabled on this system”): the command [Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned] enables it for the current user. You can also bypass activation by directly calling the environment’s interpreter: [.venv\Scripts\python manage.py runserver].

The [.venv] folder cannot be copied from one machine to another (it contains absolute paths and system-specific programs): it must be recreated using the commands above. This is why it is not included in the course materials. The [exemples] folder has its own environment, shared by all 28 examples; the case study has its own.

The [mysqlclient] library and the [MySQL] driver (Example 28 and the case study) are written in C. Under [Windows], [pip] downloads a precompiled version: no action is required. Under [Linux] and [macOS], [pip] compiles it, and to do so requires the development files from [MySQL] and a compiler:

sudo apt install python3-dev default-libmysqlclient-dev build-essential pkg-config     # Ubuntu, Debian
brew install mysql-client pkg-config                                                    # macOS
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(brew --prefix)/opt/mysql-client/lib/pkgconfig"                # macOS, before `pip install`

Without them, [pip install -r requirements.txt] fails on [mysqlclient], with an error message referring to [pkg-config] or [mysql_config].

docs.title: 13.3. Installing Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
[Visual Studio Code] downloads from code.visualstudio.com. Add three extensions (View menu / Extensions):

  • Python (from Microsoft): for running and debugging [Python] code, and managing virtual environments. It installs the Python Debugger extension along with it;
  • Pylance (from Microsoft, also installed with the Python extension): code completion, code navigation (including the code for [Django], located in the [.venv] folder), error reporting, and type annotation checking;
  • Django (by Baptiste Darthenay): syntax highlighting and shortcuts for the [Django] templates ([.html] files in the [templates] folder).

Open the [exemples] folder or the case study folder (File menu / Open Folder), then select the interpreter for the folder’s virtual environment (Command Palette, Ctrl+Shift+P, Python: Select Interpreter, then the one for [.venv]). The built-in terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal) then automatically activates the environment and allows you to run applications and commands from [python manage.py ...] without leaving the editor.

To run an application step by step, create a debug configuration (Run menu / Add Configuration, then Python Debugger and Django): the editor launches [manage.py runserver] under the debugger’s control and pauses at the breakpoints set in the views.

docs.title: 13.4. Installing MySQL with Laragon
docs.text:
[Laragon] installs a ready-to-use [MySQL] server under [Windows], along with the [HeidiSQL] administration tool (see “Installing Laragon” in the introduction). After installation:

  • the “Start All” button launches the [MySQL] server on port 3306;
  • the user [root] has no password: these are the values from the [DATABASES] setting in Example 28 ([config/settings.py]), and the variables [DB_USER] and [DB_PASSWORD] from the [.env] file in the case study;
  • the Database button opens [HeidiSQL], where the File menu / Run a File menu item (SQL) runs the scripts [dbpersonnes.sql] (Example 28) and [dbrdvmedecins2.sql] (case study).

In [Linux] or [macOS], install [MySQL] or [MariaDB] using the system’s package manager, and run the scripts using the command-line client [mysql] ([mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql]). The [mysqlclient] driver and the [MySQL] engine from [Django] work with both without any configuration. Under [Linux], the [root] account from [MariaDB] is often configured to log in only via the system account [root] ([sudo mysql]): a user is then created for the applications:

sudo mysql -e "CREATE USER 'cours'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'cours'; GRANT ALL ON dbpersonnes.* TO 'cours'@'localhost'; GRANT ALL ON dbrdvmedecins2.* TO 'cours'@'localhost';"

and we specify this to the applications: the keys [USER] and [PASSWORD] from the setting [DATABASES] for Example 28, the lines [DB_USER=cours] and [DB_PASSWORD=cours] from the file [.env] for the case study.

docs.title: 13.5. Installing curl
docs.text: [curl] is included with [Windows] 10 and 11, [macOS], and most [Linux] distributions. On [PowerShell], you must type [curl.exe], not [curl]: In older versions of [PowerShell], [curl] is an alias for another command ([Invoke-WebRequest]), which has different options. In the command prompt for [Windows] ([cmd]), the quotation marks for a string JSON are written as [\"] (example 11), and a string URL that contains [&] must be enclosed in double quotes.

docs.title: 13.6. The django-admin tool
docs.text:
[Django] installs a command, [django-admin], which is not required to follow this document (the examples are provided ready-to-use), but is used to start a new project. The [manage.py] file for each project is a [django-admin] file that also knows the project’s settings: within a project, you type [python manage.py] instead of [django-admin]. The most useful commands:

django-admin startproject config .        # a new project, whose configuration is the config package
python manage.py startapp pages           # a new application, the `pages` folder
python manage.py runserver 8000           # the development server
python manage.py check                    # Check the project (settings, routes, templates, etc.)
python manage.py check --deploy           # Check the security settings for a production deployment
python manage.py shell                    # a Python console with Django loaded
python manage.py dbshell                  # the database client, with the project settings
python manage.py inspectdb                # Write the models for an existing database (to be reviewed and corrected)
python manage.py makemessages -l en       # identify text to be translated (.po file)
python manage.py compilemessages          # compile the dictionaries (.mo files)
python manage.py collectstatic            # Gather static files for production
python manage.py diffsettings             # Settings that differ from the default values

The period at the end of the command [startproject] creates the project in the current folder (without it, the project is created in a new folder named [config]). An application created by [startapp] must be added to the [INSTALLED_APPS] settings list. The [inspectdb] command is a valuable tool for an existing database, such as the one in the case study: it reads the tables and generates a first draft of the models using [managed = False]; all that remains is to name the relationships, choose the types, and add the methods. The commands [makemigrations] and [migrate], which create and update tables based on the models, were not used in this document: its databases are created by SQL scripts, which are shared with other versions of the application.

docs.title: 8. Authentication and Authorization
docs.text:
Two distinct questions arise for each request:

  • Who is the user? This is authentication: the user has identified themselves with a username and password, and each subsequent request must prove that it comes from them;
  • Do they have permission to access this page? This is authorization: in the case study, only a user with the role ADMIN manages doctors and clients.

Proof of identity must accompany every request. [Django] has a complete authentication application, [django.contrib.auth]: a [User] model (a database table), middleware that stores the logged-in user in [request.user], login and logout views, permissions, groups, and the administration interface that manages them. It stores the logged-in user in their session (see the chapter on scopes), which is the simplest solution for a web application. The case study, in all its versions ([ASP.NET Core MVC], [Spring MVC], [NestJS], [Flask], [Laravel], [Symfony]), instead uses a JWT token (JSON Web Token), which we will use here: After login, the server generates a token containing the user’s identity and signs it with a secret key (this is the principle behind the signed cookie in Example 23). The token is stored in a cookie; the browser sends it back with every request; the server verifies the signature. The user can read their token but cannot modify it: any modification invalidates the signature. The format is standardized (RFC 7519), understood by all programming languages, and the token includes its expiration date. Most importantly, the server doesn’t have to store anything: any server that knows the key can verify the token.

The users in the case study are those in their own table, [users], and not those in [django.contrib.auth]; the tokens themselves have no place in [django.contrib.auth]. So we’ll implement the authentication ourselves, using the tools we’re already familiar with, which has the advantage of making everything transparent:

  • a middleware component (Example 03) determines, for each request, who the user is based on the token in their cookie, and includes it in the request ([request.utilisateur], Example 12). The rest of the application sees only this result;
  • decorators (example 08) protect the views: [@connexion_requise], [@role_requis("ADMIN")];
  • passwords are verified using the hashing functions of [Django] ([django.contrib.auth.hashers], which can be used without the rest of the application [auth]);
  • access denials are [PermissionDenied] exceptions, converted into an error page by a [handler403] view (Example 24);
  • Login attempts are limited using the cache in [Django] (Example 27).

The creation and verification of tokens are handled by the [PyJWT] library, the most commonly used one in [Python], installed by the example file [requirements.txt] (it is imported under the name [jwt]). (There are JWT token libraries for [Django], such as [djangorestframework-simplejwt], designed for API; for a web application, just a few lines are enough, and they better illustrate the mechanism.)

docs.title: 8.1.1. Configuration: config/settings.py
docs.text:
The token is signed with a secret key, which must not be hardcoded in production application code. It’s time to truly separate the configuration from the code:

# config/settings.py: the configuration from Example 25

import os
from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-jr8u&rl2ff+bpg(h18&^u2dtu^qtulf9yoy!e&la+nt_z-vb*8"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "securite",
    "comptes",
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
     # the AUTHENTIFICATION: with each request, the user is identified based on the
     # token JWT in their cookie (see security/middleware.py)
    "securite.middleware.Authentification",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
    },
]

STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR.parent / "commun" / "static",
]

# our own settings: the key that signs the JWT tokens (at least 32 characters), and
# their lifetime. os.environ.get: the environment variable of the same name if it
# exists (in production); otherwise, the value listed here applies (in development)
JWT_SECRET = os.environ.get("JWT_SECRET", "une-cle-secrete-d-au-moins-32-caracteres-pour-l-exemple-25")
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES = int(os.environ.get("JWT_DUREE_MINUTES", "60"))
  • lines 21–26: two middleware components: anti-CSRF protection (Example 18), followed by our authentication middleware;
  • lines 43–44: two application-specific settings (Example 06): the key that signs the tokens, and their lifetime, in minutes. [os.environ.get("NOM", défaut)] sets the value of the environment variable to [NOM] if it exists; otherwise, it uses the default value. During development, the value written to the file is sufficient; in production, the actual key is provided via an environment variable, which takes precedence. An environment variable is always a string: [int] converts the duration to an integer.

The standard requires, for the algorithm used (HMAC-SHA256), a key of at least 256 bits, or 32 bytes: [PyJWT] issues a warning for a shorter key. With [Linux] or [macOS], the application would be launched with a different key as follows:

JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres" python manage.py runserver

and for [Windows] ([PowerShell]):

$env:JWT_SECRET="une-autre-cle-d-au-moins-trente-deux-caracteres"
python manage.py runserver

The secret key for [Django] itself, [SECRET_KEY], would require the same treatment; the case study reads all its secrets from a file named [.env], or from the environment.

docs.title: 8.1.2. Users: securite/utilisateurs.py
docs.text:
# security/utilisateurs.py: users, in memory (example 28 and the study of
# will be stored in a database)

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Utilisateur:
    login: str
    nom: str
     # role: USER or ADMIN
    role: str
     # the password (empty for a user read from a token)
    hachage_mot_de_passe: str = ""
     # the contents of the token that authenticated the user; field(default_factory=dict):
     # an empty dictionary for each object
    claims: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


# No password is stored; only its hash, calculated once for
# all by Django’s make_password function (PBKDF2-SHA256 algorithm, 1,500,000
# iterations, a random salt):
# python -c "from django.conf import settings; settings.configure();
#             from django.contrib.auth.hashers import make_password; print(make_password('marie'))"
UTILISATEURS = {
    "marie": ("Marie Pélissier", "USER",
              "pbkdf2_sha256$1500000$pjnFn2tL1G4bu5rVFTv6sZ$Y6v+fj3dC+Y0LZYJGxeE1OOi9beaZVuMVm6R6tljEwI="),
    "admin": ("Administrateur", "ADMIN",
              "pbkdf2_sha256$1500000$UTT2hXVaLIEAuGHPFxgnv9$D9+Owt9lDG14VrvArR3n0GGQXWjY9Sg8cgFwip4+yx4="),
}


def chercher(login: str) -> Utilisateur | None:
    if login not in UTILISATEURS:
        return None
     # "unpacking" a tuple: its three elements into three variables
    nom, role, hachage = UTILISATEURS[login]
    return Utilisateur(login, nom, role, hachage)
  • lines 7–17: a user: the login, the name, the role, the password hash, and the content of the token that authenticated the user (empty for a user read from the user list). The last two attributes have a default value. For a dictionary, this value cannot be written to [claims: dict = {}]: this dictionary would be created only once and shared by all objects. [field(default_factory=dict)] instructs [@dataclass] to call [dict()] for each new object;
  • Lines 20–24: A server never stores a password, even in encrypted form: if the database were stolen, the passwords would be stolen as well (and many people use the same password everywhere). It stores the result of a hash function, a one-way function: you can calculate the hash of a password, but you cannot recover a password from its hash. To verify an entered password, you calculate its hash and compare it to the one stored in the database;
  • lines 25–30: two test users, hard-coded into the program (Example 28 and the case study will populate a database with them): for each login, the name, role, and password hash. The hash was calculated once and for all by the function [make_password] from [Django] (the command is provided in a comment), using its default algorithm, PBKDF2-SHA256. The stored hash has four parts, separated by [$]: the algorithm ([pbkdf2_sha256]), the number of iterations, the salt, and then the result. A good password hashing algorithm has two characteristics. It is intentionally slow, with an adjustable level of slowness: PBKDF2 applies the function SHA-256 1,500,000 times, which takes a few hundred milliseconds—imperceptible to a user, but makes it very costly for a hacker to try billions of passwords; [Django] increases this number with each version to keep pace with computing power (its [auth] application then updates the hashes stored during logins); older hashes remain verifiable, since they include their iteration count. It is salted: a randomly generated salt is mixed with the password before hashing and stored within the hash itself; thus, two users with the same password will have different hashes. [Django] can also use [Argon2] and [bcrypt] (setting [PASSWORD_HASHERS]); the case study, whose database contains hashes [bcrypt], uses the library [bcrypt] directly;
  • lines 33–38: the user of a login, or [None]. [not in] checks for the absence of a key; the assignment [nom, role, hachage = ...] unpacks a tuple: each variable receives the corresponding element.

docs.title: 8.1.3. The authentication service: securite/auth.py
docs.text:
# security/auth.py: password verification and tokens JWT

import time

import jwt
from django.conf import settings
from django.contrib.auth.hashers import check_password

from . import utilisateurs
from .utilisateurs import Utilisateur

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
COOKIE = "jeton"


# the user, or None if the login is unknown or the password is incorrect.
# check_password hashes the entered password using the salt and the hashing algorithm
# stored, then compares the two results
def valider(login: str, mot_de_passe: str) -> Utilisateur | None:
    if not login or not mot_de_passe:
        return None
    utilisateur = utilisateurs.chercher(login)
    if utilisateur is None or not check_password(mot_de_passe, utilisateur.hachage_mot_de_passe):
        return None
    return utilisateur


# the user’s token (JWT), signed with the secret key (HMAC-SHA256)
def creer_jeton(utilisateur: Utilisateur) -> str:
    maintenant = int(time.time())
     # the token’s content: the “claims” (statements about the user)
    claims = {
        "sub": utilisateur.login,
        "nom": utilisateur.nom,
        "role": utilisateur.role,
        "iat": maintenant,
        "exp": maintenant + settings.JWT_DUREE_MINUTES * 60,
    }
    return jwt.encode(claims, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithm="HS256")


# the user described by a token whose signature and expiration date are
# valid; None otherwise (token is forged, expired, or unreadable)
def verifier(jeton: str) -> Utilisateur | None:
    try:
         # Decode verifies the signature ET and the expiration date (claim exp)
        claims = jwt.decode(jeton, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        return None
    return Utilisateur(claims["sub"], claims["nom"], claims["role"], claims=claims)
  • Line 5: the [PyJWT] library;
  • line 7: the function [check_password] from [Django];
  • line 13: the name of the cookie that carries the token;
  • lines 19–25: verification of a username and password. [check_password] reads the algorithm, the number of iterations, and the salt from the stored hash, hashes the entered password using them, and compares the two results (in constant time, e.g., 23). An unknown username and an incorrect password yield the same result, [None];
  • lines 29–39: token generation. Its content is a dictionary of claims about the user. Some have standardized names: [sub] (subject), the user’s identifier; [iat] (issued at), the creation date; [exp] (expiration), the expiration date. Dates are expressed in seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970 ([time.time()] returns this number, including decimals, which [int] omits). The other fields are optional: here, the name and role. [jwt.encode] generates the token and signs it using the algorithm [HS256] (HMAC-SHA256, a signature using a shared secret key);
  • lines 44–50: token verification. [jwt.decode] verifies the signature and expiration date, then returns the assertions. Any anomaly (forged, expired, or malformed token) raises an exception of class [jwt.InvalidTokenError] or one of its subclasses, which the [except] block intercepts. The parameter [algorithms] specifies the list of accepted algorithms: a token that declares a different algorithm (or none at all, [none]) would be rejected. The valid token becomes a [Utilisateur], without a hash, along with its claims (parameter named [claims]).

docs.title: 8.1.4. The authentication middleware: securite/middleware.py
docs.text:
# security/middleware.py: AUTHENTIFICATION: for each request, who is the user?

from django.shortcuts import redirect

from . import auth


class Authentification:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
         # By default, the visitor is anonymous
        request.utilisateur = None
        jeton = request.COOKIES.get(auth.COOKIE)
        if jeton is not None:
            utilisateur = auth.verifier(jeton)
            if utilisateur is None:
                 # an invalid token (expired, forged): redirect to /login, and then
                 # the cookie is deleted
                reponse = redirect("login")
                reponse.delete_cookie(auth.COOKIE)
                return reponse
            request.utilisateur = utilisateur
        return self.get_response(request)

For each request, before the view:

  • line 14: by default, the visitor is anonymous: [request.utilisateur] equals [None];
  • lines 15–17: if the request contains the token cookie, the token is verified;
  • lines 18–23: an invalid token (expired or forged): the middleware responds on its own, without invoking the rest of the process, by redirecting to the login page, and takes the opportunity to delete the cookie: [delete_cookie] adds an empty, already expired cookie to the response;
  • line 24: a valid token: the user it identifies is included in the request. The user is not looked up in the user list: the token is sufficient, since it is signed.

The middleware does not deny access: it determines who the user is, or determines that the user is anonymous. This is authentication. Denials are handled by access control.

docs.title: 8.1.5. Access control: securite/decorateurs.py
docs.text:
# security/decorateurs.py: view access control

from functools import wraps

from django.shortcuts import redirect


# @connexion_requise: the view is executed only for an authenticated user; an
# anonymous visitors are redirected to the login page
def connexion_requise(vue):
    @wraps(vue)
    def enveloppe(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if request.utilisateur is None:
            return redirect("login")
        return vue(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return enveloppe

The decorator [@connexion_requise] wraps a view (Example 08): if the user is anonymous, it responds by redirecting to the login page without calling the view; otherwise, it calls the view. [django.contrib.auth] provides a decorator with the same role, [@login_required], which is based on [request.user].

docs.title: 8.1.6. Views: accounts/views.py
docs.text:
# accounts/views.py: login, logout, and a page reserved for
#

from django.conf import settings
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods, require_POST

from securite import auth
from securite.decorateurs import connexion_requise


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return redirect("profil")


# GET: the form; POST: login (the anti-CSRF token was verified by
# CsrfViewMiddleware)
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def login(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        return render(request, "auth/login.html")
    login = request.POST.get("login", "")
    utilisateur = auth.valider(login, request.POST.get("mot_de_passe", ""))
    if utilisateur is None:
         # a deliberately vague message: it doesn’t specify whether it’s the username or the password
        return render(request, "auth/login.html",
                      {"login": login, "erreur": "Login ou mot de passe incorrect."})
     # the token, in a cookie: the page’s JavaScript cannot read it
     # (httponly); it does not accompany requests like POST coming from other sites
     # (samesite); it disappears when the token expires (max_age)
    reponse = redirect("profil")
    reponse.set_cookie(auth.COOKIE, auth.creer_jeton(utilisateur),
                       max_age=settings.JWT_DUREE_MINUTES * 60, httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# Logout: POST only (a simple link placed on another site cannot
# log the user out without their knowledge); the cookie is deleted
@require_POST
def logout(request):
    reponse = redirect("login")
    reponse.delete_cookie(auth.COOKIE)
    return reponse


# request.utilisateur: the authenticated user, identified by the middleware
@require_GET
@connexion_requise
def profil(request):
    return render(request, "profil/profil.html", {"utilisateur": request.utilisateur})
  • lines 19–22: The login form, hand-coded in the template, is protected against forged requests by the [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware, just like all POST forms (Example 18);
  • lines 23–28: the login process. If the login fails, the form is redisplayed with the entered username and a deliberately vague message: stating “unknown username” would reveal to a hacker which usernames exist;
  • lines 32–35: if successful, the token is stored in a cookie, and the user is redirected to the protected page (schema PRG). The cookie is [httponly]: the page’s [JavaScript] cannot read it, which protects the token against script injection (XSS); it is [SameSite=Lax]: the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site, which protects the application against CSRF attacks; its lifetime ([max_age], in seconds) is the same as that of the token. In production, for HTTPS, we would add [secure=True]: the cookie would never be sent over an unencrypted connection;
  • Lines 40–44: Logging out deletes the cookie ([delete_cookie]). This is a view of POST, protected by the anti-CSRF token: a simple link to [/logout], placed on another site or within an image, cannot log the user out without their knowledge. Note a limitation of tokens: the token itself remains valid until it expires. Someone who has made a copy of it could still use it. That is why their lifetime is limited;
  • Lines 48–51: The protected page. The decorator [@connexion_requise] ensures that [request.utilisateur] is not [None].

docs.title: 8.1.8. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s request the protected page [/profil] without being logged in:

curl -i http://localhost:8000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /login

An incorrect password:

Login successful. With [curl], you must first request the form to obtain the anti-CSRF token and its cookie (example 18), then submit the form while retaining the received cookie:

curl -c jeton.txt -b jeton.txt http://localhost:8000/login
curl -i -c jeton.txt -b jeton.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=...&login=marie&mot_de_passe=marie" http://localhost:8000/login

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /profil
Set-Cookie: jeton=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJtYXJpZSIsIm5vbSI6Ik1hcmllIFBcdTAwZTlsaXNzaWVyIiwicm9sZSI6IlVTRVIiLCJpYXQiOjE3OTA1MzA5MzksImV4cCI6MTc5MDUzNDUzOX0.Ui3suZbbc_T83_kehZinNIlKEoyPmnoywZpv3WymcwE; expires=Sun, 27 Sep 2026 18:42:19 GMT; HttpOnly; Max-Age=3600; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

The token consists of three parts, separated by periods, each encoded in Base64: the header, the content, and the signature. The first two parts can be decoded without any key:

{"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
{"sub":"marie","nom":"Marie Pélissier","role":"USER","iat":1790530939,"exp":1790534539}

(The [é] is written in its escaped form, JSON, [é].) The expiration time is one hour (3,600 seconds) after creation. In the browser, the profile page displays this same content:

A malicious user modifies their token: they replace the role ***[USER]*** with ***[ADMIN]*** in the content, re-encode this part in Base64, and keep the original signature. The server recalculates the signature of the modified content, which no longer matches:

curl -i -b "jeton=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.<contenu modifié>.Ui3suZbbc_T83_kehZinNIlKEoyPmnoywZpv3WymcwE" http://localhost:8000/profile

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /login
Set-Cookie: jeton=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/

The forged token is rejected and deleted (the empty value and expired date instruct the browser to delete the cookie). To generate a valid signature, one would need to know the secret key—hence the importance of keeping it secret and choosing a long, random key.

docs.title: 8.2.1. Roles: securite/utilisateurs.py
docs.text:
# security/utilisateurs.py: users, in memory (Example 28 and the study in
# will store them in a database)

from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Utilisateur:
    login: str
    nom: str
     # role: USER or ADMIN
    role: str
     # the password (empty for a user read from a token)
    hachage_mot_de_passe: str = ""
     # the contents of the token that authenticated the user; field(default_factory=dict):
     # an empty dictionary for each object
    claims: dict = field(default_factory=dict)

     # the HIÉRARCHIE for roles: an administrator also has the rights of a user
    def a_le_role(self, role: str) -> bool:
        return role in HIERARCHIE.get(self.role, set())

     # for templates, which cannot call a method with a parameter
    @property
    def est_admin(self) -> bool:
        return self.a_le_role("ADMIN")


# each role, and the set of roles it possesses ({...}: a set)
HIERARCHIE = {
    "ADMIN": {"ADMIN", "USER"},
    "USER": {"USER"},
}


# we do not store JAMAIS a password, only its hash, calculated once for
# all by Django’s make_password function (PBKDF2-SHA256 algorithm, 1,500,000
# iterations, a random salt):
# python -c "from django.conf import settings; settings.configure();
#             from django.contrib.auth.hashers import make_password; print(make_password('marie'))"
UTILISATEURS = {
    "marie": ("Marie Pélissier", "USER",
              "pbkdf2_sha256$1500000$pjnFn2tL1G4bu5rVFTv6sZ$Y6v+fj3dC+Y0LZYJGxeE1OOi9beaZVuMVm6R6tljEwI="),
    "admin": ("Administrateur", "ADMIN",
              "pbkdf2_sha256$1500000$UTT2hXVaLIEAuGHPFxgnv9$D9+Owt9lDG14VrvArR3n0GGQXWjY9Sg8cgFwip4+yx4="),
}


def chercher(login: str) -> Utilisateur | None:
    if login not in UTILISATEURS:
        return None
     # "unpacking" a tuple: its three elements into three variables
    nom, role, hachage = UTILISATEURS[login]
    return Utilisateur(login, nom, role, hachage)
  • lines 20–21: The [a_le_role] method determines whether the user has a role, based on the role hierarchy;
  • lines 24–26: a property (example 14), for templates: DTL cannot call a method with a parameter ([a_le_role("ADMIN")]), but it can read a property ([utilisateur.est_admin]);
  • lines 30–33: the role hierarchy: for each role, the set ([set], enclosed in curly braces) of roles it possesses. The role [ADMIN] includes the role [USER]: an administrator thus has all the rights of a user without needing to be assigned both roles. The method [a_le_role] can use [HIERARCHIE], even though it is defined further down in the file: the name is looked up only at the time of the call, once the entire module has been loaded.

docs.title: 8.2.2. Access control: securite/decorateurs.py
docs.text:
# security/decorateurs.py: view access control

from functools import wraps

from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.shortcuts import redirect


# @connexion_requise: the view is executed only for an authenticated user; an
# anonymous visitors are redirected to the login page
def connexion_requise(vue):
    @wraps(vue)
    def enveloppe(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if request.utilisateur is None:
            return redirect("login")
        return vue(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return enveloppe


# @role_requis("ADMIN"): a PARAMÉTRÉ decorator (see Example 08). The view is
# executed only if the authenticated user has the requested role; otherwise, the exception
# PermissionDenied returns a 403 response (see security/erreurs.py)
def role_requis(role):
    def decorateur(vue):
        @wraps(vue)
        @connexion_requise
        def enveloppe(request, *args, **kwargs):
            if not request.utilisateur.a_le_role(role):
                raise PermissionDenied(f"rôle {role} requis")
            return vue(request, *args, **kwargs)
        return enveloppe
    return decorateur
  • lines 23–32: a parameterized decorator (example 08), [@role_requis("ADMIN")]. The wrapper is itself wrapped by [@connexion_requise]: an anonymous visitor is first sent to the login page; an authenticated user who does not have the requested role triggers the [PermissionDenied] exception (example 24), which will result in a 403 (Forbidden) error.

The difference between the two denial scenarios is significant: an anonymous visitor requesting a protected page is redirected to the login page; an authenticated user who does not have the requested role receives a 403 error—logging in would serve no purpose, since they are already authenticated.

# security/erreurs.py: the response sent to a user AUTHENTIFIÉ who requests a
# page that is restricted to them (see handler403 in config/urls.py)

from django.shortcuts import render


def acces_refuse(request, exception):
    return render(request, "erreurs/403.html", status=403)

# config/urls.py: the main routing table

from django.urls import path

from comptes import views
from securite.erreurs import acces_refuse

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.accueil),
    path("login", views.login, name="login"),
    path("logout", views.logout, name="logout"),
    path("profil", views.profil, name="profil"),
    path("admin", views.admin, name="admin"),
]

# the 403 error view (exception PermissionDenied)
handler403 = acces_refuse

The view [acces_refuse] is the application’s 403 error view (variable [handler403], example 24) : [Django] calls it for any [PermissionDenied] exception, in both debug and production modes. The [templates/erreurs/403.html] page is a standard error page with a link back to the profile. Without this view, the user would see the plain 403 page from [Django] (“403 Forbidden”).

docs.title: 8.2.4. Views: accounts/views.py
docs.text:
# accounts/views.py: login, logout, and user-restricted pages
# Authenticated

from django.conf import settings
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods, require_POST

from securite import auth
from securite.decorateurs import connexion_requise, role_requis


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return redirect("profil")


# GET: the form; POST: login (the anti-CSRF token was verified by
# CsrfViewMiddleware)
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def login(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        return render(request, "auth/login.html")
    login = request.POST.get("login", "")
    utilisateur = auth.valider(login, request.POST.get("mot_de_passe", ""))
    if utilisateur is None:
         # a deliberately vague message: it doesn’t specify whether it’s the username or the password
        return render(request, "auth/login.html",
                      {"login": login, "erreur": "Login ou mot de passe incorrect."})
     # the token, stored in a cookie: the page’s JavaScript cannot read it
     # (httponly); it does not accompany requests like POST coming from other sites
     # (samesite); it disappears when the token expires (max_age)
    reponse = redirect("profil")
    reponse.set_cookie(auth.COOKIE, auth.creer_jeton(utilisateur),
                       max_age=settings.JWT_DUREE_MINUTES * 60, httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# logout: POST only (a simple link placed on another site cannot
# log the user out without their knowledge); the cookie is deleted
@require_POST
def logout(request):
    reponse = redirect("login")
    reponse.delete_cookie(auth.COOKIE)
    return reponse


# request.utilisateur: the authenticated user, identified by the middleware
@require_GET
@connexion_requise
def profil(request):
    return render(request, "profil/profil.html", {"utilisateur": request.utilisateur})


# a page reserved for the role ADMIN
@require_GET
@role_requis("ADMIN")
def admin(request):
    return render(request, "admin/admin.html", {"nom": request.utilisateur.nom})
  • Lines 55–58: the administration page, protected by the decorator [@role_requis("ADMIN")]. The view itself performs no checks.

For rules that are more granular than a role (“a user can only edit their own appointments”), the view performs the validation itself and raises [PermissionDenied] as needed. The case study provides examples of this.

docs.text:
Marie, with role USER, follows the link to the administration page:

The administrator, on the other hand, has access to it:

With [curl]: a user with role USER (logged in as in Example 25, with cookies stored in the file [jeton.txt]), followed by an anonymous visitor:

curl -i -b jeton.txt http://localhost:8000/admin
curl -i http://localhost:8000/admin

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
...
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Erreur 403</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">Accès refusé : cette page est réservée aux administrateurs.</p>
  </div>
...
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /login

Protecting views one by one has a flaw: if one is overlooked, the page becomes accessible to everyone. The case study will reverse this logic: all URL pages are protected by default through access control middleware, and only a few URL pages (the login page, the registration page) are exempt.

docs.title: 8.3. Example 27: CAPTCHA and Attempt Limits
docs.text:
A login form is a target: a program can try thousands of passwords per minute (brute-force attack). Two protective measures complement each other:

  • a CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart): an image containing a distorted code that is easy for a human to read but difficult for a program;
  • an attempt limit: after three failed attempts, the client’s address IP is blocked for one minute.

Example 27 is based on Example 25 and adds these two security measures:

27-captcha/
├── comptes/
│   └── views.py
├── config/
│   └── settings.py
├── securite/
│   ├── auth.py
│   ├── captchas.py
│   ├── decorateurs.py
│   ├── dessin_captcha.py
│   ├── limiteur.py
│   ├── middleware.py
│   └── utilisateurs.py
├── templates/
│   └── auth/
│       └── login.html
└── ...

docs.title: 8.3.1. The CAPTCHA image: securite/dessin_captcha.py
docs.text:
# security/dessin_captcha.py: a CAPTCHA image, SVG (text: XML)
# handcrafted

import math
import secrets

LARGEUR = 150
HAUTEUR = 50

# The "font": each character is a list of strokes, each stroke a sequence of
# x and y points in a 4 x 6 grid (y down).
# Characters that are too easily confused with one another: excluded (0 O, 1 I L).
POLICE = {
    "A": [[0, 6, 2, 0, 4, 6], [0.8, 3.8, 3.2, 3.8]],
    "B": [[0, 0, 0, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 0, 3], [0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3]],
    "C": [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5]],
    "D": [[0, 0, 0, 6, 2.5, 6, 4, 4.5, 4, 1.5, 2.5, 0, 0, 0]],
    "E": [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6, 4, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
    "F": [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 6], [0, 3, 3, 3]],
    "G": [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 3.5, 2.5, 3.5]],
    "H": [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 4, 6], [0, 3, 4, 3]],
    "J": [[4, 0, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
    "K": [[0, 0, 0, 6], [4, 0, 0, 3.5], [1.3, 2.6, 4, 6]],
    "M": [[0, 6, 0, 0, 2, 3.5, 4, 0, 4, 6]],
    "N": [[0, 6, 0, 0, 4, 6, 4, 0]],
    "P": [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3]],
    "Q": [[1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5, 0, 1, 1, 0], [2.5, 4.5, 4, 6.3]],
    "R": [[0, 6, 0, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 0, 3], [2, 3, 4, 6]],
    "S": [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
    "T": [[0, 0, 4, 0], [2, 0, 2, 6]],
    "U": [[0, 0, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 0]],
    "V": [[0, 0, 2, 6, 4, 0]],
    "W": [[0, 0, 1, 6, 2, 2.5, 3, 6, 4, 0]],
    "X": [[0, 0, 4, 6], [4, 0, 0, 6]],
    "Y": [[0, 0, 2, 3, 4, 0], [2, 3, 2, 6]],
    "Z": [[0, 0, 4, 0, 0, 6, 4, 6]],
    "2": [[0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 0, 6, 4, 6]],
    "3": [[0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 1.5, 3], [3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
    "4": [[3, 6, 3, 0, 0, 4, 4, 4]],
    "5": [[4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
    "6": [[4, 1, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5, 4, 4, 3, 3, 0, 3]],
    "7": [[0, 0, 4, 0, 1.5, 6]],
    "8": [[1, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 2, 3, 3, 1, 3, 0, 4, 0, 5, 1, 6, 3, 6, 4, 5,
           4, 4, 3, 3]],
    "9": [[4, 3, 1, 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 3, 0, 4, 1, 4, 5, 3, 6, 1, 6, 0, 5]],
}

# a few dark colors, clearly legible against the light background
COULEURS = ["#1f4e79", "#7b2d26", "#2e6b30", "#5b2c83", "#8a5a00", "#23395d", "#9c2a5b"]

# A "cryptographic" generator, unpredictable (unlike the random module,
# whose sequence could be guessed)
_hasard = secrets.SystemRandom()


def texte_aleatoire(longueur: int) -> str:
    alphabet = list(POLICE)
    return "".join(secrets.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(longueur))


# a random decimal number between minimum and maximum
def hasard(minimum: float, maximum: float) -> float:
    return _hasard.uniform(minimum, maximum)


def couleur() -> str:
    return secrets.choice(COULEURS)


def svg(texte: str) -> str:
    l, h = LARGEUR, HAUTEUR
    morceaux = [f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{l}" height="{h}" viewBox="0 0 {l} {h}">',
                 '<rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#f5f7fa"/>']
     # the characters: each enlarged, tilted, offset, and each dot slightly
     # randomly shifted
    pas = (l - 20) / len(texte)
    for i, caractere in enumerate(texte):
        echelle = hasard(4.6, 5.6)    # one grid unit in pixels
        angle = hasard(-0.35, 0.35)   # rotation, in radians (approximately ±20°)
        cx = 10 + pas * (i + 0.5) + hasard(-3, 3)    # center of the character
        cy = h / 2 + hasard(-4, 4)
        for trait in POLICE[caractere]:
            d = []
             # range(0, n, 2): 0, 2, 4... one point = two numbers
            for k in range(0, len(trait), 2):
                 # grid point, centered at (2, 3), distorted, rotated, positioned
                x = (trait[k] - 2 + hasard(-0.2, 0.2)) * echelle
                y = (trait[k + 1] - 3 + hasard(-0.2, 0.2)) * echelle
                px = cx + x * math.cos(angle) - y * math.sin(angle)
                py = cy + x * math.sin(angle) + y * math.cos(angle)
                d.append(f"{'M' if k == 0 else 'L'}{px:.1f} {py:.1f}")
            morceaux.append(f'<path d="{" ".join(d)}" fill="none" stroke="{couleur()}" '
                            f'stroke-width="{hasard(2.2, 3):.1f}" stroke-linecap="round" '
                            f'stroke-linejoin="round"/>')
     # 3 scrambling lines: curves that cross the image
    for _ in range(3):
        morceaux.append(f'<path d="M{hasard(0, 20):.1f} {hasard(5, 45):.1f} '
                        f'C{hasard(30, 60):.1f} {hasard(0, 50):.1f} {hasard(90, 120):.1f} '
                        f'{hasard(0, 50):.1f} {hasard(130, 150):.1f} {hasard(5, 45):.1f}" '
                        f'fill="none" stroke="{couleur()}" stroke-width="1.3"/>')
    morceaux.append("</svg>")
    return "".join(morceaux)

The image is in SVG format (Scalable Vector Graphics): a vector graphic described in XML—that is, text—which the server generates without a graphics library and which the browser displays directly on the page. This module is pure [Python], with nothing specific to [Django]: it is the [Python] implementation of the classes from the [Laravel] and [Symfony] versions of this course.

  • Lines 13–46: a minimalist “font”: each character is a list of strokes, and each stroke is a list of x and y coordinates in a 4 × 6 grid. Characters that are easily confused ([0] and [O], [1], [I], and [L]) are excluded;
  • lines 53–58: random text, drawn from the characters in the font ([list(POLICE)]: the list of dictionary keys). The [random] module of [Python] produces predictable number sequences (anyone who knows a few values can guess the next ones): it is suitable for simulations, not for security. The [secrets] module is a cryptographic generator that is unpredictable: [secrets.choice] draws an element from a list, and [secrets.SystemRandom] provides the functions of [random] ([uniform]: a floating-point number between two bounds) using this generator. [for _ in range(longueur)] repeats [longueur] times; the name [_] indicates a variable that is not used;
  • Lines 70–102: the drawing. Each character is enlarged, rotated, and moved at random, and each of its points is slightly offset; each stroke becomes an element [<path>] of SVG ([M]: displacement, [L]: line). Three curves ([C]: Bézier curve) cross the image to interfere with recognition programs. In an f-string, [{px:.1f}] writes a number with one decimal place; a conditional expression may be included ([{'M' if k == 0 else 'L'}]). The [math] module provides [cos] and [sin]. The parts of SVG are assembled by [join].

docs.title: 8.3.2. The CAPTCHA service: security/captchas.py
docs.text:
# security/captchas.py: pending CAPTCHAs, stored by the server in the cache

import secrets
from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.core.cache import cache

from . import dessin_captcha

# the lifespan of a CAPTCHA, in seconds
DUREE_VIE = 600


# a CAPTCHA: its ID and its image (SVG)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Captcha:
    id: str
    svg: str


def generer() -> Captcha:
    texte = dessin_captcha.texte_aleatoire(5)
     # a random identifier that is impossible to guess: 12 bytes generated by a
     # cryptographic generator, written in hexadecimal
    id = secrets.token_hex(12)
     # the expected response, cached for 10 minutes: the cache will then forget it
     # on its own afterward
    cache.set(f"captcha.{id}", texte, DUREE_VIE)
    return Captcha(id, dessin_captcha.svg(texte))


# the CAPTCHA is CONSOMMÉ in all cases: an image is used only once
def verifier(id: str, saisie: str) -> bool:
    if not id or not saisie:
        return False
     # `get` returns the value, or `None`; `delete` removes the response from the cache, whether it is
     # correct or not
    attendu = cache.get(f"captcha.{id}")
    cache.delete(f"captcha.{id}")
    if attendu is None:
        return False    # unknown ID, or expired captcha
     # casefold: the string in lowercase, for a case-insensitive comparison
    return attendu.casefold() == saisie.strip().casefold()
  • line 6: the cache for [Django]: a store of key→value pairs shared by all modules. Where it stores these values depends on the setting [CACHES] (see below);
  • Lines 21–29: a new CAPTCHA: a random text string, a random identifier that is impossible to guess ([secrets.token_hex(12)]: 12 random bytes, written in hexadecimal, or 24 characters), and the image. For each identifier, the server stores the expected response in the cache for ten minutes: the third parameter of [cache.set] is the lifetime, in seconds. After this time, the cache automatically discards it. The page receives only the identifier and the image: the response never leaves the server;
  • lines 33–43: the verification. The expected response is read ([cache.get] yields [None] for a missing key), then retrieved from the cache ([cache.delete]): The CAPTCHA is consumed in all cases, whether successful or not. Without this, a program could try every possible answer on the same image. The comparison ignores case ([casefold] converts a string to lowercase, correctly handling all alphabets) and spaces around the input ([strip]).

docs.title: 8.3.3. Attempt Limit: security/limiteur.py
docs.text:
# security/limiteur.py: the limit on login attempts per address IP

import time

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.cache import cache


# A client’s failed attempts are counted within a fixed time window: at most
# LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS failures per window of LOGIN_FENETRE_SECONDES seconds
class Limiteur:
    def __init__(self, ip: str):
        self.cle = f"login.{ip}"

     # seconds to wait if the client is blocked, 0 otherwise
    def attente(self) -> int:
        etat = cache.get(self.cle)
        if etat is None or etat["echecs"] < settings.LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS:
            return 0
        return max(1, int(etat["fin"] - time.time()))

     # one more failure
    def echec(self) -> None:
        etat = cache.get(self.cle)
        if etat is None:
             # a new window begins
            etat = {"echecs": 0, "fin": time.time() + settings.LOGIN_FENETRE_SECONDES}
        etat["echecs"] += 1
         # the key is removed from the cache at the end of the window (timeout, in seconds)
        cache.set(self.cle, etat, timeout=max(1, int(etat["fin"] - time.time())))

     # A successful connection clears the failures
    def effacer(self) -> None:
        cache.delete(self.cle)

The limiter counts a client’s failed attempts within a fixed time window: no more than three failed attempts per 60-second window, counted from the first failed attempt. Each client is identified by its address IP.

  • line 13: the cache key, specific to the client: [login.127.0.0.1];
  • lines 16–20: the number of seconds to wait if the client is blocked (the number of failures has reached the maximum), 0 otherwise. The state stored in the cache is a dictionary: the number of failures and the end time of the window;
  • lines 23–30: one more failure. If there is no state in the cache, a new window begins. The state is rewritten with a lifetime that expires at the end of the window: the cache will then automatically forget it, and the client will start over from scratch;
  • lines 33–34: a successful connection clears the failures.

This limiter, written for illustrative purposes, has a weakness: two simultaneous failures could read the same state and count it as only one. The cache in [Django] offers atomic operations ([cache.add], which writes only if the key does not exist, and [cache.incr], which increments a number), which are used in the case study version. Ready-made libraries are also available ([django-ratelimit], [django-axes]).

docs.title: 8.3.5. The view: accounts/views.py
docs.text:
# accounts/views.py: login (with CAPTCHA and limited attempts),
# logout, and a page reserved for authenticated users

from django.conf import settings
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods, require_POST

from securite import auth, captchas
from securite.decorateurs import connexion_requise
from securite.limiteur import Limiteur


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return redirect("profil")


# GET: the form; POST: login, with CAPTCHA and attempt limit
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def login(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        return page_login(request)
    login = request.POST.get("login", "")
     # the client limiter for CE: its failed attempts are counted under its address IP
    limiteur = Limiteur(request.META["REMOTE_ADDR"])
     # 1. A blocked address is not even listened to
    secondes = limiteur.attente()
    if secondes > 0:
        return page_login(request, login, f"Trop de tentatives : réessayez dans {secondes} s.")
     # 2. First the CAPTCHA (low-cost), then the password (PBKDF2, high-cost)
    if not captchas.verifier(request.POST.get("captcha_id", ""), request.POST.get("captcha", "")):
        limiteur.echec()
        return page_login(request, login, "Le code de l'image est incorrect.")
    utilisateur = auth.valider(login, request.POST.get("mot_de_passe", ""))
    if utilisateur is None:
        limiteur.echec()
        return page_login(request, login, "Login ou mot de passe incorrect.")
    limiteur.effacer()
    reponse = redirect("profil")
    reponse.set_cookie(auth.COOKIE, auth.creer_jeton(utilisateur),
                       max_age=settings.JWT_DUREE_MINUTES * 60, httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# Each time the form is displayed, a NOUVEAU CAPTCHA is generated
def page_login(request, login="", erreur=None):
    return render(request, "auth/login.html",
                  {"login": login, "erreur": erreur, "captcha": captchas.generer()})


# Logout: POST only (a simple link placed on another site cannot
# log the user out without their knowledge); the cookie is deleted
@require_POST
def logout(request):
    reponse = redirect("login")
    reponse.delete_cookie(auth.COOKIE)
    return reponse


# request.utilisateur: the authenticated user, identified by the middleware
@require_GET
@connexion_requise
def profil(request):
    return render(request, "profil/profil.html", {"utilisateur": request.utilisateur})
  • line 25: this client’s limiter, based on its address IP ([REMOTE_ADDR], example 05);
  • Lines 27–29: A blocked address is not even listened to;
  • lines 31–37: The CAPTCHA is verified before the password; verifying it costs almost nothing, whereas the hash PBKDF2 is intentionally slow. A program that gets the CAPTCHA wrong would therefore not put any load on the server. Every failure—whether for the CAPTCHA or the password—is counted. On the third failure, the address is blocked until the end of the 60-second window, counted from the first failure;
  • line 38: a successful login clears the failure count;
  • lines 46–48: each time the form is displayed, a new CAPTCHA is generated, even after a failure.

docs.title: 11.1. The Problem
docs.text:
The RdvMedecins application manages appointments for a medical practice. Each doctor has time slots (from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments, for example); an appointment consists of a day, a time slot, and a client (a patient). This is the exact port, in [Django], of the [Symfony] application from the previous lesson (which was itself ported from versions [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], and [ASP.NET Core MVC]): same database, same business rules, same pages, same URLs, same text. The HTML pages are generated by the server using templates from [Django]; access to the database is routed through ORM from [Django].

Three user roles share the application:

RoleWhoPermissionsADMINThe administrator ([admin])View schedules, make and cancel appointments for any patient; manage (list, add, edit, delete) doctors and clientsDOCTORDoctorsView schedules, make appointments, and cancel appointments for any patientUSERclients (patients)view schedules without seeing other patients’ names; book an appointment for themselves; cancel their appointment; manage their account; create an account

Key management rules:

  • No appointments in the past;
  • A time slot is reserved only once a day;
  • a patient has only one upcoming appointment at a time;
  • two doctors (or two clients) cannot have the same first and last names, and a login belongs to only one account;
  • A doctor with appointments cannot be deleted; A client is deleted along with their appointments;
  • the login page is protected against bots (CAPTCHA, limited attempts), and creating a client account requires first solving the CAPTCHA on that page.

After the booking, a message confirms the appointment:

docs.text:
A patient (role USER) arrives at “My Account”: their upcoming appointment, which they can cancel, and links to manage their account and view their calendar. Here, they do not yet have an appointment:

In the calendar, they do not see the names of other patients; these are replaced by “Reserved”: this name does not even appear in the page’s source code. They can book an available time slot:

His dashboard now shows his upcoming appointment, which he can cancel:

docs.title: 11.3. Installation and Execution
docs.text: The application is located in the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder, next to the [exemples] folder. It is a standalone project, with its own [requirements.txt] and [.env] files, and its own virtual environment. The [README.md] file in the folder contains all of the following. The introduction to this document has already described the installation; we’ll provide additional details here.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Required Software
docs.text:
Two software packages are sufficient:

  • [Python] 3.12 or later ([Django] 6.1 requires [Python] 3.12). Verify the installation in a terminal:
python --version
  • Under [Linux] and [macOS], the command is often referred to as [python3]. Under [Linux], compiling [mysqlclient] also requires a few system packages (see appendices);
  • a [MySQL] server version 8.4 or later, such as the one from [Laragon] running under [Windows] (see appendices). [MariaDB] 10.11 or later is also suitable. These are the minimum versions of [Django] 6.1: with [MySQL] 8.0, [Django] refuses to connect ([MySQL 8.4 or later is required]).

The recommended editor is [Visual Studio Code], along with the extensions [Python] and [Django] (see appendices); however, everything can be done via the command line.

docs.title: 11.3.2. Install the libraries
docs.text:
The libraries are not provided: create a virtual environment once and for all in the application folder, and install the libraries there in a terminal opened to the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder (you must be connected to the Internet):

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

(under [Linux] and [macOS], the second command is written as [source .venv/bin/activate]). [pip] reads the file [requirements.txt] (discussed below), downloads [Django], [mysqlclient], [PyJWT], [bcrypt], and the libraries they depend on, and installs them in the [.venv] folder. The environment must be activated in each new terminal ([Visual Studio Code] does this automatically once the environment interpreter has been selected; see the introduction).

docs.title: 11.3.3. Create the database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database is created by the [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu (see introduction). At the command line, in the application folder:

mysql -u root -p < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql

The [-p] option prompts for the [root] password; omit it if the account does not have one (as is the case with [Laragon]). This is the same database as in other versions of the application: if it already exists, this step is optional. The script can be run at any time to revert to the original data.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Configure Database Access
docs.text: All installation configuration is contained in the file [.env] (discussed further below). By default, the application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password: these are the default settings for [Laragon]. If your [root] account has a password, enter it in this file on the [DB_PASSWORD=] line. A system environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25): this allows you to specify the password without writing it to a project file.

docs.title: 11.3.5. Run the application
docs.text:
In a terminal window open to the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder, with the virtual environment activated:

python manage.py runserver 8081

Watching for file changes with StatReloader
Performing system checks...

System check identified no issues (0 silenced).
September 27, 2026 - 19:30:12
Django version 6.1.1, using settings 'config.settings'
Starting WSGI development server at http://127.0.0.1:8081/
Quit the server with CONTROL-C.

Next, open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser, and stop the application using [Ctrl-C]. Port 8081 allows you to run a course example (port 8000) at the same time; other versions of the application also use port 8081: do not run them simultaneously.

docs.title: 11.3.6. Demo Accounts
docs.text:
The password for each account is its username; you must also enter the characters shown in the image, in uppercase or lowercase:

UsernameRole[admin]ADMIN (the administrator)[pelissier], [tatou], [dupont]DOCTOR (the doctors)[martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german]USER (patients)

A guide to exploring the app:

  • [admin]: Calendar, Ms. Marie PELISSIER, today: a time slot is already booked by Ms. Brigitte BISTROU. Book a slot for Mr. Jean MARTIN, then try to book a second appointment for him (declined). Doctors and Clients menus: add, edit, delete (Dr. PELISSIER, who has appointments, cannot be deleted);
  • [pelissier]: his daily schedule is displayed directly; the address [/medecins], entered manually, returns a 403 error page;
  • [martin]: My Account, their appointment, the calendar where other patients appear as “Reserved” (view the page’s source code: their names do not appear there); Manage My Account;
  • Login page: Create a customer account, then log in with the new account;
  • buttons FR / EN: the entire interface changes languages, including dates.

docs.title: 11.3.7. Development Mode
docs.text:
The provided [.env] file configures the application for development ([DJANGO_DEBUG=1]):

  • the server console displays every request and every SQL command sent to the database (Example 28). For example, to display a calendar (after the two commands to open the connection, Example 28; lines abbreviated):
(0.000) SELECT `medecins`.`id`, ..., `users`.`role` FROM `medecins` INNER JOIN `users` ON (`medecins`.`user` = `users`.`id`) WHERE `medecins`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `medecins`.`id` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.003) SELECT `rv`.`id`, ..., `clients`.`user` FROM `rv` INNER JOIN `creneaux` ON (`rv`.`id_creneau` = `creneaux`.`id`) INNER JOIN `clients` ON (`rv`.`id_client` = `clients`.`id`) WHERE (`creneaux`.`id_medecin` = 1 AND `rv`.`jour` = '2026-09-28'); args=(1, '2026-09-28'); alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `creneaux`.`id`, ..., `creneaux`.`mfin` FROM `creneaux` WHERE `creneaux`.`id_medecin` = 1 ORDER BY `creneaux`.`hdebut` ASC, `creneaux`.`mdebut` ASC; args=(1,); alias=default
[27/Sep/2026 19:50:21] "GET /agenda?idMedecin=1&jour=2026-09-28 HTTP/1.1" 200 9377

Three requests can be identified here: the doctor and their account (a join), today’s appointments and their patients, and the doctor’s available time slots. The list of doctors in the drop-down menu, however, is not retrieved; it comes from the cache (see below). The logged-in user is not retrieved either; they are identified by their token (Example 25);

  • an unexpected exception displays the [Django] debug page (example 03), along with the exception message and the call stack. In production, the application displays its own 500 error page instead;
  • there is nothing to restart after a change: the development server restarts automatically when a [Python] file changes (example 01), and a modified template is re-read on the next request.

The debugger for the [Python] extension of [Visual Studio Code] also allows you to step through the application: all you need is a “Django”-style launch configuration (file [.vscode/launch.json], which the extension offers to create), with the parameters [runserver 8081 --noreload]. The [django-debug-toolbar] extension (to be installed via [pip]) displays, next to each page, the details of the request: the SQL commands and their durations, the templates used, the settings, the signals...

docs.title: 11.3.8. A production server
docs.text:
The [Django] development server is not intended for production. In production, the application is served by a WSGI server (example 01): [gunicorn] under [Linux] ([gunicorn config.wsgi:application --workers 4]), [waitress] under [Windows] ([waitress-serve --port=8081 config.wsgi:application]), typically behind a web server ([nginx], [Apache]) that receives connections from HTTPS, serves the static files itself, and delegates the rest to the WSGI server. In the [.env] file, you must specify production mode, change the secret keys, declare the site name, and specify that the site is served by HTTPS:

DJANGO_DEBUG=0
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=une-longue-chaîne-aléatoire
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=rdvmedecins.exemple.fr
JWT_SECRET=une-autre-longue-chaîne-aléatoire
COOKIE_SECURE=1

A suitable random string can be obtained using [Python] itself: [python -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))"]. The application is then prepared using two commands:

python manage.py collectstatic
python manage.py check --deploy

The first command copies all static files (those from the application and those from [Django]) to the [var/static] folder (setting [STATIC_ROOT]), which the web server will serve (Example 15). The second script checks the security settings of a deployment and flags any missing ones (the HSTS headers, the redirect to HTTPS, etc.). To test production mode with the development server, which no longer serves static files: [python manage.py runserver 8081 --insecure].

docs.title: 11.3.9. Common Issues
docs.text:
With [MySQL], the [runserver] command connects to the database as soon as it starts up: its project checks (system checks, example 01) require knowledge of the server version. An inaccessible database therefore prevents it from starting: the console displays a long call stack, which ends with the error. For example, with a database that does not exist:

django.db.utils.OperationalError: (1049, "Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'")

A production server ([gunicorn]...) does not perform these checks: the error then appears in the log on the first page that queries the database (the login page does not query the database; the login process itself does). The most common messages:

MessageCause[ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django']The virtual environment is not enabled, or [pip install -r requirements.txt] has not been executed[Django 6.1 requires Python 3.12 or later] (during installation)The version of [Python] is earlier than 3.12[OperationalError: (2002, "Can't connect to server on '127.0.0.1' ...")][MySQL] has not been started, or is not listening on [127.0.0.1:3306][OperationalError: (1045, "Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' ...")]The password for [MySQL] must be entered in [DB_PASSWORD] (see “Configuring Database Access”)[OperationalError: (1049, "Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'")]The script [database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] was not executed[NotSupportedError: MySQL 8.4 or later is required]The [MySQL] server is too old: upgrade to [MySQL] 8.4 or [MariaDB] 10.11[ImproperlyConfigured: JWT_SECRET doit comporter au moins 32 caractères (cf. .env).]The token secret key is too short in [.env][Error: That port is already in use.]Port 8081 is already in use (is another version of the application running?): stop it, or choose a different port

docs.title: 11.4. Application Architecture
docs.text:
• The browser sends its requests to the server ([runserver], or [nginx] + [gunicorn]), which forwards them to [Django] via the WSGI application in the [config/wsgi.py] file. The request passes through the middleware layers (see the chapter on the lifecycle): the request language ([FixerLangue]), anti-CSRF protection, flash messages, and then authentication: the user is identified based on the JWT token in their cookie ([Authentification]); after routing, [ControleAcces] denies access to protected pages for visitors who are not authorized. Errors are handled by pages HTML ([PageErreur], and the error views);
  • [web]: the web layer. Views ([web/vues]), a family of pages per module, and their routes ([web/urls.py]); forms and their constraints ([web/formulaires.py]); the template models ([web/modeles_vues.py]). They all pass through a single object, [ApplicationModel] ([web/application.py]), which caches the lists of doctors and clients and forwards other requests to the business layer;
  • [securite]: JWT tokens, authentication and access control middleware, CAPTCHA, attempt limits, and account creation pass;
  • [metier]: business rules and transactions; [domaine]: calendar objects, calculated by the business layer;
  • [dao]: the DAO layer, one module per table (or family of tables);
  • [modeles]: the templates from ORM (Example 28), which the DAO layer reads from and writes to the database;
  • [templates]: the templates, which generate the HTML pages; [locale]: the English dictionary; [static]: the style sheet, the page script, and [Bootstrap];
  • The [config] folder and the [.env] file: the configuration that brings it all together.

The application folder (excluding [.venv] and [var]):
