Only two of these are [Django] applications, declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]: [modeles], because it contains templates from ORM (which [Django] searches for only in applications), and [web], because it contains a tag library ([templatetags], example 16). The others ([dao], [metier], [securite], [domaine]) are simply [Python] packages that the others import: they have nothing to report to [Django]. [Django] does not enforce any of these folders, and a typical project would instead have one application per domain (calendars, accounts, etc.), each with its own models, views, and templates; we preferred, as in the other versions of the case study, a layer-based organization, as shown in Example 28. [Bootstrap] is part of the application this time (folder [static/lib/bootstrap]): the case study is self-contained.

docs.title: 11.5. The Database
docs.text:
The [dbrdvmedecins2] database has five tables:

  • [users]: users authorized to log in;
  • [medecins] and [clients]: doctors and patients, each linked to their user account;
  • [creneaux]: each doctor’s available time slots;
  • [rv]: appointments, one client per time slot on a given day.

docs.title: 11.5.1. database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
docs.text:
-- =========================================================================
-- Database [dbrdvmedecins2] - MySQL 8
--
-- Changes to [dbrdvmedecins]:
--    1. The tables [medecins] and [clients] are added with a column named [user],
--       foreign key to users(id): each doctor and each client is
--       now also a user capable of logging in;
--    2. A third role appears: DOCTOR (in addition to ADMIN and USER);
--    3. The script creates a row [users] for each doctor (role DOCTOR)
--       and for each client (role USER):
--         -        login = name in lowercase
--         - password = name in lowercase, hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds)
--         - displ ay name = first name + last name
--
--    4. uniqueness constraints, all NOMMÉES (the application recognizes
--       the name of the violated constraint in the error message MySQL):
--         - unq_users         _login : a login belongs to only one account;
--         - unq_medecins_pren om_nom : Two doctors cannot have the
--                                      same first and last names;
--         - unq_clients_pren  om_nom : the same applies to clients.
--       Note: The utf8mb4_unicode_ci collation compares without taking into account
--       capital letters or accents—"Hélène DUPONT" and "helene dupont"
--       are therefore considered identical.
--
-- The table [users] must now be created AVANT [medecins] and [clients]
-- (they reference it), and delete APRÈS them.
-- =========================================================================

-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- we start with an empty database each time the script runs (useful during development)
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS dbrdvmedecins2 CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbrdvmedecins2;

-- Deletion order: from “child” tables to “parent” tables
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS rv;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS creneaux;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS clients;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS medecins;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS users;

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [users]: users authorized to log in to the application
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE users (
  id       INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version  INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  login    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,                 -- login ID
  password VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,                -- HACHÉ password (bcrypt) — never stored in plain text
  nom      VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,                 -- display name after login
  role     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,                 -- 'ADMIN', 'DOCTOR', or 'USER'
   -- A login can belong to only one account
  CONSTRAINT unq_users_login UNIQUE (login)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [medecins]: the practice’s doctors
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE medecins (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,      -- primary key (technical identifier)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,               -- row version number (optimistic lock)
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,                 -- Ms., Mrs., Mr.
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- Foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_medecins_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- one account per doctor, and one doctor per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- No two doctors can have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_medecins_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [clients]: doctors' patients
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE clients (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  titre   VARCHAR(5)  NOT NULL,
  nom     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  prenom  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
  `user`  INT NOT NULL,                         -- foreign key -> users(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_clients_user FOREIGN KEY (`user`) REFERENCES users(id),
   -- One account per customer, and one customer per account
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_user UNIQUE (`user`),
   -- Two clients cannot have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_clients_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [creneaux]: each doctor’s appointment slots
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE creneaux (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  id_medecin INT NOT NULL,                      -- foreign key -> doctors(id)
  hdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start time of the time slot
  mdebut     INT NOT NULL,                       -- start minute of the time slot
  hfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- slot end hour
  mfin       INT NOT NULL,                       -- end minute of the time slot
  CONSTRAINT fk_creneaux_medecin FOREIGN KEY (id_medecin) REFERENCES medecins(id)
);

-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- table [rv]: appointments made by customers
-- -------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TABLE rv (
  id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  version    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  jour       DATE NOT NULL,                      -- appointment date
  id_creneau INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> time slots (id)
  id_client  INT NOT NULL,                        -- foreign key -> customers(id)
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_creneau FOREIGN KEY (id_creneau) REFERENCES creneaux(id),
  CONSTRAINT fk_rv_client  FOREIGN KEY (id_client)  REFERENCES clients(id),
   -- The same time slot on the same day can only be booked once
  CONSTRAINT unq1_rv UNIQUE (jour, id_creneau)
);

-- =========================================================================
-- Demo data
-- =========================================================================

-- Users: Passwords hashed with bcrypt (10 rounds of salting)
--    admin/admin (ADMIN)
--    one DOCTOR account per doctor, one USER account per client
--    (the demo account user/user has been removed: a USER account is
--    now TOUJOURS, which belongs to a client who can make reservations and manage their account)
--    (login = password = name in lowercase)
INSERT INTO users (login, password, nom, role) VALUES
  ('admin',     '$2b$10$YSNBJXXHX9mp13nPZb6YGu8M1jR6uvPwO1s2X73z0QAqBR7TOQjoq', 'Administrateur',   'ADMIN'),
   -- doctors
  ('pelissier', '$2b$10$DnSDOK5ONrdMxTTr1NKCHOphR3WSp5QAyG9S9ueruw9HwlxI.16ba', 'Marie PELISSIER',  'DOCTOR'),
  ('tatou',     '$2b$10$PeovBO.gmJUKP4PglI/fwu4xtWOYSxoM5VTWjTj7uQ4wcd9P9.htS', 'Paul TATOU',       'DOCTOR'),
  ('dupont',    '$2b$10$az7wvPKC1h0EiAxXwu/PU.vYjzmB04rd5B7QnK0mvxp4niYIHVoc.', 'Sophie DUPONT',    'DOCTOR'),
   -- clients
  ('martin',    '$2b$10$GT6S5pp.WdGapFw/UmocXesbC6LEjJfZzgatCUyG9Sf4o1iBNlqZW', 'Jean MARTIN',      'USER'),
  ('durand',    '$2b$10$l2gl/zCder8E7Nh4VxGRX.0.SsO3FDiXt6YwqYq3v9nFzgC/jQCy6', 'Alice DURAND',     'USER'),
  ('bistrou',   '$2b$10$naeRp2YUU6c.QDl5itJMAum3Y5aHdUV6jwIcsbp0D.64jPG4F6E9m', 'Brigitte BISTROU', 'USER'),
  ('german',    '$2b$10$tTWxh3ROWF7NjhZOMnWDMOsZcnSWUiwwfy5C3G0.xhccTXALKyLeW', 'Luc GERMAN',       'USER');

-- doctors: the column [user] is retrieved based on the login,
-- rather than assuming the values of the primary keys from [users]
INSERT INTO medecins (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mme',  'PELISSIER', 'Marie',  (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'pelissier')),
  ('Mr',   'TATOU',     'Paul',   (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'tatou')),
  ('Melle','DUPONT',    'Sophie', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'dupont'));

INSERT INTO clients (titre, nom, prenom, `user`) VALUES
  ('Mr',   'MARTIN',  'Jean',     (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'martin')),
  ('Mme',  'DURAND',  'Alice',    (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'durand')),
  ('Melle','BISTROU', 'Brigitte', (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'bistrou')),
  ('Mr',   'GERMAN',  'Luc',      (SELECT id FROM users WHERE login = 'german'));

-- Dr. PELISSIER’s time slots (id_medecin = 1): from 8:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (1, 8, 0, 8, 20), (1, 8, 20, 8, 40), (1, 8, 40, 9, 0),
  (1, 9, 0, 9, 20), (1, 9, 20, 9, 40), (1, 9, 40, 10, 0),
  (1, 10, 0, 10, 20), (1, 10, 20, 10, 40), (1, 10, 40, 11, 0),
  (1, 11, 0, 11, 20), (1, 11, 20, 11, 40), (1, 11, 40, 12, 0);

-- Dr. TATOU’s time slots (id_medecin = 2): 2:00 PM to 6:00 PM in 20-minute increments
INSERT INTO creneaux (id_medecin, hdebut, mdebut, hfin, mfin) VALUES
  (2, 14, 0, 14, 20), (2, 14, 20, 14, 40), (2, 14, 40, 15, 0),
  (2, 15, 0, 15, 20), (2, 15, 20, 15, 40), (2, 15, 40, 16, 0),
  (2, 16, 0, 16, 20), (2, 16, 20, 16, 40), (2, 16, 40, 17, 0),
  (2, 17, 0, 17, 20), (2, 17, 20, 17, 40), (2, 17, 40, 18, 0);

-- an appointment already scheduled, to immediately see a slot that is occupied in the calendar
INSERT INTO rv (jour, id_creneau, id_client) VALUES
  (CURDATE(), 2, 3);
  • line 33: the database is created if it does not exist, with the character set [utf8mb4] and the collation [utf8mb4_unicode_ci], which compares strings without regard to uppercase letters or accents (example 28);
  • lines 37–41: The tables are dropped and then recreated; the script restores the database to its initial state. The order matters: a table cannot be dropped as long as another table references it via a foreign key;
  • lines 46–55: users: a login, a password hashed by [bcrypt] (example 25), the display name once logged in, and the role ([ADMIN], [DOCTOR], or [USER]). The constraint [unq_users_login] ensures that a username belongs to only one account;
  • Lines 60–72: Each table has a primary key [id], generated by the database, and a column [version], which is the optimistic lock (Example 28). The column [user] is a foreign key to [users(id)]: the database rejects any value that is not the ID of an existing user. Since [user] is a word in the SQL language, it is surrounded by grave accents. Three constraints: [fk_medecins_user] (the foreign key), [unq_medecins_user] (one account per doctor, and one doctor per account), and [unq_medecins_prenom_nom] (no homonyms). All constraints are named: the application recognizes a violated constraint by its name;
  • lines 77–89: the customer table has exactly the same columns;
  • lines 94–103: a time slot belongs to a doctor; its start and end times are stored in hours and minutes;
  • lines 108–118: an appointment consists of a day (type [DATE], without a time), a time slot, and a client. The constraint [unq1_rv] prevents the same time slot from being booked twice on the same day: the database enforces this rule, even if two users attempt to book it at the same time;
  • Lines 130–140: Demo users, whose password is their login. The hashes begin with [$2b$10$]: the algorithm ([bcrypt], variant [2b]) and the cost (10: 2^10 computation rounds). Next come the salt (22 characters) and the hash. These hashes were calculated by the [Flask] version of the application, using the [bcrypt] library from [Python], which is also used by this version;
  • lines 144–147: the [user] column for each doctor is retrieved via a subquery based on the login, rather than by assuming the values of the primary keys;
  • lines 170–171: an appointment already scheduled for today ([CURDATE()]) in Dr. PELISSIER’s second time slot for Ms. BISTROU: the calendar thus immediately shows that the time slot is booked.

Unlike in the case of [Django], the database is not created by the migrations for [Django] (Example 28): it is shared with the other versions of the application, and the script SQL is common to all of them. The templates are therefore declared as [managed = False], and the [python manage.py makemigrations] command has no action to perform. The [python manage.py inspectdb] command is used to compare the database to the templates.

docs.title: 11.6.1. requirements.txt
docs.text:
# the application's libraries: pip install -r requirements.txt
Django==6.1.1
mysqlclient==2.3.0
PyJWT==2.15.0
bcrypt==5.0.0

The four libraries required by the application, with their exact versions (see introduction): [Django], the driver [MySQL] ([mysqlclient], Example 28), the tokens JWT ([PyJWT], Example 25), and [bcrypt], for the database passwords (see below). [pip] also installs the libraries on which they depend ([asgiref] and [sqlparse], for [Django]). The command [pip freeze] outputs the exact list of what is installed in the environment, including dependencies: this is the way to obtain a file that locks in all versions. A larger project would use a project management tool, such as [uv] or [Poetry], which separates the requested libraries (file [pyproject.toml]) from the exact versions installed (a lock file, such as [composer.lock] for [PHP]).

docs.title: 11.6.2. .env
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# .env: settings specific to the CETTE installation, read at startup by
# config/settings.py. Each line NOM=value becomes a
# process environment variable; a true system environment variable
# takes precedence over this file.
# =========================================================================

# 1: development (detailed error pages); 0: production (see README.md)
DJANGO_DEBUG=1
# Django’s secret key (signatures, anti-CSRF tokens, etc.). In production: a
# another value, long and random
DJANGO_SECRET_KEY=Hayf1oPBd4cm9qXHUGusMtUqCFqEyyj1nnwGxKvuJKYI0EDjjn
# the hostnames that the application is configured to serve (separated by commas)
DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS=localhost,127.0.0.1

# ---- the database MySQL [dbrdvmedecins2] (script: database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql): the
# server, its port, the database, the username, and its password (Laragon’s:
# root, no password)
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=3306
DB_NAME=dbrdvmedecins2
DB_USER=root
DB_PASSWORD=

# ---- authentication (see security/auth.py)
# secret key for JWT tokens: at least 32 characters (HMAC-SHA256)
JWT_SECRET=229b83fd9cc502aaebd911d2662753a8393b340edb296724
# token validity period, in minutes (120 min = 2 h)
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES=120
# 1 in production (site served as HTTPS): cookies are never transmitted in plain text
COOKIE_SECURE=0

# ---- protection against bots (see security/limiteur.py)
# allowed login failures for the same login from the same address IP, then
# blocked for this duration (in minutes); an address IP is also blocked if it
# accumulates LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP failed attempts across all logins (a bot attempting
# thousands of different logins)
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS=5
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP=25
LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES=15
# customer accounts created per hour and per IP address. In the classroom, all
# workstations often connect via the same IP address: increase this limit if necessary
INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE=10

The file containing settings specific to this installation (example 25): these vary from one machine to another (the database, its credentials) or are secrets (the keys). In a real-world project, this file is never released with the code: each installation has its own, and production secrets are often provided via actual environment variables. [Django] does not read a [.env] file on its own: the [config/settings.py] file reads it (as described later). The [python-dotenv] library would do the same, and [django-environ] would add value conversion to it.

  • Line 9: debug mode (example 01): 1 during development (detailed error pages, SQL commands in the console), 0 in production;
  • line 12: the secret key for [Django], which is used for anti-CSRF tokens (example 18) and all signatures (signed cookies, flash messages, examples 20 and 23);
  • line 14: accepted hostnames (example 01);
  • lines 19–23: the database connection (example 28);
  • lines 25–43: application-specific settings: the JWT tokens (example 25), setting cookies to [Secure] mode (discussed later), and protection against bots (example 27).

docs.title: 11.6.3. config/settings.py
docs.text:
The settings file contains the entire configuration, written in [Python] (example 01):

# =========================================================================
# config/settings.py: the configuration of the RdvMedecins application.
#
# Installation-specific settings (passwords, secret keys, thresholds)
# are read from environment variables, which the .env file provides during
# the development environment (see lire_env). Everything else is written here.
# =========================================================================

import os
from pathlib import Path

# the project folder (the one containing manage.py)
BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# reads the .env file: each line NOM=value becomes a variable
# environment variable, SAUF if it already exists (setdefault): a true
# system environment variables take precedence over the file. Empty lines and
# comments (#) are ignored; quotation marks around the value are removed
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def lire_env(fichier: Path) -> None:
    if not fichier.exists():
        return
    for ligne in fichier.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        ligne = ligne.strip()
        if ligne and not ligne.startswith("#") and "=" in ligne:
            nom, valeur = ligne.split("=", 1)
            os.environ.setdefault(nom.strip(), valeur.strip().strip('"'))


lire_env(BASE_DIR / ".env")


# an environment variable: text, an integer, a boolean (1/0)
def env(nom: str, defaut: str = "") -> str:
    return os.environ.get(nom, defaut)


def env_int(nom: str, defaut: int) -> int:
    return int(env(nom, str(defaut)))


def env_bool(nom: str, defaut: bool) -> bool:
    return env(nom, "1" if defaut else "0") == "1"


# ---- debug mode and security
DEBUG = env_bool("DJANGO_DEBUG", False)
SECRET_KEY = env("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY")
ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h.strip() for h in env("DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS", "localhost").split(",")]

# ---- applications: Django itself (static files, flash messages,
# forms), and our two applications: models (the tables) and web (the
# template tags). The other folders (dao, business, security...) contain
# simple Python packages: they have neither models nor templates
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "django.contrib.messages",
    "django.forms",
    "modeles",
    "web",
]

# ---- the middleware components, in order (see Example 24):
#    - FixerLangue: the request language (cookie rdvmedecins_langue);
#    - CsrfViewMiddleware: the anti-CSRF token for any request POST;
#    - MessageMiddleware: flash messages;
#    - Authentication: the user, based on the token JWT in their cookie;
#    - ControleAcces: the access rule for each URL (after routing);
#    - PageErreur: errors are converted into application pages
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "web.middleware.FixerLangue",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
    "securite.middleware.Authentification",
    "securite.middleware.ControleAcces",
    "web.middleware.PageErreur",
]

ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

# ---- the database: MySQL (or MariaDB), the dbrdvmedecins2 database
DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.mysql",
        "HOST": env("DB_HOST", "127.0.0.1"),
        "PORT": env("DB_PORT", "3306"),
        "NAME": env("DB_NAME", "dbrdvmedecins2"),
        "USER": env("DB_USER", "root"),
        "PASSWORD": env("DB_PASSWORD"),
        "OPTIONS": {"charset": "utf8mb4"},
    },
}

# ---- CACHE: files in the var/cache folder, PARTAGÉS by all
# server processes (captchas, failure counters, passes, lists of
# doctors and clients). An in-memory cache (LocMemCache) is specific to
# each process: a production server launches several
CACHES = {
    "default": {
        "BACKEND": "django.core.cache.backends.filebased.FileBasedCache",
        "LOCATION": BASE_DIR / "var" / "cache",
    },
}

# ---- the templates (templates folder) and their context processors
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "APP_DIRS": True,
        "OPTIONS": {
            "context_processors": [
                "django.template.context_processors.request",
                "django.template.context_processors.i18n",
                "django.contrib.messages.context_processors.messages",
                 # the logged-in user, in all templates (see web/contextes.py)
                "web.contextes.utilisateur",
            ],
        },
    },
]

# form fields are styled using Bootstrap 5 classes (see
# Example 18 and templates/forms/champ.html)
FORM_RENDERER = "web.rendu.RenduBootstrap"

# ---- Languages (see Example 22): French by default, English; the
# dictionaries are in the local folder
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
LANGUAGES = [("fr", "Français"), ("en", "English")]
LOCALE_PATHS = [BASE_DIR / "locale"]
# the cookie that stores the selected language (see web/vues/langue.py)
LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME = "rdvmedecins_langue"

# ---- the time zone: that of the doctor’s office. It sets the current date (not
# for appointments in the past; see business/dates.py)
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
USE_TZ = True

# ---- static files (static folder): Bootstrap, the stylesheet, the script
STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [BASE_DIR / "static"]
# in production, `collectstatic` gathers all static files there (see README.md)
STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / "var" / "static"

# ---- Flash messages: in a signed cookie (see example 20)
MESSAGE_STORAGE = "django.contrib.messages.storage.cookie.CookieStorage"

# ---- cookies: never readable by the JavaScript on the page (HttpOnly, not even the
# anti-CSRF cookie, which Django leaves readable by default), never sent with a
# POST request originating from another site (Lax), never in plain text in production (Secure)
COOKIE_SECURE = env_bool("COOKIE_SECURE", False)
CSRF_COOKIE_NAME = "rdvmedecins_csrf"
CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = COOKIE_SECURE
CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True
CSRF_COOKIE_SAMESITE = "Lax"
# a missing or invalid anti-CSRF token: our 419 error page (see web/views/erreurs.py)
CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW = "web.vues.erreurs.csrf_refuse"

# ---- our own settings: authentication (see security/auth.py)...
JWT_SECRET = env("JWT_SECRET")
JWT_DUREE_MINUTES = env_int("JWT_DUREE_MINUTES", 120)
# ... and bot protection (see security/limiteur.py)
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS = env_int("LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS", 5)
LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP = env_int("LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP", 25)
LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES = env_int("LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES", 15)
INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE = env_int("INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE", 10)

# ---- the log: in debug mode, the SQL commands sent to the database are written to
# the console (see Example 28)
LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "handlers": {"console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler"}},
    "loggers": {
        "django.db.backends": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "DEBUG"},
    },
}
  • Lines 22–32: Reading the file [.env]. [read_text] reads the entire file, while [splitlines] splits it into lines. Each line of [NOM=valeur], excluding comments, becomes an environment variable for the process ([split("=", 1)]: split only at the first occurrence of [=], as a value may contain it). [setdefault] does not overwrite an existing variable: a real environment variable takes precedence over the file (example 25);
  • lines 36–45: three small functions that read an environment variable—with a default value—and convert it (to an integer or a Boolean value of 1 or 0);
  • lines 49–51: debug mode, the secret key, and the hostnames, read from the environment. If [.env] is not present, debug mode is disabled: this is the safe choice. [ALLOWED_HOSTS] is a list, constructed from a string of names separated by commas;
  • lines 57–63: the applications (see the architecture): three applications from [Django] (static files, Example 15; flash messages, Example 20; form templates, Example 18) and our two;
  • lines 72–79: the six middleware components, in the order in which the request passes through them (example 24). The order matters: the language is set first, so that all pages—even error pages—are in the correct language; anti-CSRF protection comes before authentication; authentication (which identifies the user) comes before access control (which evaluates the user); and [PageErreur], the last one, is the first to handle exceptions thrown by the views ([process_exception] is called in the reverse order, Example 24);
  • lines 85–95: the database (Example 28), whose parameters come from the environment;
  • lines 101–106: the application cache (Example 27). It is stored in files ([FileBasedCache]) within the [var/cache] folder, which [Django] creates itself: unlike the in-memory cache in Example 27, it survives server restarts (on a development server, after every code change), and it is shared by all processes on a production server (see the chapter on scopes). The application stores lists of doctors and clients, CAPTCHAs, attempt counters, and passes in this cache. With multiple servers, one would choose a shared cache, such as [Redis];
  • lines 109–124: the templates (Example 13), along with the application templates ([APP_DIRS], for those in [django.forms], Example 18), and four context processors: the request, the language (Example 22), flash messages (Example 20), and ours, which makes the logged-in user available to all templates (see below);
  • line 128: the form rendering engine, with the classes from [Bootstrap] (example 18);
  • lines 132–136: the languages and the dictionary (Example 22). The language cookie has a name specific to the application;
  • lines 140–141: the firm’s time zone. [USE_TZ = True] (the default value) causes [Django] to operate in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) and convert times to this time zone for display; [timezone.localdate()] returns the current date in this time zone. The current date is used for a business rule (no appointments in the past): in Paris, between midnight and 2:00 a.m. during daylight saving time, the date in Coordinated Universal Time is still the previous day; therefore, the firm’s time zone takes precedence;
  • lines 144–147: static files (example 15): the application’s [static] folder, and the folder where [collectstatic] collects them for production;
  • line 150: flash messages, in a signed cookie (example 20);
  • lines 155–161: the cookies from [Django]. [COOKIE_SECURE], read from [.env], will also be used for our own cookies (the token, language, etc.) : In production, on HTTPS, no cookies are transmitted in plain text. The anti-CSRF token cookie is given a name specific to the application; it is rendered as [HttpOnly] (the [JavaScript] on the page does not need it: it does not send any requests itself) and [SameSite=Lax]. A missing or invalid anti-CSRF token will display a page from the application (see below), rather than the 403 page for [Django] (Example 18);
  • lines 164–170: application-specific settings, read from the environment: the tokens JWT (Example 25) and bot protection (Example 27);
  • lines 174–181: the SQL command log, in debug mode (example 28).

The [python manage.py diffsettings] command displays all settings that differ from the default values of [Django].

docs.title: 11.7.1. manage.py and config/wsgi.py
docs.text:
The files [manage.py] and [config/wsgi.py] are from Example 01: the command-line tool, and the application WSGI, which is launched by the development server and the production servers. Upon startup, [Django] reads the settings (the [config/settings.py] file then reads the [.env] file), loads the applications from [INSTALLED_APPS] (their models, their configuration, example 24), creates an object for each middleware component (example 03), and then waits for requests. Everything built at startup is shared by all requests as long as the process is running: this applies to unique application objects (the business layer, the [ApplicationModel] facade), which are created by their providers when first used (example 06).

Two things are checked at startup, and an error shuts down the server before any requests are processed: the JWT token key (if it is too short, it is rejected; see [securite/auth.py]) and, with [MySQL], the database connection (see “Common Problems”).

docs.title: 11.8. The Templates
docs.text: The templates for ORM (Example 28): one class per table, in the [modeles/models.py] file of the [modeles] application.

# models/apps.py: the application configuration for models

from django.apps import AppConfig


class ModelesConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "modeles"

The application configuration (example 24), reduced to its name. It is not required: [Django] would generate one; we write it so that each application has its own.

docs.title: 11.8.2. modeles/models.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# modeles/models.py: Django, one class per database table
# dbrdvmedecins2 (see Example 28).
#
# The tables already exist: they are created by the script
# database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql, the same as in other versions of
# the application. Each model tells Django this via `managed = False`: Django never
# ever creates, modifies, or deletes these tables (no migrations).
#
# Foreign keys (ForeignKey, OneToOneField) are declared with
# on_delete=DO_NOTHING: when a row is deleted, Django does not itself search for
# the rows that reference it. It is the business layer that deletes them, in the correct
# order, which must be done (see business/service.py); the database constraints
# would prevent an incomplete deletion anyway.
#
# All tables have a column [version]: the optimistic lock that the layer
# DAO uses for its UPDATE (see dao/personnes.py).
# =========================================================================

from django.db import models


# the three roles of a user (column users.role):
#    - ADMI N: the administrator—appointments + management of doctors and clients;
#    - DOCTOR: a doctor—books and cancels appointments;
#    - USE  R : a client (patient)—books appointments for themselves, manages their account.
# TextChoices: a Django ÉNUMÉRATION, where each value is a string (the one
# is stored in the database); Role("ADMIN") performs the reverse lookup
class Role(models.TextChoices):
    ADMIN = "ADMIN"
    DOCTOR = "DOCTOR"
    USER = "USER"


# an authorized user (table [users]). Each doctor and each
# client has an account (column [user] in tables [medecins] and [clients]).
# Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq_users_login (a login belongs to only one
# account), identified by its NOM in the business layer (see business/service.py)
class User(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
    login = models.CharField(max_length=30)
     # the password HACHÉ (bcrypt), never the password itself
    password = models.CharField(max_length=100)
     # the display name once logged in: "Marie PELISSIER"
    nom = models.CharField(max_length=40)
     # choices: the possible values in the column
    role = models.CharField(max_length=10, choices=Role.choices)

    class Meta:
        db_table = "users"
        managed = False

    def __str__(self):
        return self.login


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# what doctors (table [medecins]) and customers (table
# [clients]): a title, a last name, a first name—and the associated user account
# (column [user]).
#
# Both tables have exactly the same columns: they are described UNE times,
# in this model ABSTRAIT (abstract = True: a “Person” is never created, and
# it does not have its own table), from which Doctor and Client inherit; each specifies
# specifies only the name of its table.
#
# Note: [Client] here refers to a PATIENT from the medical practice, not a client
# HTTP! This is the vocabulary of the original business domain, retained as-is.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class Personne(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
     # Mr., Mrs., Ms.
    titre = models.CharField(max_length=5)
    nom = models.CharField(max_length=20)
    prenom = models.CharField(max_length=20)
     # the RELATION linked to the user account: a person has a UN account, identified by
     # the foreign key [user] (db_column). OneToOneField: one account per person,
     #: one person per account. personne.compte returns a User object, retrieved from the database upon
     # first access—or upon the request itself, if requested (select_related, see
     # dao/personnes.py). related_name: the name of the inverse relationship,
     # user.medecin or user.client (%(class)s: the model name, in lowercase)
    compte = models.OneToOneField(User, db_column="user", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                                  related_name="%(class)s")

    class Meta:
        abstract = True

     # "Ms. Alice DURAND"
    def libelle(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.titre} {self.prenom} {self.nom}"

    def __str__(self):
        return self.libelle()


# a doctor (table [medecins]). Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq_medecins_prenom_nom
# (Two doctors cannot have the same first and last names)
class Medecin(Personne):
    class Meta:
        db_table = "medecins"
        managed = False


# a customer, i.e., a PATIENT (table [clients]). Uniqueness constraint SQL:
# unq_clients_prenom_nom
class Client(Personne):
    class Meta:
        db_table = "clients"
        managed = False


# a doctor’s time slot (table [creneaux]): 8:00 a.m. – 8:20 a.m., etc. The
# slots are created by the SQL script: the application simply reads them
class Creneau(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
     # multiple time slots for the same doctor: a foreign key, [id_medecin]
    medecin = models.ForeignKey(Medecin, db_column="id_medecin", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                                related_name="creneaux")
    hdebut = models.IntegerField()
    mdebut = models.IntegerField()
    hfin = models.IntegerField()
    mfin = models.IntegerField()

    class Meta:
        db_table = "creneaux"
        managed = False

     # "8:00 - 8:20"; :02d: two digits, "8:05" rather than "8:5"
    def horaire(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.hdebut}:{self.mdebut:02d} - {self.hfin}:{self.mfin:02d}"


# an appointment (table [rv]): a client, in a time slot, on a given day.
# Uniqueness constraint SQL: unq1_rv (day, id_creneau) — a time slot is reserved
# only once per day; identified by its name in the business layer
class Rv(models.Model):
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
     # DateField: the column [jour] (type SQL DATE) becomes a Python date object
    jour = models.DateField()
    creneau = models.ForeignKey(Creneau, db_column="id_creneau", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                                related_name="rvs")
    client = models.ForeignKey(Client, db_column="id_client", on_delete=models.DO_NOTHING,
                               related_name="rvs")

    class Meta:
        db_table = "rv"
        managed = False
  • lines 29–32: the three roles, in the form of an enumeration of [Django] ([models.TextChoices]), itself built on the enumerations of [Python] (the [enum] module): a type whose only possible values are its members: [Role.ADMIN], [Role.DOCTOR], and [Role.USER]. Each element has a value, in this case the string in base; an element of [TextChoices] is itself a string: [Role.ADMIN == "ADMIN"] is true. [Role("ADMIN")] returns the corresponding element (and sets [ValueError] to an unknown value). [Role.choices] returns the list of (value, label) pairs, which can be passed to the [choices] parameter of a field;
  • lines 39–55: the schema for table [users]: the primary key, the version (the optimistic lock, example 28), followed by the columns. [choices] (line 48) documents the possible values for the column; [Django] uses this to validate a form based on the schema and for the administration interface; the database itself does not perform any checks. [managed = False]: the table is created by the script SQL (Example 28);
  • lines 71–95: the tables [medecins] and [clients] have the same columns. Their shared description is written once, in an abstract template ([abstract = True], line 88): a template that has no table of its own and serves only to be inherited. The templates [Medecin] and [Client] inherit from it: each has the fields of [Personne] in its own table. ([Django] also supports true template hierarchies, where each child class has a table linked to that of the parent class; this is not the case here, where the two tables are independent);
  • Lines 84–85: The relationship to the account. [OneToOneField]: A person has an account, and an account belongs to at most one person. [db_column] refers to the foreign key column, [user] (without this parameter, [Django] would refer to it as [compte_id], the field name followed by [_id]). [on_delete] specifies what [Django] does when the account is deleted: [DO_NOTHING], nothing (the comment on lines 10–14 explains this choice; [CASCADE] would also delete the person, while [PROTECT] would reject the deletion). The attribute [compte] is a [User] object, not a number: that is the purpose of a ORM. When the ORM reads a person, it also reads their account if the request specifies it ([select_related]; see the DAO layer); otherwise, it will retrieve it via an additional request upon the first access to [personne.compte]. The number itself is always available, without a query, under the name [compte_id]. [related_name] refers to the inverse relationship: [user.medecin] or [user.client], the person associated with an account; [%(class)s] is replaced by the template name, in lowercase, which gives a different name to each of the two templates that inherit the field;
  • lines 91–95: the name of a person, “Ms. Alice DURAND,” used by all pages;
  • lines 100–111: two templates that specify only their table; everything else is inherited. A [Client] is a patient at the practice, not a client HTTP: this is the vocabulary of the original business domain, preserved in all versions of the application;
  • lines 116–133: an appointment slot. [ForeignKey] (line 120): multiple appointment slots for the same doctor, via the foreign key [id_medecin]; the inverse relationship, [medecin.creneaux], returns a doctor’s time slots. The method [horaire] returns “8:00 - 8:20”: in an f-string, [{self.mdebut:02d}] writes an integer of at least two digits, padded with zeros ([8:05] rather than [8:5]);
  • lines 139–151: an appointment. The column [jour] (type SQL [DATE]) becomes a [date] object of type [Python] ([DateField]); the [date] objects are immutable ([jour + timedelta(days=1)] is returned the next day, [jour] remains unchanged). Two relationships: one to the time slot and one to the appointment’s client.

docs.title: 11.9.1. domain/agenda.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# domain/agenda.py: a doctor’s schedule for a given day. Objects
# "business" objects CALCULÉS by the business layer (MetierService.get_agenda_medecin_jour),
# that do not correspond to any table, and then formatted for the template by the
# calendar view (web/views/agenda.py).
#
# frozen=True: the attributes are set once and for all by the constructor—
# exactly what is needed for a calculated object that no one modifies afterward.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

from modeles.models import Creneau, Medecin, Rv


# a time slot, and any appointment scheduled within that slot on a given day
# (None if the time slot is available)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CreneauMedecinJour:
    creneau: Creneau
    rv: Rv | None


# a doctor’s complete schedule for a given day: the list of their time slots,
# each of which is either available or booked
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgendaMedecinJour:
    medecin: Medecin
    jour: date
    creneaux_medecin_jour: list[CreneauMedecinJour]

Two calculated objects that do not correspond to any table: a time slot and its potential appointment on a given day; a doctor’s schedule for a single day, the list of their time slots. These are immutable data classes (example 03), whose attributes are typed: [Rv | None] (an appointment, or [None] for an available time slot), [list[CreneauMedecinJour]] (a list of time slots). [Python] does not validate these types at runtime, but the editors ([Pylance]) and analysis tools ([mypy]) read them.

docs.title: 11.10. The DAO layer
docs.text: The DAO layer (Example 28) groups the queries: one module per table (doctors and clients share theirs), with no business rules. Its methods do not start a transaction: the business layer calls them within its own transactions. They are written using the [QuerySet] from the ORM (Example 28); the values there are query parameters: no SQL injection is possible. The DAO are classes, of which the business layer creates one object for each; they have no state: they are collections of functions.

docs.title: 11.10.1. dao/personnes.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# dao/personnes.py: the DAO layer common to both doctors and clients.
#
# The DAO values for doctors and clients would be identical: the class PersonneDao
# writes them only once. self.modele is the relevant model (Doctor or
# Client): the queries target the SA table.
#
# The queries are written using Django’s ORM (see Example 28), which translates them
# into SQL. The values (first name, last name, etc.) become PARAMÈTRES in the SQL format:
# no string concatenation, so no injection of SQL. These methods do not open
# any transactions: the business layer calls them within its own transactions.
# =========================================================================

from django.db.models import F, QuerySet

from modeles.models import Client, Medecin, Personne


class PersonneDao:
     # model: the CLASSE of the model, Doctor or Client (in Python, a class is
     # a value like any other, which can be stored in a variable)
    def __init__(self, modele: type[Personne]):
        self.modele = modele

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # a query on the model’s table, including the user account.
     # select_related("account"): the join SQL with the table [users]
        # SELECT doctors.*, users.* FROM doctors INNER JOIN users ON ...
     # the accounts are loaded PAR LA MÊME query. Without this, every access to
     # personne.compte would trigger its own query
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _requete(self) -> QuerySet:
        return self.modele.objects.select_related("compte")

     # list sorted by last name then first name
    def lister(self) -> list[Personne]:
        return list(self._requete().order_by("nom", "prenom"))

     # a person and their account; None if they do not exist
    def lire(self, id: int) -> Personne | None:
        return self._requete().filter(id=id).first()

     # the person whose user account is [id_user]; compte_id: the
     # the foreign key column itself, without a join
    def lire_par_user(self, id_user: int) -> Personne | None:
        return self._requete().filter(compte_id=id_user).first()

     # the person with that first and last name, if there is one. The comparison is
     # performed by MySQL, i.e., using the database’s collation (utf8mb4_unicode_ci: without
     # case or accents taken into account)—exactly the same rule as
     # the one used for the uniqueness constraint SQL
    def homonyme(self, prenom: str, nom: str) -> Personne | None:
        return self._requete().filter(prenom=prenom, nom=nom).first()

     # INSERT: the database generates the ID, which Django stores in the created object
    def ajouter(self, titre: str, nom: str, prenom: str, compte) -> Personne:
        return self.modele.objects.create(titre=titre, nom=nom, prenom=prenom, compte=compte)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # UPDATE with VERROU OPTIMISTE (see Example 28):
        # UPDATE doctors SET title = ?, last name = ?, first name = ?, version = version + 1
        # WHERE id = ? AND version = ?
     # returns False if no rows have been modified: the record has changed (or been deleted)
     # since it was last read
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def modifier(self, id: int, version: int, titre: str, nom: str, prenom: str) -> bool:
        return self.modele.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(
            titre=titre, nom=nom, prenom=prenom, version=F("version") + 1) == 1

     # DELETE FROM doctors WHERE id = ?
    def supprimer(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.modele.objects.filter(id=id).delete()


# the DAO for doctors: everything is inherited from PersonneDao
class MedecinDao(PersonneDao):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(Medecin)


# the DAO for customers: that of individuals, plus a locking method
class ClientDao(PersonneDao):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(Client)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # places a VERROU on a customer’s line until the end of the transaction in
     # progress (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), and returns its ID (None if the client does
     # does not exist). A second transaction that requests the same lock ATTEND as the
     # first one must be completed. select_for_update: the "pessimistic" lock from
     # Django, which requires an open transaction.
     # Used for scheduling appointments (see MetierService.ajouter_rv): two
     # simultaneous appointments for the same patient are thus processed one
     # APRÈS the other, and the second reservation sees the appointment created by the first.
     # values_list("id", flat=True): only the "id" column, without a Client object
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def verrouiller(self, id: int) -> int | None:
        return Client.objects.select_for_update().filter(id=id).values_list("id", flat=True).first()
  • Lines 19–23: The DAO objects for doctors and clients would be identical, except for the template: the [PersonneDao] class creates them once and receives the template as a parameter to its constructor. [type[Personne]] is the annotation of a class (not an object): [Personne] or one of its child classes;
  • lines 32–33: the base query, common to all methods. [select_related("compte")] instructs ORM to also retrieve each person’s account using a join ([INNER JOIN users]; see the console output above): a single query, instead of one additional query per person. Without it, displaying the list of doctors with their logins would require one query for the list, then one per doctor: this is the so-called “N + 1 queries” problem, the most common pitfall of ORM. The underscore at the beginning of the method name indicates that it is internal to the class (example 06);
  • lines 36–46: the reads. [compte_id] (line 46) refers to the foreign key column itself: the condition applies to the people table, without a join;
  • lines 52–53: searching for a homonym. The comparison is performed by [MySQL], using the database’s collation: case-insensitive and ignoring accents, exactly like the uniqueness constraint (example 28);
  • lines 56–57: the insert; [compte] is an instance of [User], which has already been inserted;
  • lines 66–68: the update, with its optimistic lock (Example 28): [update] returns the number of modified lines, 0 if the version has changed;
  • lines 71–72: the deletion, via a [QuerySet]: [delete()] sends a [DELETE] for all the lines it designates;
  • lines 76–78: the DAO for doctors, which inherits everything. [super().__init__(Medecin)] calls the parent class constructor with the template;
  • lines 82–98: the DAO for clients, with one additional method. [select_for_update()] adds to the [FOR UPDATE] query: [MySQL] places a lock on the read rows until the end of the current transaction. A second transaction requesting the same lock waits until the first one is complete. This is a “pessimistic” lock: it blocks the transaction, rather than detecting conflicts after the fact like an optimistic lock. It is only permitted within a transaction (otherwise, ORM throws an exception). [values_list("id", flat=True)] reads only the [id] column: a list of integers, not objects. The code comment explains the purpose of this lock; we’ll revisit this when discussing the business layer.

docs.text:
# dao/creneaux.py: the DAO layer of time slots

from modeles.models import Creneau


class CreneauDao:
     #: a time slot and its doctor (a join)
    def lire(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None:
        return Creneau.objects.select_related("medecin").filter(id=id).first()

     # a doctor’s time slots, in chronological order. medecin_id: the column
     # of the foreign key, compared to an ID
    def lister_par_medecin(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]:
        return list(Creneau.objects.filter(medecin_id=id_medecin).order_by("hdebut", "mdebut"))

     # deletes all time slots for a doctor (deletion of a doctor):
        # DELETE FROM time slots WHERE id_medecin = ?
    def supprimer_par_medecin(self, id_medecin: int) -> None:
        Creneau.objects.filter(medecin_id=id_medecin).delete()

A doctor’s appointment slots, in chronological order; an appointment slot and its doctor (a join); the deletion of a doctor’s appointment slots (which precedes the deletion of the doctor, due to the foreign key constraint).

docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# dao/rvs.py: the DAO layer for appointments.
#
# The [rv] table does not directly reference the doctor: it goes through the appointment slot.
# Django’s ORM writes the join itself when a filter follows a relationship:
# creneau__medecin_id (two underscores: “the doctor for the time slot”).
# =========================================================================

from datetime import date

from modeles.models import Client, Creneau, Rv


class RvDao:
     # an appointment, its client, and its time slot
    def lire(self, id: int) -> Rv | None:
        return Rv.objects.select_related("client", "creneau").filter(id=id).first()

     # a doctor’s appointments on a given day, with their clients
    def rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]:
        return list(Rv.objects.select_related("client")
                    .filter(jour=jour, creneau__medecin_id=id_medecin))

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # a client’s appointments starting from the day [depuis] (inclusive), in chronological order
     # chronological order, with the time slot ET and the doctor for that time slot (two joins:
     # select_related("creneau__medecin")). jour__gte: days >= since (gte:
     # "greater than or equal")
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int, depuis: date) -> list[Rv]:
        return list(Rv.objects.select_related("creneau__medecin")
                    .filter(client_id=id_client, jour__gte=depuis)
                    .order_by("jour", "creneau__hdebut", "creneau__mdebut"))

     # number of appointments for a client starting on day [depuis] (inclusive):
     # count() counts the database (SELECT COUNT(*) ...)
    def compter_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int, depuis: date) -> int:
        return Rv.objects.filter(client_id=id_client, jour__gte=depuis).count()

     # number of appointments (past or future) for a doctor
    def compter_par_medecin(self, id_medecin: int) -> int:
        return Rv.objects.filter(creneau__medecin_id=id_medecin).count()

     # INSERT INTO rv ...
    def ajouter(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv:
        return Rv.objects.create(jour=jour, creneau=creneau, client=client)

    def supprimer(self, id: int) -> None:
        Rv.objects.filter(id=id).delete()

     # deletes TOUS a client’s appointments (past and future)
    def supprimer_par_client(self, id_client: int) -> None:
        Rv.objects.filter(client_id=id_client).delete()
  • Lines 20–22: a doctor’s appointments on a given day. The [rv] table does not directly reference the doctor: [creneau__medecin_id] (two underscores) follows the relationship to the time slot, then compares the [id_medecin] column of the time slot. ORM writes the join itself ([INNER JOIN creneaux]; see the console output above). The client for each appointment is retrieved by the same query;
  • lines 30–33: a client’s upcoming appointments. [select_related("creneau__medecin")] joins two tables: the time slot, then the client’s doctor (two joins). [jour__gte]: The suffix [gte] (“greater than or equal,” example 28) performs a comparison using [>=]. The sort also follows the relationships;
  • lines 37–42: [count()] counts the base ([SELECT COUNT(*)]) without reading the lines;
  • lines 45–53: insertions and deletions.

docs.title: 11.10.4. dao/users.py
docs.text:
# dao/users.py: the DAO layer for user accounts. Create (or delete) a
# A doctor or a client also creates (or deletes) their own account—see business/service.py

from django.db.models import F

from modeles.models import User


class UserDao:
     # None if no user has this login
    def lire_par_login(self, login: str) -> User | None:
        return User.objects.filter(login=login).first()

    def ajouter(self, login: str, hachage: str, nom: str, role: str) -> User:
        return User.objects.create(login=login, password=hachage, nom=nom, role=role)

     # UPDATE with optimistic lock (see DAO/personnes.py); hash None: the
     # password remains unchanged. **fields: the dictionary, "unpacked" into named parameters
    def modifier(self, id: int, version: int, login: str, nom: str, hachage: str | None) -> bool:
        champs = {"login": login, "nom": nom, "version": F("version") + 1}
        if hachage is not None:
            champs["password"] = hachage
        return User.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(**champs) == 1

    def supprimer(self, id: int) -> None:
        User.objects.filter(id=id).delete()

User accounts. The modification (lines 19–23) has an optional parameter: the hash of the new password, or [None] to keep the existing one. The columns to be modified are grouped into a dictionary, which [**champs] passes to [update] as named parameters (the “unpacking” of a dictionary, example 08).

docs.title: 11.11. The business layer
docs.text: The business layer (example 28): business rules and transactions. It knows nothing about the web: no requests, no responses, no templates.

docs.title: 11.11.1. business/dates.py
docs.text:
# business/dates.py: today’s date. It is used for RÈGLES DE GESTION (no
# past appointments, only one appointment per patient at VENIR): it resides
# in the business layer. The web layer reuses it.

from datetime import date

from django.utils import timezone


# today, in the application’s time zone (setting TIME_ZONE)
def aujourdhui() -> date:
    return timezone.localdate()

Today's date, in the application's time zone ([TIME_ZONE], see [config/settings.py]): [timezone.localdate()] converts Coordinated Universal Time to this time zone and then returns the date. The current date is used for two business rules (no appointments in the past, only one upcoming appointment): it is therefore calculated here, in a single location.

docs.title: 11.11.2. business/erreurs.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/erreurs.py: the exception thrown by the business layer when a RÈGLE DE
# GESTION is violated (login already taken, doctor still has appointments,
# time slot already reserved...).
#
# It carries a CODE (LOGIN_PRIS...), which the web layer can validate, and the message
# intended for the user. This message is translated into French or English at the
# the moment it is displayed, in the page’s language: gettext_lazy yields a
# "lazy" translation, which is calculated only when the text
# (str), and not when the module loads (see Example 22 and the `locale` directory).
#
# A MetierErreur is not an error: it is a normal response (“this login
# is already in use”), displayed to the user. Any other exception is a true
# exception, which results in a 500 error page.
# =========================================================================

from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

# the business error codes
LOGIN_PRIS = "LOGIN_PRIS"
MEDECIN_EXISTE_DEJA = "MEDECIN_EXISTE_DEJA"
CLIENT_EXISTE_DEJA = "CLIENT_EXISTE_DEJA"
MEDECIN_A_DES_RV = "MEDECIN_A_DES_RV"
CRENEAU_DEJA_RESERVE = "CRENEAU_DEJA_RESERVE"
MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE = "MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE"
MEDECIN_INTROUVABLE = "MEDECIN_INTROUVABLE"
CLIENT_INTROUVABLE = "CLIENT_INTROUVABLE"
DATE_PASSEE = "DATE_PASSEE"
PATIENT_A_UN_RV = "PATIENT_A_UN_RV"

# the message for each code
MESSAGES = {
    LOGIN_PRIS: _("Ce login est déjà utilisé par un autre compte."),
    MEDECIN_EXISTE_DEJA: _("Un médecin portant ce prénom et ce nom existe déjà."),
    CLIENT_EXISTE_DEJA: _("Un client portant ce prénom et ce nom existe déjà."),
    MEDECIN_A_DES_RV: _("Ce médecin a des rendez-vous : annulez-les avant de le supprimer."),
    CRENEAU_DEJA_RESERVE: _("Ce créneau vient d'être réservé par quelqu'un d'autre."),
    MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE: _("Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps par un autre utilisateur. "
                                "Revenez à la liste et rouvrez-la avant de recommencer."),
    MEDECIN_INTROUVABLE: _("Ce médecin n'existe pas (ou plus)."),
    CLIENT_INTROUVABLE: _("Ce client n'existe pas (ou plus)."),
    DATE_PASSEE: _("On ne peut pas prendre de rendez-vous à une date passée."),
    PATIENT_A_UN_RV: _("Ce patient a déjà un rendez-vous à venir : il faut l'annuler "
                       "avant d'en prendre un autre."),
}


class MetierErreur(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code: str):
        super().__init__(code)
        self.code = code

     # the message, in the language of the current request; @property: it is written
     # erreur.message, without parentheses
    @property
    def message(self) -> str:
        return str(MESSAGES[self.code])
  • lines 20–29: business error codes and constants (e.g., 09). The web layer can check an error code to associate it with the correct field in a form (see below);
  • Lines 32–45: The message for each code, marked “to be translated.” [gettext_lazy], imported under the short name [_] (as used in Example 22), provides a lazy translation: an object that retrieves its translation only when the text is requested. A standard translation ([gettext]) would be performed when the module loads, at startup, once and for all, in the default language; the lazy translation is performed each time the content is displayed, in the language of the current request. Two strings written side by side are concatenated by [Python] (line 38);
  • lines 48–57: the business-layer exception (example 28), which carries its own code. The [message] property (example 14) renders the message in the language of the request; [str] forces lazy translation.

A [MetierErreur] is not an error: it is a normal response (“this login is already in use”), displayed to the user. Any other exception is a true error, which results in a 500 error page.
