# business/donnees.py: the data entered in a "doctor" or "client" form,
# as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DonneesPersonne:
    titre: str          # Mr., Mrs., Ms.
    nom: str
    prenom: str
     # creation: optional (None), defaults to the name in lowercase
     # modification: optional; the login remains unchanged if absent
    login: str | None = None
     # creation: optional; defaults to the login
     # modification: optional; the password remains unchanged if omitted
    password: str | None = None
     # update: the record version at the time the form was
     # displayed (optimistic lock)
    version: int | None = None

A person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer (example 28). The last three attributes have a default value, [None]: they are optional. A comment following an attribute (line 9) is allowed: the comment extends from [#] to the end of the line.

docs.title: 11.11.4. business/metier.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business layer/metier.py: the CONTRAT of the business layer: read operations, calendar,
# appointments, doctor and client management.
#
# An abstract class (ABC, see Example 06) describes the methods that a class must
# have, without specifying how they are implemented. MetierService (the business layer) and
# ApplicationModel (the web layer cache) both inherit from it; Python
# refuses to create an object of a class that is missing an abstract method.
#
# X | None: a result that may be absent (a doctor who doesn’t exist...).
# =========================================================================

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from datetime import date

from domaine.agenda import AgendaMedecinJour
from modeles.models import Client, Creneau, Medecin, Rv

from .donnees import DonneesPersonne


class Metier(ABC):
     # ------------------------------------------------ readings
    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_medecins(self) -> list[Medecin]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_all_creneaux(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_medecin_by_id(self, id: int) -> Medecin | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_rv_by_id(self, id: int) -> Rv | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_creneau_by_id(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def get_agenda_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> AgendaMedecinJour | None: ...

     # the client (patient) whose user account is [id_user]
    @abstractmethod
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Client | None: ...

     # a client’s appointments, for today or in the future, with time slot and doctor
    @abstractmethod
    def get_rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int) -> list[Rv]: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ appointments (ADMIN, DOCTOR, USER)
     # triggers a MetierErreur if:
       # - the day has passed (DATE_PASSEE);
       # - the patient already has an upcoming appointment (PATIENT_A_UN_RV);
       # - the time slot is already booked for that day (CRENEAU_DEJA_RESERVE).
    @abstractmethod
    def ajouter_rv(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def supprimer_rv(self, rv: Rv) -> None: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ doctors (ADMIN)
     # creates the doctor ET's user account (role DOCTOR)
    @abstractmethod
    def ajouter_medecin(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin: ...

     # modifies the doctor ET's user account
    @abstractmethod
    def modifier_medecin(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin: ...

     # deletes the doctor, his time slots, and his account—ET—rejected if he has appointments
    @abstractmethod
    def supprimer_medecin(self, id: int) -> None: ...

     # ------------------------------------------------ patients
     # (ADMIN; ajouter_client is also used to register a patient,
     # modifier_client and supprimer_client for the patient to create their own account)
     #creates the client ET and their user account (role USER)
    @abstractmethod
    def ajouter_client(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def modifier_client(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client: ...

     # deletes the client, their account ET, and all their appointments (past and future)
    @abstractmethod
    def supprimer_client(self, id: int) -> None: ...

The business layer contract, an abstract class (example 06): all methods, along with their parameters and types, and, in comments, the rules they enforce. The body of an abstract method can be written on the same line as its signature ([: ...]). Two classes inherit from this contract: [MetierService], the business layer itself, and [ApplicationModel], the web layer facade (discussed later), which can thus replace the business layer wherever a [Metier] object is expected.

docs.title: 11.11.5. business/descripteur.py
docs.text:
# business domain/descripteur.py: everything that distinguishes a doctor from a client for the
# management rules (see business/service.py). Doctors and clients follow the
# same rules: the common code is written UNE times and configured by a descriptor.

from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass

from dao.personnes import PersonneDao


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Descripteur:
    dao: PersonneDao
    role: str                   # DOCTOR or USER
    code_introuvable: str       # error if the person does not exist
    code_existe_deja: str       # error if the same first and last names already exist
     # optional (None): if present, the deletion is REFUSÉE as long as the
     # person has appointments (compter_rv(id) > 0), with the error code_avec_rv.
     # Callable[[int], int]: a function that takes an integer and returns an integer
    compter_rv: Callable[[int], int] | None
    code_avec_rv: str | None
     # optional: what needs to be deleted—AVANT the person (the rows that
     # refer to them via a foreign key); receives their ID
    avant_suppression: Callable[[int], None] | None

Doctors and clients follow the same management rules, with a few minor differences: their account roles, their error codes, and what prevents or facilitates their deletion. A descriptor consolidates these details; the common code, in [MetierService], is defined once and receives the descriptor. The last three attributes are functions: [Callable[[int], int]] declares a function that takes an integer and returns an integer (the module [collections.abc] provides these abstract types); [| None]: or nothing.

docs.title: 11.11.6. business/fournisseur.py
docs.text:
# business layer/fournisseur.py: the business layer provider (see example 06):
# UN object MetierService, created upon the first request, then shared by all
# requests as long as the server is running. It has no request-specific state:
# sharing it is safe, even among multiple threads

from functools import cache

from .service import MetierService


@cache
def metier() -> MetierService:
    return MetierService()

The business layer provider (example 06): a single [MetierService] object, created on the first request, then shared by all requests. This is safe, even with multiple execution threads (example 20): the object has no request-specific state (its DAO objects do not have any either), and each thread has its own connection to the database (the ORM of [Django] opens one connection per execution thread).

docs.title: 11.11.7. business/service.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# business/service.py: the business layer implementation.
#
# The management of doctors and clients follows three business rules:
#
#    1. A person (doctor or client) and their user account are TOUJOURS
#       as a pair: they are created, modified, and deleted together, within the same
#       TRANSACTION—either everything succeeds, or nothing is written;
#    2. The login is unique throughout the application, and two doctors (or two
#       customers) cannot have the same first and last names;
#    3. Deletion:
#       - A MÉDECIN with appointments cannot be deleted (their patients
#         would lose their appointments without being notified): you must first
#         canceled first. Its time slots disappear along with it;
#       - a CLIENT, on the other hand, disappears along with TOUS its appointments (past and future) -
#         whether the deletion comes from the ADMIN or the patient themselves.
#
# And two rules for scheduling appointments, regardless of the role of the person
# making the appointment (ADMIN, DOCTOR, or the patient themselves):
#    4. No appointments in the past;
#    5. A patient can have only one upcoming appointment at a time.
#
# Doctors and patients follow exactly the same rules: the common code is
# is written UNE times (methods _xxx_personne), and configured by a descriptor that specifies
# what type of person we are dealing with.
#
# The TRANSACTIONS are opened by the _transaction method (at the end of the file),
# which also translates the errors reported by the database into MetierErreur.
# =========================================================================

import re
from collections.abc import Callable
from datetime import date

from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction

from dao.creneaux import CreneauDao
from dao.personnes import ClientDao, MedecinDao
from dao.rvs import RvDao
from dao.users import UserDao
from domaine.agenda import AgendaMedecinJour, CreneauMedecinJour
from modeles.models import Client, Creneau, Medecin, Personne, Role, Rv
from securite import mots_de_passe

from . import erreurs
from .dates import aujourdhui
from .descripteur import Descripteur
from .donnees import DonneesPersonne
from .erreurs import MetierErreur
from .metier import Metier

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Database errors -> MetierErreur
#
# When a constraint UNIQUE rejects a write operation, Django raises a IntegrityError,
# whose message is that of MySQL. It references the NOM of the constraint:
#    (1062, "Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'medecins.unq_medecins_prenom_nom'")
# (MySQL prefixes the name with the table name, MariaDB does not). That is why
# the script SQL NOMME has all these constraints. The regular expression CONTRAINTE
# extracts this name: (?:[^'.]*\.)? skips any prefix, ([^']+) captures the name
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
ERREURS_CONTRAINTES = {
    "unq_users_login": erreurs.LOGIN_PRIS,
    "unq_medecins_prenom_nom": erreurs.MEDECIN_EXISTE_DEJA,
    "unq_clients_prenom_nom": erreurs.CLIENT_EXISTE_DEJA,
    "unq1_rv": erreurs.CRENEAU_DEJA_RESERVE,
}

CONTRAINTE = re.compile(r"for key '(?:[^'.]*\.)?([^']+)'")


# a MetierErreur MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE, DANS lifted a transaction so that it
# is rolled back: a UPDATE did not modify any rows (optimistic lock)
class _VersionPerimee(Exception):
    pass


class MetierService(Metier):
     # the DAO objects, created once and for all; they have no state: a single
     # each one is used for all queries
    def __init__(self):
        self.medecins = MedecinDao()
        self.clients = ClientDao()
        self.creneaux = CreneauDao()
        self.rvs = RvDao()
        self.users = UserDao()

        self.medecin = Descripteur(
            dao=self.medecins,
            role=Role.DOCTOR,
            code_introuvable=erreurs.MEDECIN_INTROUVABLE,
            code_existe_deja=erreurs.MEDECIN_EXISTE_DEJA,
             # self.rvs.compter_par_medecin: the method itself, without calling it (a
             # "method bound" to the object self.rvs, which will be called later)
            compter_rv=self.rvs.compter_par_medecin,
            code_avec_rv=erreurs.MEDECIN_A_DES_RV,
             # A walk-in clinic may still have available time slots:
             # they no longer make sense without it, so they are deleted along with it (otherwise the
             # foreign key creneaux.id_medecin would prevent the deletion)
            avant_suppression=self.creneaux.supprimer_par_medecin)

        self.client = Descripteur(
            dao=self.clients,
            role=Role.USER,
            code_introuvable=erreurs.CLIENT_INTROUVABLE,
            code_existe_deja=erreurs.CLIENT_EXISTE_DEJA,
             # no compter_rv: deleting a client is never denied;
             # their appointments (past and future) are deleted along with them (otherwise
             # the foreign key rv.id_client would prevent deletion)
            compter_rv=None,
            code_avec_rv=None,
            avant_suppression=self.rvs.supprimer_par_client)

    # =======================================================================
     # read operations
    # =======================================================================

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return self.clients.lister()

    def get_all_medecins(self) -> list[Medecin]:
        return self.medecins.lister()

    def get_all_creneaux(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]:
        return self.creneaux.lister_par_medecin(id_medecin)

    def get_rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]:
        return self.rvs.rv_medecin_jour(id_medecin, jour)

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.clients.lire(id)

    def get_medecin_by_id(self, id: int) -> Medecin | None:
        return self.medecins.lire(id)

    def get_rv_by_id(self, id: int) -> Rv | None:
        return self.rvs.lire(id)

    def get_creneau_by_id(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None:
        return self.creneaux.lire(id)

    def get_client_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.clients.lire_par_user(id_user)

    def get_rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int) -> list[Rv]:
        return self.rvs.rv_a_venir_client(id_client, aujourdhui())

     # a doctor's schedule for a given day: their time slots, and for each one, the
     # appointments scheduled for that day (None if the doctor is available)
    def get_agenda_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> AgendaMedecinJour | None:
        medecin = self.get_medecin_by_id(id_medecin)
        if medecin is None:
            return None
         # a dictionary in COMPRÉHENSION format: slot number -> appointment scheduled for that slot
        reservations = {rv.creneau_id: rv for rv in self.get_rv_medecin_jour(id_medecin, jour)}
         # get(key): the value, or None if the key is missing
        creneaux_medecin_jour = [CreneauMedecinJour(creneau, reservations.get(creneau.id))
                                 for creneau in self.get_all_creneaux(id_medecin)]
        return AgendaMedecinJour(medecin, jour, creneaux_medecin_jour)

    # =======================================================================
     # appointment
    # =======================================================================

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # scheduling an appointment, within a transaction:
        # 1. no past appointments;
        # 2. on the patient’s line (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE): if the same
           # patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, double
           # click...), the second transaction waits for the first one to finish—and sees
           # the appointment it has just created;
        # 3. only one upcoming appointment per patient;
        # 4. Finally, the insertion. If the time slot has just been booked by a AUTRE patient,
           # it is the constraint SQL unq1_rv (day, id_creneau) that rejects
           # the insertion—translated to MetierErreur by _transaction.
     # A function defined as DANS—a method (task)—sees the variables of
     # that method (job) (day, time slot, customer): this is a “closure”
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def ajouter_rv(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv:
        def travail():
            if jour < aujourdhui():
                raise MetierErreur(erreurs.DATE_PASSEE)
            id_patient = self.clients.verrouiller(client.id)
            if id_patient is None:
                raise MetierErreur(erreurs.CLIENT_INTROUVABLE)
            if self.rvs.compter_a_venir_client(id_patient, aujourdhui()) > 0:
                raise MetierErreur(erreurs.PATIENT_A_UN_RV)
            return self.rvs.ajouter(jour, creneau, client)
        return self._transaction(travail)

    def supprimer_rv(self, rv: Rv) -> None:
         # lambda: an anonymous function reduced to an expression
        self._transaction(lambda: self.rvs.supprimer(rv.id))

    # =======================================================================
     # doctors and clients—public methods delegate to
     # shared methods, with the correct descriptor
    # =======================================================================

    def ajouter_medecin(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        return self._ajouter_personne(self.medecin, donnees)

    def modifier_medecin(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        return self._modifier_personne(self.medecin, id, donnees)

    def supprimer_medecin(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._supprimer_personne(self.medecin, id)

    def ajouter_client(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        return self._ajouter_personne(self.client, donnees)

    def modifier_client(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        return self._modifier_personne(self.client, id, donnees)

     # the client, their account ET all their appointments (ADMIN, or the patient themselves
     # from “Manage My Account”: same method, same rule)
    def supprimer_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self._supprimer_personne(self.client, id)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # creation: the user account, PUIS the person (who references it by their
     # foreign key [user]), in UNE transaction
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _ajouter_personne(self, d: Descripteur, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
        nom = donnees.nom.strip().upper()
        prenom = donnees.prenom.strip()
         # the rules of the dbrdvmedecins2 database: login = name in lowercase, password
         # password = login—unless the ADMIN (or the patient) has entered others
        login = (donnees.login or nom).lower()
        password = donnees.password or login

        def travail():
            self._verifier_personne_unique(d, prenom, nom, None)
            self._verifier_login_libre(login)
            compte = self.users.ajouter(login, mots_de_passe.hacher(password), f"{prenom} {nom}", d.role)
            return d.dao.ajouter(donnees.titre, nom, prenom, compte)
        return self._transaction(travail)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # change: the person ET their account (the displayed name "first name NOM" must
     # be updated; the login and password change only if they were entered).
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _modifier_personne(self, d: Descripteur, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
        def travail():
            personne = d.dao.lire(id)
            if personne is None:
                raise MetierErreur(d.code_introuvable)
             # optimistic lock: if the version in the database is no longer the same as the
             # form, someone has modified this record in the meantime—the operation is rejected
             # rather than silently overwriting their changes
            if donnees.version is not None and donnees.version != personne.version:
                raise MetierErreur(erreurs.MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE)
            nom = donnees.nom.strip().upper()
            prenom = donnees.prenom.strip()
            self._verifier_personne_unique(d, prenom, nom, id)
             # their account: the displayed name, and, if entered, the username and
             # password
            compte = personne.compte
            login = donnees.login.lower() if donnees.login else compte.login
            if login != compte.login:
                self._verifier_login_libre(login)
            hachage = mots_de_passe.hacher(donnees.password) if donnees.password else None
             # the UPDATE, with their optimistic lock: if the record (or account) has
             # been modified since the read operation above, no rows are modified
            if not d.dao.modifier(id, personne.version, donnees.titre, nom, prenom):
                raise _VersionPerimee()
            if not self.users.modifier(compte.id, compte.version, login, f"{prenom} {nom}", hachage):
                raise _VersionPerimee()
             # the person re-read, along with their account: the recorded values
            return d.dao.lire(id)
        return self._transaction(travail)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # deletion, in UNE transaction, in the order dictated by the keys
     # external:
        # 1. possible rejection if there are remaining appointments (with a doctor);
        # 2. what identifies the person (a doctor’s time slots, a
           # client);
        # 3. the person (who references their account), then their account.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _supprimer_personne(self, d: Descripteur, id: int) -> None:
        def travail():
            personne = d.dao.lire(id)
            if personne is None:
                raise MetierErreur(d.code_introuvable)
            if d.compter_rv is not None and d.compter_rv(id) > 0:
                raise MetierErreur(d.code_avec_rv)
            if d.avant_suppression is not None:
                d.avant_suppression(id)
            d.dao.supprimer(id)
            self.users.supprimer(personne.compte_id)
        self._transaction(travail)

     # Rejects first and last names already used by a AUTRE person of the same type
     # (id_courant: the person being edited, who obviously has the right
     # to keep their own first and last names; None for a new creation)
    def _verifier_personne_unique(self, d: Descripteur, prenom: str, nom: str,
                                  id_courant: int | None) -> None:
        homonyme = d.dao.homonyme(prenom, nom)
        if homonyme is not None and homonyme.id != id_courant:
            raise MetierErreur(d.code_existe_deja)

    def _verifier_login_libre(self, login: str) -> None:
        if self.users.lire_par_login(login) is not None:
            raise MetierErreur(erreurs.LOGIN_PRIS)

    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
     # executes [travail] in a transaction (transaction.atomic, see Example 28):
     # if the function completes normally, the transaction is committed (COMMIT);
     # if an exception occurs (including MetierErreur), the transaction is rolled back
     # (ROLLBACK): nothing is written.
    #
     # The "free login" and "unique first name + last name" checks are performed AVANT
     # the entry, to provide a clear message. But two ADMIN entries could
     # register the same login (or the same doctor) at the same time: in this case
     # — though rare — a uniqueness constraint SQL prevents the second write.
     # Similarly, two simultaneous modifications to the same record are resolved by the
     # optimistic lock. We therefore intercept these transaction errors AUTOUR,
     # and convert them to MetierErreur. Any other error is a true anomaly:
     # it is allowed to be escalated.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _transaction(self, travail: Callable):
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                return travail()
        except IntegrityError as e:
             # str(e): the message from MySQL
            trouve = CONTRAINTE.search(str(e))
            if trouve and trouve.group(1) in ERREURS_CONTRAINTES:
                 # from e: the new exception tracks the one that caused it
                raise MetierErreur(ERREURS_CONTRAINTES[trouve.group(1)]) from e
            raise
        except _VersionPerimee as e:
            raise MetierErreur(erreurs.MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE) from e

docs.title: 11.11.7.1. Dependencies and Descriptors
docs.text:
• lines 62–69: translation of database errors into business errors (see “Transactions,” below);
  • lines 74–75: an internal exception, which signals a [UPDATE] with no effect (the optimistic lock);
  • lines 81–86: the DAO objects, created once and for all by the constructor;
  • lines 88–112: the two descriptors. The functions are methods of the DAO, passed without parentheses (line 95): these are bound methods—functions that retain a reference to their object—and will be called later ([d.compter_rv(id)], line 286). A doctor who has appointments cannot be deleted; their time slots are deleted along with them. A client is deleted along with their appointments. The parameters are named: you can immediately see what each value is for.

docs.title: 11.11.7.2. Read operations and the calendar
docs.text:
• lines 118–146: the readings, delegated to the DAO layer. The current date is calculated here (line 146), not by DAO: this is a business rule (“upcoming”);
  • lines 150–159: a doctor’s schedule for a given day. A read-only dictionary (example 18) associates each time slot number with the appointment booked for that slot on that day ([rv.creneau_id]: the foreign key, without a query; see the templates); then, for each of the doctor’s time slots, the corresponding appointment, or [None]. Only two queries, regardless of the number of time slots: the day’s appointments and the time slots (plus the doctor’s notes), as shown in the console (“Development Mode”).

docs.title: 11.11.7.3. Appointment Scheduling
docs.text:
• Lines 179–189: Scheduling an appointment in a transaction. The function [travail], defined in the method, receives its parameters ([jour], [creneau], [client]): this is a closure (example 08). It is passed to [_transaction], which executes it within a transaction;
  • lines 181–182: no appointments in the past;
  • lines 183–185: the “pessimistic” lock on the patient’s record ([SELECT ... FOR UPDATE]; see layer DAO). Here’s why. The “only one upcoming appointment” rule is verified by a count (line 186), then the appointment is inserted (line 188). If the same patient books two time slots at the same time (two tabs, a double-click), two transactions could both count zero appointments and then both insert the appointment: no database constraint would prevent this, since the two time slots are different. The lock on the patient’s row causes the second transaction to wait until the first one is complete: it then counts one appointment and fails. The database cannot enforce this rule on its own: it is the business layer that enforces it, with the database’s assistance;
  • lines 186–187: only one upcoming appointment per patient;
  • line 188: the insertion. If the time slot has just been taken by another patient, it is the database constraint [unq1_rv] that rejects the insertion, and [_transaction] translates the error (further on);
  • lines 191–193: canceling an appointment. [lambda: ...] is an anonymous function, reduced to a single expression (in this case, a call): the equivalent of a three-line function [def].

docs.title: 11.11.7.4. Managing Doctors and Clients
docs.text:
• lines 200–218: public methods delegate to common methods, using the correct descriptor;
  • lines 224–237: creating a person. The name is capitalized ([PELISSIER], the database convention), and spaces surrounding the input are removed. The rules of the [dbrdvmedecins2] database: By default, the login is the name in lowercase, and the password is, by default, the login ([a or b]: [a] if it is “true” (a non-empty string), [b] otherwise). In the transaction: the validations (homonym check, free username), then the account (with the password hash; see [securite/mots_de_passe.py]), then the person, who references the account by its foreign key: the order is fixed;
  • lines 243–271: modifying a person and their account. The form version is compared to the version read (line 251): this is the first level of the optimistic lock, which returns a clear message. The second level is that of the [UPDATE] (lines 265–268): if the record has been modified between the read operation (line 245) and the write operation, [UPDATE] does not modify anything, and the exception [_VersionPerimee] rolls back the entire transaction (so the account is not modified either). The login and password change only if they have been entered; the displayed account name follows the person;
  • lines 281–292: deletion, in the order dictated by the foreign keys: the reference to the person (their time slots or appointments), the person, then their account. [personne.compte_id] is the foreign key, read without a query;
  • lines 297–305: the two uniqueness checks, performed before the write operation, to ensure a clear message. A person being edited has the right to retain their own first and last names: [id_courant] excludes this.

docs.title: 11.11.7.5. Database Transactions and Errors
docs.text:
• lines 322–334: every write operation is executed within a transaction ([transaction.atomic], example 28): if [travail] completes normally, the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]); if an exception occurs (including a [MetierErreur]), it is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): nothing is written. The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation, one transaction;
  • Lines 326–332: The checks performed before writing are not always sufficient: two administrators could save the same login at the same time. In this case, a database uniqueness constraint rejects the second write, and ORM triggers a [IntegrityError], whose message is that of [MySQL]: [(1062, "Duplicate entry 'Marie-PELISSIER' for key 'medecins.unq_medecins_prenom_nom'")]. The regular expression [CONTRAINTE] (line 69) extracts the name of the constraint ([search] searches for the expression in the string; [group(1)] returns what the first group captured in parentheses; [(?:...)] is a non-capturing group, and [?] makes it optional: [MySQL] 8 prefixes the name with the table name, [MariaDB] does not). This is why the script SQL names all its constraints. A known constraint becomes the corresponding [MetierErreur]; another, [IntegrityError], is re-raised as-is ([raise] with no parameters): this is a genuine anomaly. [raise ... from e] attaches the original exception to the new one (example 28);
  • Lines 333–334: A failed optimistic lock results in the error [MODIFICATION_CONCURRENTE]. The exception [_VersionPerimee] is thrown within the block [atomic] to roll back the transaction, then propagated outside the block.

Exceptions are caught outside the [with transaction.atomic()] block, not inside it: after a database error, the transaction is no longer valid and must first be rolled back, which is what exiting the block does (Example 28).

docs.title: 11.12. Authentication and Security
docs.text: The [securite] file covers everything related to authentication (who is the user?), permissions (does the user have access to this page?), and protection against bots. This is the complete version of Examples 25 through 27.

docs.title: 11.12.1. security/mots_de_passe.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/mots_de_passe.py: password hashing using the bcrypt algorithm
# (bcrypt library), 10 rounds, like the hashes in the SQL script.
#
# A HACHAGE hash is one-way: you cannot recover the password from
# it. To verify an entered password, it is hashed with the “salt” (a
# random value) contained in the stored hash, and the two
# results: that’s what bcrypt.checkpw does.
#
# The hashes of the SQL script begin with $2b$; those of the other versions of
# the application—which share the same base—with $2y$ (PHP) or $2a$ (Java):
# bcrypt verifies all three forms.
#
# bcrypt only takes into account the first 72 characters OCTETS of the password (and the
# library refuses to hash any more): forms therefore limit the
# password length (see web/formulaires.py).
# =========================================================================

import bcrypt

# the number of rounds: hashing costs 2^10 elementary calculations
TOURS = 10
MAX_OCTETS = 72


def hacher(mot_de_passe: str) -> str:
     # encode: the byte string (UTF-8); decode: the bytes as a string
    return bcrypt.hashpw(mot_de_passe.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(TOURS)).decode()


def verifier(mot_de_passe: str, hachage: str) -> bool:
    octets = mot_de_passe.encode()
    if len(octets) > MAX_OCTETS:
        return False
    return bcrypt.checkpw(octets, hachage.encode())

Passwords in the database are hashed by [bcrypt] (the SQL script mentioned above), not by PBKDF2, the default algorithm of [Django] (Example 25). The [bcrypt] library verifies them directly:

  • lines 26–28: the hash of a password. [gensalt(10)] generates a random salt with a cost of 10; [hashpw] calculates the hash, which contains the algorithm, the cost, and the salt (Example 25). The library operates on bytes: [encode()] converts the string to bytes ([UTF-8]), and [decode()] performs the reverse operation;
  • lines 31–35: verification. [checkpw] retrieves the cost and salt from the stored hash, hashes the entered password using them, and compares the results (in constant time, Example 23). [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password, and the library, since version 5, refuses to hash any more than that (it throws an exception): a longer password is therefore rejected outright. Forms also limit password length (web layer, discussed later).

[Django] could have verified these hashes itself, using its [BCryptPasswordHasher] algorithm (setting [PASSWORD_HASHERS]): but it expects hashes prefixed with [bcrypt$], and the database is shared with other versions of the application, which do not recognize this prefix.
