docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/utilisateur.py: the logged-in user, as described by their token JWT
# (see Example 25).
#
# The claims in our tokens (see security/auth.py):
#    su  b : the user account ID (convention JWT: "subject"), in plain text
#    login: the login
#    na  me: the display name (“Marie PELISSIER”), for the navigation bar
#    rol e: ADMIN, DOCTOR, or USER
#    iat, exp: token creation and expiration dates
#
# This object does not come from the database: it is reconstructed with each request
# from the token, whose signature guarantees its content.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass

from modeles.models import Role


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UtilisateurConnecte:
    user_id: int
    login: str
    nom: str
    role: str

     # the user described by the claims of an already verified token; None if a claim
     # is missing or does not have the expected format. @staticmethod: a function belonging to
     # the class, which accepts neither an object nor a class
    @staticmethod
    def de(claims: dict) -> "UtilisateurConnecte | None":
        role = claims.get("role")
        sub = str(claims.get("sub", ""))
         # Role.values: the values of the enumeration; isdigit: only digits
        if role not in Role.values or not sub.isdigit() or "login" not in claims or "nom" not in claims:
            return None
        return UtilisateurConnecte(int(sub), str(claims["login"]), str(claims["nom"]), role)

    @property
    def est_admin(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.ADMIN

    @property
    def est_medecin(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.DOCTOR

    @property
    def est_patient(self) -> bool:
        return self.role == Role.USER

The logged-in user, as described by their token (example 25). This object does not come from the database: it is reconstructed with each request from the token, whose signature guarantees its content.

  • Lines 31–38: a static method ([@staticmethod]): a method defined within the class that takes neither an object nor a class as an argument, and is called [UtilisateurConnecte.de(claims)]. It constructs the user object based on the claims in a token that has already been verified. Even if signed by us, a token is carefully verified: an unknown role, an identifier that is not a number, or a missing claim will result in the user being denied access ([None]). [Role.values] is the list of enumeration values; [isdigit] verifies that a string consists only of digits. The annotation for the returned type is enclosed in quotation marks: the class is not yet fully defined at this point;
  • lines 40–50: three properties for templates (example 26).

docs.title: 11.12.3. security/auth.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/auth.py: the authentication logic:
#    - validate         () : verifies a username/password pair;
#    - poser_jeton(     ) : generates the JWT token for a validated user, and
#                           stores it in a cookie in the response;
#    - user()      : the user described by a token.
#
# Where does the JWT token travel? In a COOKIE (see Example 25): a browser that
# displays ordinary HTML pages presents it on its own with every request.
# The settings in this cookie are important for security:
#    - HttpOnly: the page’s JavaScript cannot read the cookie (an injected script
#      injected script could not steal the token);
#    - SameSite=Lax: the browser does not send the cookie with a PAS value originating from a
#      another site (first line of defense against the so-called CSRF attack; the second is
#      the anti-CSRF token for forms);
#    - Secure: in production (HTTPS), the cookie is never transmitted in plain text;
#    - Lifetime: the cookie is deleted when the token expires.
# =========================================================================

import time

import jwt
from django.conf import settings
from django.core.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured

from dao.users import UserDao
from modeles.models import User

from . import mots_de_passe
from .utilisateur import UtilisateurConnecte

# the name of the cookie that carries the token
COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_jwt"

# HMAC-SHA256 requires a key of at least 256 bits: this is clearly stated right from the
# the module loads, rather than letting the library fail later
if len(settings.JWT_SECRET) < 32:
    raise ImproperlyConfigured("JWT_SECRET doit comporter au moins 32 caractères (cf. .env).")

_users = UserDao()


# None if the login does not exist or if the password is incorrect
def valider(login: str, password: str) -> User | None:
    user = _users.lire_par_login(login)
    if user is None or not mots_de_passe.verifier(password, user.password):
        return None
    return user


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the token JWT from [user], stored in the cookie that carries it. The token is
# SIGNÉ (HMAC-SHA256) with the secret key: the browser can read it (it is
# not encrypted), but it cannot modify it—any modification would render the signature
# invalid.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def poser_jeton(reponse, user: User):
    maintenant = int(time.time())
    duree = settings.JWT_DUREE_MINUTES * 60
    claims = {
        "sub": str(user.id),
        "login": user.login,
        "nom": user.nom,
        "role": user.role,
        "iat": maintenant,
        "exp": maintenant + duree,
    }
    jeton = jwt.encode(claims, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithm="HS256")
    reponse.set_cookie(COOKIE, jeton, max_age=duree, secure=settings.COOKIE_SECURE,
                       httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# deletes the token cookie: the response contains an empty cookie with the same name that has already expired
def effacer_jeton(reponse):
    reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the user identified by a token; None if the token has expired, is forged, or is incorrectly
# formatted. jwt.decode verifies the signature; ET verifies the expiration date (claim exp).
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def utilisateur(jeton: str) -> UtilisateurConnecte | None:
    try:
        claims = jwt.decode(jeton, settings.JWT_SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])
    except jwt.InvalidTokenError:
        return None
    return UtilisateurConnecte.de(claims)

The authentication service from Example 25, with a few differences:

  • Lines 37–38: The token key is verified when the module loads, that is, when the application starts: If the key is too short, the process stops entirely, with a clear error message ([ImproperlyConfigured] is the exception to [Django] for an incorrect configuration), rather than a simple warning like [PyJWT] (Example 25);
  • lines 44–48: verification of a username and password by the DAO layer (the account, retrieved from the database) and by the password module. The web layer calls this module directly: authentication is a security matter, not a business rule;
  • lines 57–71: generating the token and storing it in a cookie in the response (Example 25). The account ID ([sub]) is written in plain text: the JWT standard requires this. The cookie is [Secure] in production ([COOKIE_SECURE], see [config/settings.py]);
  • lines 75–77: Deletion of the cookie: a cookie with the same name, empty, and already expired (Example 25);
  • lines 84–89: the user is identified by a token, or [None] (example 25).

docs.title: 11.12.4. security/acces.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/acces.py: LA RÈGLE from ACCÈS for each URL.
#
# The rules are evaluated in order; the first one whose pattern (a
# regular expression) matches the path of the URL is applied:
#    - a few URL PUBLIQUES: the welcome page, login, language selection,
#      account creation;
#    - URL reserved for certain roles (any one of these roles is sufficient);
#    - all AUTRES require an authenticated user (last rule).
# This is the “everything is prohibited unless explicitly permitted” rule: a URL added later
# later—and which we might have forgotten to protect—is automatically protected.
#
# The ControleAcces middleware (see securite/middleware.py) enforces these rules: an
# An anonymous visitor who is denied access is redirected to the login page; a user
# authenticated user without the requested role receives a 403 error page.
# =========================================================================

import re

from modeles.models import Role

# two specific values instead of a set of roles
PUBLIC = "PUBLIC"
AUTHENTIFIE = "AUTHENTIFIE"

# re.compile: the regular expression, parsed once and for all
REGLES = [
    (re.compile(r"^/$"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/(login|logout)$"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/langue/"), PUBLIC),
    (re.compile(r"^/inscription"), PUBLIC),
     # A patient cancels an appointment (SON) from “My Account,” not from the calendar
    (re.compile(r"^/agenda/annuler$"), {Role.ADMIN, Role.DOCTOR}),
    (re.compile(r"^/(medecins|clients)"), {Role.ADMIN}),
    (re.compile(r"^/mon-"), {Role.USER}),
    (re.compile(r"^/"), AUTHENTIFIE),
]


# The path rule [chemin]: PUBLIC, AUTHENTIFIE, or a set of roles
def regle(chemin: str):
    for motif, exigence in REGLES:
        if motif.match(chemin):
            return exigence
    return AUTHENTIFIE

The application’s access rules, grouped into a single list. Example 26 protected each view with a decorator; here, protection is centralized, as was done by the rules [access_control] and [Symfony]:

  • lines 27–37: Each rule associates a pattern (a regular expression, compiled once and for all by [re.compile]) with a requirement: [PUBLIC], [AUTHENTIFIE], or a set of roles, any one of which is sufficient. [^] marks the start of the path, [$] marks its end; [(login|logout)]: either one. The public URL pages are the home page, login, language selection, and account creation. Next are the URL pages reserved for certain roles: cancellation from the calendar (a patient cancels from “My Account”), management of doctors and clients, and the patient’s account. The last rule, [^/], applies to all remaining URL rules and requires an authenticated user;
  • lines 41–45: the path rule: the first one that matches ([match]: the recognized expression at the beginning of the string).

This is the “everything is prohibited except what is permitted” rule: a URL added later—which might have been forgotten to be protected—is automatically protected. The opposite error (a public URL that was forgotten to be made public) is immediately obvious; the error of a forgotten protected page is much less so.

docs.title: 11.12.5. security/middleware.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/middleware.py: the two security middleware components (see examples 24 through 26).
#
#    1. Authentication, AVANT routing: who is the user? Based on the
#       token JWT from their cookie. It does not reject anything on its own: a missing token or
#       invalid token allows the visitor to proceed (ANONYME; request.utilisateur is equivalent to None); the
#       An invalid token cookie is removed from the response;
#    2. ControleAcces, APRÈS routing (process_view): Does the user have
#       permission to access this URL? The rules are in security/acces.py. A URL
#       that has no route does not reach this point: it receives a 404 page.
# =========================================================================

from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

from . import acces, auth


class Authentification:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        jeton = request.COOKIES.get(auth.COOKIE, "")
        request.utilisateur = auth.utilisateur(jeton) if jeton else None
        reponse = self.get_response(request)
         # an invalid token (expired, forged): the cookie is deleted in the response
         # whatever it may be—unless the request has just set a new one (a
         # successful login)
        if jeton and request.utilisateur is None and auth.COOKIE not in reponse.cookies:
            auth.effacer_jeton(reponse)
        return reponse


class ControleAcces:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
         # path_info: the path to URL, without its parameters
        exigence = acces.regle(request.path_info)
        if exigence == acces.PUBLIC:
            return None
        utilisateur = request.utilisateur
        if utilisateur is None:
             # an anonymous visitor: redirect to the login page. If they had a
             # token cookie, it means their token is no longer valid (expired,
             # forged): their session has expired, and they are notified of this
            if auth.COOKIE in request.COOKIES:
                messages.error(request, _("Votre session a expiré : reconnectez-vous."))
            return redirect("login")
        if exigence != acces.AUTHENTIFIE and utilisateur.role not in exigence:
             # authenticated, but without the requested role: error 403 (view handler403, see config/urls.py)
            raise PermissionDenied("rôle insuffisant")
        return None

The two security middleware components:

  • lines 21–34: authentication (example 25), before routing. It does not reject anything: a missing or invalid token leaves the visitor anonymous. It deletes the cookie associated with an invalid token in the response, regardless of what that response is, unless the response sets a new one (a successful login): [reponse.cookies] is the dictionary of cookies that the response sets;
  • Lines 37–60: access control, after routing (its method [process_view], Example 24). A URL that has no route therefore does not reach this point: it receives a 404 page directly, without the visitor being asked to log in. [request.path_info] is the path of URL, without its parameters. An anonymous visitor who is denied access is sent to the login page; if they had a token cookie, it means their token is no longer valid: a pop-up message informs them that their session has expired (see the screenshot titled “End of Session”). An authenticated user who does not have the required role triggers [PermissionDenied]: since the exception is thrown in [process_view]—not in the view—[Django] itself transforms it into a response via the application’s [handler403] view (Example 24), in both debug and production modes.

The message is translated by [gettext] (line 16), not by [gettext_lazy]: it is translated during the request, in its language; lazy translation is only useful for text defined when a module is loaded.

docs.title: 11.12.6. security/erreurs.py
docs.text:
# security/erreurs.py: the token is valid, but the account it refers to does not exist
# anymore: it has been deleted since the login (by the patient themselves in another
# tab, or by the ADMIN). This case is treated as an expired session: the
# PageErreur middleware deletes the cookie and redirects to the login page.


class SessionInvalide(Exception):
    pass

A special case: the token is valid, but the account it refers to no longer exists (the patient deleted it in another tab, or the administrator deleted it). Views that require the account then throw this exception, which the [PageErreur] middleware treats as an expired session (see below).

docs.title: 11.12.7. security/captchas.py and dessin_captcha.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/captchas.py: a CAPTCHA ("test to distinguish a human from a robot")
# generated by the server itself, without an external service (see example 27).
#
# How it works:
#    1. `generer()` generates a random text, turns it into an image, and stores the correct one
#       response DANS LE CACHE from the server under a random identifier;
#    2. The page displays the image and places the identifier in a hidden field on the
#       form (the response itself never leaves the server);
#    3. verify(id, input) compares the input to the expected response, then OUBLIE
#       this CAPTCHA: each image is used only once, so a bot cannot replay
#       a response that has already been found.
#
# Why use a cache instead of a simple module variable? Because a server
# production server launches PLUSIEURS processes (see README.md), which do not share their
# memory: the request that verifies the CAPTCHA is not necessarily processed by the
# process that generated it. The application cache (for files, see
# config/settings.py) is shared by all processes.
# =========================================================================

import secrets
from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.core.cache import cache

from . import dessin_captcha

# image validity period, in seconds: 10 minutes to fill out the form
DUREE_VIE = 600


# a CAPTCHA: its ID, to be placed in the hidden field [captcha_id] of the
# form, and its image (SVG), to be inserted as-is into the page
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Captcha:
    id: str
    svg: str


def generer() -> Captcha:
    texte = dessin_captcha.texte_aleatoire(5)     # 5 characters
    id = secrets.token_hex(12)                     # a username that cannot be guessed
     # the cache will automatically forget the answer after 10 minutes
    cache.set(f"captcha.{id}", texte, DUREE_VIE)
    return Captcha(id, dessin_captcha.svg(texte))


# true if [saisie] is the correct answer to the captcha [id] (regardless of
# case). The CAPTCHA is consumed in all cases.
def verifier(id: str, saisie: str) -> bool:
     # The identifier comes from the browser: 24 hexadecimal digits, or nothing
    if len(id) != 24 or any(c not in "0123456789abcdef" for c in id) or not saisie:
        return False
    attendu = cache.get(f"captcha.{id}")
     # `delete` returns `True` if the element existed: if two requests have the same
     # captcha at the same time, only one actually deletes it—the other fails
    if attendu is None or not cache.delete(f"captcha.{id}"):
        return False
    return attendu.casefold() == saisie.strip().casefold()

The CAPTCHA service from Example 27, with two additional precautions:

  • lines 51–52: The identifier comes from the browser; we verify that it consists of 24 hexadecimal digits (those of [token_hex(12)]) before using it as the cache key. [any] returns [True] if any of the elements produced by the generating expression is true;
  • lines 53–56: [cache.delete] returns [True] if the element existed. If two requests present the same CAPTCHA at the same time, only one actually removes it; the other fails. An image is used only once.

The file's comment (lines 17–22) explains why the CAPTCHAs are stored in the cache (a set of files shared by all server processes) rather than in a module variable. The file [securite/dessin_captcha.py] is the one from Example 27, with a longer header comment: each character is drawn with lines, never written as text, otherwise a bot would simply have to read the image’s source code.

docs.title: 11.12.8. security/limiteur.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/limiteur.py: second line of defense against bots (the first is the
# captcha): we track attempts, and once a threshold is exceeded, we block access for a
# for a while (see example 27).
#
#    - Login: After LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS failed attempts (incorrect CAPTCHA or incorrect
#      ) for the same login from the same IP address IP, this pair is blocked
#      until the end of a LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES-minute window, counted from
#      the first failed attempt. The same IP address is also blocked if it accumulates
#      LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP failed attempts across all logins (a bot attempting
#      thousands of different logins);
#    - account creation: no more than INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE accounts created per hour
#      from the same IP address IP.
#
# Caution in the classroom: all computers often connect to the Internet via the
# MÊME address IP. This is why the connection block first targets the
# pair (IP, login)—a student who enters the wrong password does not block their
# neighbors—and why the thresholds are adjustable (in the .env file).
#
# Each counter is stored in the cache (see securite/captchas.py), with the end
# of its window: {"count": 3, "end": 1790531419.2}.
# =========================================================================

import hashlib
import math
import time

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.cache import cache


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- connection
# number of remaining lockout minutes (0 = attempt is allowed)
def minutes_blocage_login(ip: str, login: str) -> int:
    return max(_minutes_restantes(_cle_login(ip, login), settings.LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS),
               _minutes_restantes(f"login_ip.{ip}", settings.LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS_IP))


# one more failure; the first opens a window of LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES minutes,
# at the end of which the counter resets to zero
def echec_login(ip: str, login: str) -> None:
    duree = settings.LOGIN_BLOCAGE_MINUTES * 60
    _compter(_cle_login(ip, login), duree)
    _compter(f"login_ip.{ip}", duree)


# a successful login resets the login counter to zero
def reussite_login(ip: str, login: str) -> None:
    cache.delete(_cle_login(ip, login))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- registration
def minutes_blocage_inscription(ip: str) -> int:
    return _minutes_restantes(f"inscription.{ip}", settings.INSCRIPTION_MAX_PAR_HEURE)


def inscription_reussie(ip: str) -> None:
    _compter(f"inscription.{ip}", 3600)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- common mechanism
# the pair key (IP, login). The login comes from the browser: it may contain
# anything (spaces...). Its fingerprint, SHA-256, consists of 64 digits
# hexadecimal digits, yields a cache key that is always valid
def _cle_login(ip: str, login: str) -> str:
    empreinte = hashlib.sha256(f"{ip}|{login.strip().lower()}".encode()).hexdigest()
    return f"login.{empreinte}"


# the minutes remaining until the end of the window if the counter has reached the
# limit, 0 otherwise; seconds are rounded up to the nearest minute SUPÉRIEURE (ceil):
# 30 s -> "1 minute"
def _minutes_restantes(cle: str, limite: int) -> int:
    etat = cache.get(cle)
    if etat is None or etat["compte"] < limite:
        return 0
    return max(1, math.ceil((etat["fin"] - time.time()) / 60))


# one more attempt in the current window (or in a new window of
# [duree] seconds). The cache resets the counter at the end of the window (timeout).
# Reading followed by writing is not ATOMIQUES: two simultaneous attempts
# might count as only one. For a failure counter, this is not a serious issue
def _compter(cle: str, duree: int) -> None:
    etat = cache.get(cle) or {"compte": 0, "fin": time.time() + duree}
    etat["compte"] += 1
    cache.set(cle, etat, timeout=max(1, math.ceil(etat["fin"] - time.time())))

The attempt limit in Example 27, more refined:

  • lines 34–49: the login. Failed attempts are counted for each pair (address IP, username): five failed attempts (setting [LOGIN_MAX_ECHECS]) block that username from that address for fifteen minutes, starting from the first failed attempt. In a classroom, where all computers often access the Internet via the same address IP, a student who enters the wrong password does not block their neighbors. However, the same address is also blocked if it accumulates 25 failed attempts across all logins: this is the case for a bot that tries thousands of different logins. A successful login clears the failed attempts for that login;
  • lines 53–58: account creation: a maximum of ten accounts per hour per IP address;
  • lines 65–67: the pair’s key (IP, login). The login comes from the browser: it can contain anything. Its fingerprint SHA-256 ([hashlib.sha256], from the standard library), consisting of 64 hexadecimal digits, yields a cache key that is always valid and of fixed length;
  • lines 73–77: the remaining lockout minutes, rounded up to the next minute ([math.ceil]: 30 seconds equal “1 minute”);
  • lines 84–87: the counter, within a fixed window (Example 27). [cache.get(cle) or {...}]: the current state, or a new state. The code comment acknowledges the weakness of Example 27 (two simultaneous failures may count as only one); for a failure counter, this is not a serious issue.

docs.title: 11.12.9. security/passe_inscription.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# security/passe_inscription.py: the "pass" for account creation.
#
# To open the “Create a Customer Account” page, you must first have copied the
# CAPTCHA from the authentication page (see web/vues/inscription.py, POST
# /registration/access). The server then issues a token:
#    - a random identifier, stored in a cookie named HttpOnly;
#    - valid for 15 minutes (enough time to fill out the form, even if you have to
#      several times after data entry errors);
#    - Expires as soon as an account is created: UN captcha solved = UN account at most.
#      A bot cannot create accounts in rapid succession.
#
# Without a valid pass, GET and POST /registration redirect to the
# authentication page (see the @passe_inscription_exige decorator): type
# directly; the URL /registration does not allow you to bypass the CAPTCHA.
#
# Like CAPTCHAs, passcodes are stored in the cache.
# =========================================================================

import secrets
from functools import wraps

from django.conf import settings
from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.cache import cache
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

COOKIE = "rdvmedecins_inscription"
# The cookie is sent by the browser only to the /registration... addresses
CHEMIN = "/inscription"
# Pass lifetime, in minutes
DUREE_VIE = 15


# Issues a new token in a cookie in the response
def emettre(reponse):
    id = secrets.token_hex(12)
    cache.set(f"passe.{id}", True, DUREE_VIE * 60)
    reponse.set_cookie(COOKIE, id, max_age=DUREE_VIE * 60, path=CHEMIN,
                       secure=settings.COOKIE_SECURE, httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# true if [id] is an existing, unexpired token
def est_valide(id: str | None) -> bool:
    return bool(id) and id.isalnum() and cache.get(f"passe.{id}") is not None


# The pass has been used: it is discarded...
def consommer(id: str | None) -> None:
    if id and id.isalnum():
        cache.delete(f"passe.{id}")


# ... and its cookie is overwritten by a cookie with the same name and path that has already expired
def effacer_cookie(reponse):
    reponse.delete_cookie(COOKIE, path=CHEMIN, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# @passe_inscription_exige: a decorator (see Example 26), applied to views that
# require a token (GET and POST /registration). Without a valid token,
# the view is not called: return to the authentication page, with a message
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def passe_inscription_exige(vue):
    @wraps(vue)
    def enveloppe(request, *args, **kwargs):
        if not est_valide(request.COOKIES.get(COOKIE)):
            messages.error(request, _("Pour créer un compte, recopiez d'abord correctement les "
                                      "caractères de l'image, puis cliquez sur « Créer un compte client »."))
            return redirect("login")
        return vue(request, *args, **kwargs)
    return enveloppe

The account creation token. To create an account, you must first enter the CAPTCHA from the login page (the “Create a Customer Account” button): the server then issues a token, a random identifier stored in the cache and in a cookie. Without a passcode, the account creation page redirects to the login page: typing URL or [/inscription] directly does not bypass the CAPTCHA; and a passcode is only used to create an account: a bot cannot create accounts in bulk.

  • lines 29–33: the cookie is sent by the browser only to addresses beginning with [/inscription] (cookie parameter [path]): it does not travel with other requests;
  • lines 37–42: the cookie is issued for fifteen minutes—enough time to fill out the form, even if you have to try several times after making input errors;
  • lines 46–59: verification, usage, and deletion of the cookie (which must have the same path as the cookie to be deleted). [isalnum] verifies that the identifier consists only of letters and numbers;
  • lines 67–75: the decorator [@passe_inscription_exige] (example 26), applied to the account creation view.

docs.title: 11.13. The Web Layer: Shared Services
docs.text: The [web] folder contains the [Django] application for the web layer (declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]; see [config/settings.py]; its file [web/apps.py] contains only its name). It brings together the routes, views, forms, and what all views have in common: that is the focus of this section.

docs.title: 11.13.1. web/application.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/application.py: the business layer cache/facade (the equivalent of the
# [ApplicationModel] class in other versions of the application): the lists of
# doctors and clients are read from the database once, then served from the cache.
#
# Why use Django’s CACHE, and not simply an attribute of this object? A
# Python process does indeed retain its objects from one request to the next (see Example 20);
# but a production server launches PLUSIEURS processes, each of which would have SA
# copy of the lists: the ADMIN process that adds a doctor would only update the list of the
# process that processed its request. The application cache (for files, see
# config/settings.py) is shared by all processes.
#
# These lists can be CHANGER (the ADMIN adds, modifies, or deletes doctors and
# clients): each write operation therefore goes through this facade, which OUBLIE updates the list
# in question immediately afterward; the next query that needs it reads it from the database. This is
# the whole point of an entry point UNIQUE to the business layer: the rule
# "write => cache update" is only written here.
# =========================================================================

from datetime import date
from functools import cache as une_fois

from django.core.cache import cache

from domaine.agenda import AgendaMedecinJour
from metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne
from metier.fournisseur import metier
from metier.metier import Metier
from modeles.models import Client, Creneau, Medecin, Rv

MEDECINS = "rdvmedecins.medecins"
CLIENTS = "rdvmedecins.clients"


# same contract as the business layer
class ApplicationModel(Metier):
    def __init__(self):
        self.metier = metier()

     # ------------------------------------------------ reads from the cache
     # get_or_set(key, function, timeout): the cache value if it exists; otherwise,
     # the function is called, and its result is stored in the cache (timeout=None:
     # no time limit) before being returned. Objects are stored there in serialized form
     # (pickle module): each request that reads them obtains copies
    def get_all_medecins(self) -> list[Medecin]:
        return cache.get_or_set(MEDECINS, self.metier.get_all_medecins, timeout=None)

    def get_all_clients(self) -> list[Client]:
        return cache.get_or_set(CLIENTS, self.metier.get_all_clients, timeout=None)

     # the doctor whose user account is [id_user]—used for preselection,
     # for a logged-in doctor, their own calendar
    def get_medecin_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Medecin | None:
        return next((m for m in self.get_all_medecins() if m.compte_id == id_user), None)

     # ------------------------------------------------ simple delegations
    def get_all_creneaux(self, id_medecin: int) -> list[Creneau]:
        return self.metier.get_all_creneaux(id_medecin)

    def get_rv_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> list[Rv]:
        return self.metier.get_rv_medecin_jour(id_medecin, jour)

    def get_client_by_id(self, id: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.metier.get_client_by_id(id)

    def get_medecin_by_id(self, id: int) -> Medecin | None:
        return self.metier.get_medecin_by_id(id)

    def get_rv_by_id(self, id: int) -> Rv | None:
        return self.metier.get_rv_by_id(id)

    def get_creneau_by_id(self, id: int) -> Creneau | None:
        return self.metier.get_creneau_by_id(id)

    def get_agenda_medecin_jour(self, id_medecin: int, jour: date) -> AgendaMedecinJour | None:
        return self.metier.get_agenda_medecin_jour(id_medecin, jour)

     # no cache here: the most recent data is what counts (a patient who
     # has just modified or deleted their account)
    def get_client_by_user_id(self, id_user: int) -> Client | None:
        return self.metier.get_client_by_user_id(id_user)

    def get_rv_a_venir_client(self, id_client: int) -> list[Rv]:
        return self.metier.get_rv_a_venir_client(id_client)

    def ajouter_rv(self, jour: date, creneau: Creneau, client: Client) -> Rv:
        return self.metier.ajouter_rv(jour, creneau, client)

    def supprimer_rv(self, rv: Rv) -> None:
        self.metier.supprimer_rv(rv)

     # ------------------------------------------------ entries => cache ignored
     # (delete: the item is removed from the cache)
    def ajouter_medecin(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        medecin = self.metier.ajouter_medecin(donnees)
        cache.delete(MEDECINS)
        return medecin

    def modifier_medecin(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Medecin:
        medecin = self.metier.modifier_medecin(id, donnees)
        cache.delete(MEDECINS)
        return medecin

    def supprimer_medecin(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.metier.supprimer_medecin(id)
        cache.delete(MEDECINS)

    def ajouter_client(self, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        client = self.metier.ajouter_client(donnees)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)
        return client

    def modifier_client(self, id: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Client:
        client = self.metier.modifier_client(id, donnees)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)
        return client

    def supprimer_client(self, id: int) -> None:
        self.metier.supprimer_client(id)
        cache.delete(CLIENTS)


# the facade provider: a single, shared object (see business/fournisseur.py)
@une_fois
def application() -> ApplicationModel:
    return ApplicationModel()

All versions of the application have a [ApplicationModel] class: a single entry point from the web layer to the business layer, which keeps the lists of doctors and clients in memory. These lists are requested by almost all pages (the drop-down list of doctors in the calendar, the list of patients in the booking window, the administration pages), and rarely change.

A [Python] process retains its objects from one request to the next (Example 20): the [Flask] version therefore simply stored these lists in the attributes of a single object. The header comment explains why this version instead stores them in the cache of [Django] (Example 20): a production server runs multiple processes, and each would have its own copy of the lists.

  • line 36: the class inherits the contract [Metier], just like [MetierService]: the views call the same methods, regardless of which class serves them;
  • Lines 45–49: [get_or_set(clé, fonction, timeout)] returns the value stored under this key; if it does not exist, it calls the function (here, a bound method from the business layer, passed without parentheses, which reads the list from the database), stores its result in the cache indefinitely ([timeout=None]), and returns it. The first request that needs the list reads it from the database; subsequent requests find it in the cache. The cache stores the list serialized by module [pickle] (Example 20), and reconstructs it upon retrieval, along with the already-loaded relationships: each person’s account, retrieved via the join [select_related("compte")] from layer DAO. The reconstructed objects are copies: they are used for display, never for writing (the business layer always re-reads from the database what it modifies);
  • lines 53–54: the physician associated with an account, retrieved from the cache list. [next(générateur, None)] returns the first element produced by the generating expression, or [None] if there is none (example 06);
  • Lines 57–90: The other methods in the contract simply delegate to the business layer. An account’s client ([get_client_by_user_id]) is always retrieved from the database, not from the cache: the most recent data is what matters (a patient who has just modified or deleted their account);
  • Lines 94–120: the updates. Each write operation for a doctor or client clears the relevant list ([delete]): the next query that needs it will read it from the database again. This is the whole point of a single entry point: the rule “a write operation updates the cache” is implemented only here. If the write operation fails (a [MetierErreur]), the exception exits the method before the [delete]: the list is not overwritten; it has not changed. An application that writes to the database via a different path (another program, another version of the application using the same database) would leave the cache out of date: in that case, it would suffice to clear the [var/cache] folder;
  • Lines 124–126: The facade provider, modeled after the business layer provider: a single object, created on the first request. [functools.cache], imported under the name [une_fois], stores the result of a function (example 06): the function [application()] executes only once, then always returns the same object.

docs.title: 11.13.2. web/outils.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/outils.py: small utility functions of the web layer:
#    - dates: "yyyy-mm-dd", days "Wednesday, September 23, 2026";
#    - input: reading a positive integer or a date sent by the browser;
#    - user: the logged-in user and their patient (Client model).
# =========================================================================

import re
from datetime import date, datetime

from django.utils import dateformat

from modeles.models import Client
from securite.erreurs import SessionInvalide
from securite.utilisateur import UtilisateurConnecte

from .application import application


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- dates
# the date, if [texte] is a valid date in the yyyy-mm-dd format; None otherwise.
# strptime rejects dates that do not exist ("2026-02-30")
def date_valide(texte: str | None) -> date | None:
    if texte is None or not re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}", texte):
        return None
    try:
        return datetime.strptime(texte, "%Y-%m-%d").date()
    except ValueError:
        return None


# "2026-09-23"
def iso(jour: date) -> str:
    return jour.isoformat()


# "Wednesday, September 23, 2026" / "mercredi 23 septembre 2026", in the language
# is active (see web/middleware.py). dateformat.format formats a date like the
# date filter in the templates: l is the day of the week spelled out, j is the day,
# F is the month spelled out, Y is the year; the names are translated by Django
def formater_jour(jour: date) -> str:
    return dateformat.format(jour, "l j F Y")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- input
# "3" -> 3; "", "abc", "-2", "+2", None -> None
def entier_positif(valeur: str | None) -> int | None:
    if valeur is None or not re.fullmatch(r"\d{1,9}", valeur):
        return None
    n = int(valeur)
    return n if n > 0 else None


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- user
# the logged-in user. Protected views are only called if it exists (see
# security/middleware.py); as a precaution, its absence is treated as an
# expired session
def utilisateur(request) -> UtilisateurConnecte:
    if request.utilisateur is None:
        raise SessionInvalide()
    return request.utilisateur


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The patient (Client model) corresponding to the logged-in user.
#
# The token JWT contains only the ID of COMPTE (users.id). For a role USER,
# the corresponding client is identified using the clients.user column.
#
# If there is no match, it means the account has been deleted since the login, so
# even though its token is still valid: it is treated as an expired session.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
def patient_connecte(request) -> Client:
    client = application().get_client_by_user_id(utilisateur(request).user_id)
    if client is None:
        raise SessionInvalide()
    return client


# the client’s address IP
def ip(request) -> str:
    return request.META.get("REMOTE_ADDR", "")

Some utility functions that all views require:

  • Lines 23–29: the date of a parameter [aaaa-mm-jj] or [None]. Two checks: the format (a regular expression; [fullmatch] requires that the entire string match), then the existence of the date: [strptime] raises a [ValueError] for February 30;
  • lines 41–42: “Wednesday, September 23, 2026” or “mercredi 23 septembre 2026,” depending on the language of the query. [dateformat.format] formats a date like the [date] filter in the templates (example 16), using the same codes; the names of the days and months are translated by [Django] itself, in the active language;
  • lines 47–51: a query parameter is a string, or [None]. Only digits are accepted (up to nine: a reasonable number that the database accepts), and the number must be strictly positive;
  • lines 58–61: the logged-in user, determined by the middleware [Authentification]. Protected views are called only for an authenticated user (access control), but the absence of a user is still handled as an expired session;
  • lines 73–77: the patient ([Client]) associated with the logged-in user. The token contains only the account ID; the client is identified by the [clients.user] column. If it does not exist, the account has been deleted since the user logged in: [SessionInvalide] (the [PageErreur] middleware, discussed later);
  • lines 81–82: the client’s address (IP) for the attempt limiter. [REMOTE_ADDR] is the address of the machine that established the connection. Behind a reverse proxy (see “A production server”), this would always be the proxy’s address: you would then need to read the header it adds ([X-Forwarded-For]), and only the one it adds, since the browser can send any header.

docs.title: 11.13.3. web/contextes.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/contextes.py: a context processor (see Example 15): the variables that
# TOUTES the pages require:
#    - user: the logged-in user (or None), for the navigation bar;
#    - menu: the navigation bar menu items, which depend on the role.
#
# The menu is calculated in ICI, in Python, and not in the template: "Doctors" and
# "Clients" appear only for the ADMIN. This is merely a display convenience: the
# real security comes from the access rules (a user USER who types /doctors into the
# manually gets a 403 page).
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.urls import reverse
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

from securite import auth


# a menu entry: its URL, its label, and whether it corresponds to the current page
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EntreeMenu:
    url: str
    libelle: str
    active: bool


def utilisateur(request):
     # the user established by the Authentication middleware. As a precaution, if
     # is missing (an error page due to an error that occurred before this middleware), it is
     # read directly from the token, so that the navigation bar is complete
    connecte = getattr(request, "utilisateur", None)
    if connecte is None and request.COOKIES.get(auth.COOKIE):
        connecte = auth.utilisateur(request.COOKIES[auth.COOKIE])
    return {"utilisateur": connecte, "menu": menu(request, connecte)}


# the menu entries: (route name, label, path prefixes for
# for which the entry is active)
def menu(request, connecte):
    if connecte is None:
        return []
    entrees = []
    if connecte.est_patient:
         # active for /my-space ET /my-account
        entrees.append(("espace", _("Mon espace"), ["/mon-"]))
    entrees.append(("agenda", _("Agenda"), ["/agenda"]))
    if connecte.est_admin:
        entrees.append(("medecins_liste", _("Médecins"), ["/medecins"]))
        entrees.append(("clients_liste", _("Clients"), ["/clients"]))
     # any: true if any of the prefixes match
    return [EntreeMenu(reverse(route), libelle, any(request.path.startswith(p) for p in prefixes))
            for route, libelle, prefixes in entrees]

A context processor (Example 15), declared in [config/settings.py]: the variables required by all pages, within the context of all templates:

  • [utilisateur]: the logged-in user, or [None], for the navigation bar. Usually, this is the one from the [Authentification] middleware; [getattr(objet, nom, défaut)] reads an attribute or returns the default value if it does not exist. As a precaution, if it is missing, the user is read directly from the token (lines 34–35);
  • [menu]: the navigation bar menu entries, which depend on the role (lines 41–54). Each entry is a [EntreeMenu] object (a data class, lines 22–26): the URL (generated by [reverse], example 04), the translated label, and the indicator for the active entry—the one on the currently displayed page—which the template highlights. The [Mon espace] entry is active for all URL entries that begin with [/mon-]: [/mon-espace] and [/mon-compte].

The menu is calculated in [Python], not in the template (there is no logic in the templates; more on this later). Hiding the “Doctors” and “Clients” entries is merely a display convenience: the real protection comes from the access rules.

docs.title: 11.13.4. web/templatetags/rdv.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/templatetags/rdv.py: the tags from our templates (see Example 16), loaded
# by {% load rdv %}.
#
#    {% zone_succes %}: the flash messages from SUCCÈS, at the top of the page;
#    {% zone_erreurs %}: the error area, in BAS on every page, on a pink background
#    light. It lists the three possible sources of error:
#      - [erreur]: the error on the displayed page (invalid date, incorrectly
#        entered, username already taken...), transmitted by the view;
#      - flash error messages, set by the previous view before a
#        redirect (time slot already reserved, deletion denied...);
#      - input errors from an invalid form (see example 19): their
#        messages are displayed next to the fields; here, if there are no other
#        message, a simple phrase: “The form contains errors.”
# =========================================================================

from django import template
from django.contrib import messages as flash
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

register = template.Library()


# takes_context: the function receives the context of the template that calls it; messages:
# the context processor variable for flash messages; level: the level of a message
@register.inclusion_tag("fragments/succes.html", takes_context=True)
def zone_succes(context):
    return {"textes": [m.message for m in context.get("messages", []) if m.level == flash.SUCCESS]}


@register.inclusion_tag("fragments/erreurs.html", takes_context=True)
def zone_erreurs(context):
    textes = [m.message for m in context.get("messages", []) if m.level == flash.ERROR]
    if context.get("erreur"):
        textes.insert(0, context["erreur"])
    formulaire = context.get("formulaire")
     # a LIÉ form (submitted) that is invalid, with no other message
    if not textes and formulaire is not None and formulaire.is_bound and formulaire.errors:
        textes.append(_("Le formulaire contient des erreurs."))
    return {"textes": textes}

Two inclusion tags (example 16), loaded into the templates by [{% load rdv %}]. Each returns a small template (a fragment, discussed later), containing the variables returned by the function:

  • Lines 26–28: [{% zone_succes %}]: success flash messages (example 20), displayed at the top of the page. [takes_context=True]: The function receives the context of the template that calls it, where the message context processor has stored the variable [messages]. [level] is the level of a message ([flash.SUCCESS], [flash.ERROR]...);
  • lines 31–40: [{% zone_erreurs %}]: the error area, at the bottom of each page. It groups the three possible sources of errors: the page error (the variable [erreur], passed by the view and placed at the top of the list by [insert(0, ...)]), flash error messages (set by the previous view before a redirect), and input errors from an invalid form, whose messages are displayed below the fields: the error area then simply displays the phrase, “The form contains errors.” [is_bound]: the form has received an entry (example 19).

Both tags read the same list, with each retaining only one level. A list of messages that has been read is cleared at the end of the request (example 20): each message is displayed only once.

docs.title: 11.13.5. web/middleware.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/middleware.py: two web-layer middleware components (see Example 24).
# =========================================================================

from django.conf import settings
from django.contrib import messages
from django.core.exceptions import BadRequest, PermissionDenied
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import redirect
from django.utils import translation
from django.utils.translation import gettext as _

from securite import auth
from securite.erreurs import SessionInvalide

from .vues.erreurs import page_erreur


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the request language (see Example 22): the one in the [rdvmedecins_langue] cookie
# if it is a supported language, French; otherwise, another language. Placed at the top of the list of
# middleware, it applies to TOUTES requests, even those that result in
# any route (404 page): their error page is in the correct language
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class FixerLangue:
     # the supported languages; the first is the default language
    LANGUES = [code for code, nom in settings.LANGUAGES]

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        langue = request.COOKIES.get(settings.LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME)
        if langue not in self.LANGUES:
            langue = self.LANGUES[0]
        translation.activate(langue)
         # the language of the request, sorted as in LocaleMiddleware (see example 22)
        request.LANGUAGE_CODE = langue
        return self.get_response(request)


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# how errors become HTML pages. Three cases:
#    1. a SessionInvalide (account deleted since login) -> return to the
#       login page, as with an expired session;
#    2. A HTTP error raised by a view: invalid request (BadRequest, 400),
#       insufficient (PermissionDenied, 403), unknown object (Http404) -> the
#       error page, with the original code;
#    3. any other exception (a true error): Django logs it in the
#       log, along with its call stack; in production (DEBUG false), the user
#       sees the 500 error page (handler500, see config/urls.py)—never the
#       ; in development, the Django debug page.
# A HTTP method denied (405) is not an exception: decorators
# require_GET... return an empty 405 response, which __call__ replaces with our page.
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class PageErreur:
    CODES = {BadRequest: 400, PermissionDenied: 403, Http404: 404}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        reponse = self.get_response(request)
        if reponse.status_code == 405 and not reponse.content:
            page = page_erreur(request, 405)
             # the Allow header: accepted methods
            page["Allow"] = reponse["Allow"]
            return page
        return reponse

    def process_exception(self, request, exception):
        if isinstance(exception, SessionInvalide):
            messages.error(request, _("Votre session a expiré : reconnectez-vous."))
            return auth.effacer_jeton(redirect("login"))
        for classe, code in self.CODES.items():
            if isinstance(exception, classe):
                return page_erreur(request, code)
        return None

The two middleware components of the web layer (Example 24). Recall their order in the list [MIDDLEWARE] from [config/settings.py]: [FixerLangue] first, [PageErreur] last.

  • Lines 25–39: the request language; if it matches the language of the [rdvmedecins_langue] cookie, that language is used; otherwise, French is used. This is the [FixerLangue] middleware from Example 16, not [LocaleMiddleware] (Example 22): [LocaleMiddleware] would select the browser’s preferred language if no cookie is present; the other versions of the application always start in French, and this one does the same. The supported languages are read from the [LANGUAGES] setting (line 27, a read-only list executed once when the class is loaded). [translation.activate] (line 36) sets the active language (example 16): the language used for translations, dates, and the [LANGUAGE_CODE] variable in the templates (context processor [i18n], example 22). The language is also stored in [request.LANGUAGE_CODE] (line 38), as is the case with [LocaleMiddleware], for views that need to access it. Placed at the top, this middleware applies to all requests before any other processing: all pages, including error pages, are in the correct language;
  • Lines 62–69: A rejected HTTP method (a GET call to [/logout], which only accepts POST) does not throw an exception: the decorators [require_GET], [require_POST]... return a 405 response with no content. [__call__] replaces it with the error page, retaining the [Allow] header (the accepted methods), which is required in a 405 response;
  • Lines 71–78: Exceptions thrown by views ([process_exception], Example 24). A [SessionInvalide] (the account has been deleted): the “session expired” message, deletion of the token cookie, and the login page. A HTTP error thrown by a view ([BadRequest], [PermissionDenied], [Http404]): the error page, with its code, in both production and development. Any other exception is a true anomaly: the method returns [None], and [Django] handles it itself; it logs it, along with its call stack, and then displays its debug page in development and the 500 error page ([handler500]) in production. The user never sees the call stack of an application in production.
$ curl -si http://localhost:8000/logout
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Allow: POST
...
<!doctype html>
...

Code 405 (Method Not Allowed) is presented to the user as a page not found (the error page message, discussed below). A URL that does not match any route does not go through [PageErreur]: [Django] directly calls the [handler404] view in production and displays its detailed 404 page in development (Example 24).

docs.title: 11.14. Dictionaries
docs.text:
The interface text is the same as in other versions of the application, which stored it in JSON files under keys ([LOGIN.TITLE] referred to the text in [Connexion]). [Django] works differently (example 22): the original text, in French, is written directly in the code ([_("Connexion")]) and in the templates ([{% translate "Connexion" %}]); it serves as the key in the English dictionary, the file [locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po]:

#: web/views/agenda.py:202 web/views/espace.py:75
msgid "Rendez-vous annulé."
msgstr "Appointment cancelled."

#: web/views/auth.py:62 web/views/espace.py:142
#, Python format
msgid "Trop de tentatives infructueuses. Réessayez dans %(minutes)d minute."
msgid_plural ""
"Trop de tentatives infructueuses. Réessayez dans %(minutes)d minutes."
msgstr[0] "Too many failed attempts. Try again in %(minutes)d minute."
msgstr[1] "Too many failed attempts. Try again in %(minutes)d minutes."

This file, containing approximately 140 texts, is not reproduced here. It was generated by the command [python manage.py makemessages -l en], which retrieves all texts marked with the code and templates, then completed manually, and compiled into [django.mo] by [python manage.py compilemessages] (example 22). The compiled [django.mo] file is delivered with the code: the application runs without the [gettext] tools. There is no French dictionary: text without a translation is displayed as-is, that is, in French.

The [#:] lines indicate where each text is used; [#, python-format] identifies a text with parameters ([%(minutes)d]), whose translation [makemessages] will verify. [gettext] enables something the other versions could not do: the plural (“1 minute,” “15 minutes”), with [ngettext] in the code (see below) and [msgid_plural] in the dictionary (example 22). Some text has been added: the message on page 419, which the other versions do not have.

Form error messages are translated in the same way (see below). The messages that [Django] generates itself (number too large, invalid email address, etc.) are translated using the dictionaries from [Django].

docs.title: 11.15. Forms
docs.text: “Person” forms are [Django] forms (examples 18 and 19): a class describes the fields and their constraints; the view builds the form with the user’s input ([PersonneForm(request.POST)]), then checks whether it is valid ([is_valid]). An invalid form is redisplayed, showing the user’s input and error messages below the fields (excluding passwords: a [PasswordInput] field is never redisplayed). The anti-CSRF token is verified for all forms by the [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware.

docs.title: 11.15.1. web/formulaires.py
docs.text:
# =========================================================================
# web/formulaires.py: "person" forms and their constraints (see
# examples 18 and 19). Three forms share the same identity fields
# (title, first name, last name):
#
#    ChampsPersonneFor         m title, first name, last name
#     ├─ PersonneFo           rm + login / password FACULTATIFS, version
#                                 │ (ADMIN adds or modifies a doctor/client)
#     ├─ InscriptionFo        rm + login / password / confirmation OBLIGATOIRES
#                                 │ (a patient creates an account)
#     └─ MonCompteFo          rm + username, optional new password,
#                                  ACTUEL password required, version
#                                  (a patient modifies their account)
#
# The daughter classes HÉRITENT of ChampsPersonneForm: they have its fields, plus
# their own fields. The validated entry (cleaned_data) is converted to DonneesPersonne
# for the business layer using the `données()` method.
#
# Labels, tooltips, and error messages are translated (gettext_lazy,
# see business/erreurs.py). The maximum lengths are those of the columns SQL.
# =========================================================================

from django import forms
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.core.validators import RegexValidator
from django.utils.translation import gettext_lazy as _

from metier.donnees import DonneesPersonne
from securite import mots_de_passe

TITRES = ["Mr", "Mme", "Melle"]
# minimum length of a password CHOISI entered by a patient
MOT_DE_PASSE_MIN = 6

# login: lowercase letters, numbers, period, hyphen, underscore—30 characters maximum
FORMAT_LOGIN = RegexValidator(r"^[a-z0-9._-]{1,30}$", message=_(
    "30 caractères au plus : lettres minuscules non accentuées, chiffres, point, tiret, souligné."))


# bcrypt only considers the first 72 bytes of a password (see
# security/mots_de_passe.py); an accented letter takes up two bytes in UTF-8
def longueur_bcrypt(valeur: str) -> None:
    if len(valeur.encode()) > mots_de_passe.MAX_OCTETS:
        raise ValidationError(_("Le mot de passe ne doit pas dépasser 72 caractères."))


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# a username is always in lowercase: the field converts the input AVANT to
# validation (to_python is called before the validators)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class LoginField(forms.CharField):
    def to_python(self, value):
        texte = super().to_python(value)
        return texte.lower() if texte else texte


# a password field: never redisplayed, and spaces are not removed
# (strip=False: a space is part of the password)
def champ_mot_de_passe(label, required, help_text="", min_length=None):
    messages = {
        "required": _("Le mot de passe est obligatoire."),
         # %(limit_value)d: the minimum length, inserted by Django into the message
        "min_length": _("Le mot de passe doit comporter au moins %(limit_value)d caractères."),
    }
    return forms.CharField(label=label, required=required, help_text=help_text, strip=False,
                           min_length=min_length, validators=[longueur_bcrypt],
                           error_messages=messages,
                           widget=forms.PasswordInput(attrs={"maxlength": 72,
                                                             "autocomplete": "new-password"}))


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the parent class of our forms (see Example 18): each input field receives
# the appropriate Bootstrap class (CSS); signal() highlights in red (class
# is-invalid) the fields with input errors, and those where an error MÉTIER
# (a username that’s already taken...), with the message appearing at the bottom of the page
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class FormulaireBootstrap(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for champ in self.fields.values():
            classe = "form-select" if isinstance(champ.widget, forms.Select) else "form-control"
            champ.widget.attrs["class"] = classe

    def signaler(self, champs=()):
         # errors: data entry errors; |: the union of two sets
        for nom in set(self.errors) | set(champs):
            if nom in self.fields:
                self.fields[nom].widget.attrs["class"] += " is-invalid"
        return self


class ChampsPersonneForm(FormulaireBootstrap):
    titre = forms.ChoiceField(label=_("Titre"), choices=[(t, t) for t in TITRES], error_messages={
        "required": _("Choisissez un titre dans la liste."),
        "invalid_choice": _("Choisissez un titre dans la liste.")})
    prenom = forms.CharField(label=_("Prénom"), max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": _("Le prénom est obligatoire."),
        "max_length": _("Le prénom ne doit pas dépasser 20 caractères.")})
    nom = forms.CharField(label=_("Nom"), max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": _("Le nom est obligatoire."),
        "max_length": _("Le nom ne doit pas dépasser 20 caractères.")})

     # validated input -> the data expected by the business layer. An empty field
     # that is empty is treated as None (or None: an empty string is "false")
    def donnees(self) -> DonneesPersonne:
        d = self.cleaned_data
        return DonneesPersonne(d["titre"], d["nom"], d["prenom"], d.get("login") or None,
                               d.get("password") or None, d.get("version"))


# a doctor’s or client’s form (ADMIN): username and password
# FACULTATIFS; creation=False: the update form, with the version
class PersonneForm(ChampsPersonneForm):
    def __init__(self, *args, creation=True, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
         # an empty field is accepted: validators apply only to entered values
        self.fields["login"] = LoginField(
            label=_("Login"), required=False, max_length=30, validators=[FORMAT_LOGIN],
            help_text=_("Facultatif : par défaut, le nom en minuscules.") if creation
            else _("Laisser vide pour ne pas le changer."),
            widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "autocomplete": "off"}))
        self.fields["password"] = champ_mot_de_passe(
            _("Mot de passe"), False,
            _("Facultatif : par défaut, identique au login.") if creation
            else _("Laisser vide pour ne pas le changer."))
        self.fields["password"].widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"
         # update: the version of the displayed record, in a hidden field (the
         # optimistic lock)
        if not creation:
            self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)


# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# the password and its confirmation: two fields, compared using `clean` (see
# example 19). Common to registration (required) and the patient’s account
# (optional: empty = password unchanged)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
class AvecConfirmation(ChampsPersonneForm):
    def ajouter_mots_de_passe(self, obligatoire: bool):
        self.fields["login"] = LoginField(
            label=_("Login"), max_length=30, validators=[FORMAT_LOGIN],
            help_text=_("Lettres minuscules non accentuées, chiffres, point, tiret, souligné.")
            if obligatoire else "",
            error_messages={"required": _("Le login est obligatoire.")},
            widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "autocomplete": "username"}))
        self.fields["password"] = champ_mot_de_passe(
            _("Mot de passe") if obligatoire else _("Nouveau mot de passe"), obligatoire,
            _("Au moins 6 caractères.") if obligatoire else _("Laisser vide pour ne pas le changer."),
            min_length=MOT_DE_PASSE_MIN)
        self.fields["confirmation"] = champ_mot_de_passe(_("Confirmation du mot de passe"), obligatoire)
        self.fields["confirmation"].error_messages["required"] = _("Confirmez le mot de passe.")
        for nom in ("password", "confirmation"):
            self.fields[nom].widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"

     # Validation of the entire form, following the validation of each field
    def clean(self):
        donnees = super().clean()
        password = donnees.get("password")
        confirmation = donnees.get("confirmation")
        if password and password != confirmation and "confirmation" not in self.errors:
            self.add_error("confirmation", _("La confirmation ne correspond pas au mot de passe."))
        return donnees


# "Create a customer account": username, password, and confirmation OBLIGATOIRES
class InscriptionForm(AvecConfirmation):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.ajouter_mots_de_passe(obligatoire=True)


# "Manage My Account" (one patient): username required, new password
# optional, password ACTUEL required, version
class MonCompteForm(AvecConfirmation):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self.ajouter_mots_de_passe(obligatoire=False)
         # the password ACTUEL, required for any account changes
        self.fields["current_password"] = forms.CharField(
            label=_("Mot de passe actuel"), strip=False,
            help_text=_("Obligatoire pour enregistrer une modification."),
            error_messages={"required": _("Saisissez votre mot de passe actuel.")},
            widget=forms.PasswordInput(attrs={"class": "form-control", "maxlength": 72,
                                              "autocomplete": "current-password"}))
        self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)

Three forms share the identity fields (title, first name, last name): the administrator form (for a doctor or a client), the client account creation form, and “Manage My Account.” The header comment outlines their inheritance hierarchy: their common parent class, [ChampsPersonneForm], defines the identity fields; each child adds its own. The labels, tooltips, and messages are translated lazily ([gettext_lazy]): they are defined when the module loads and translated each time the page is displayed, into the language of the request (the business layer, mentioned above).

  • Lines 36–37: a login form, a validator ([RegexValidator]) that checks for a regular expression. A validator is a callable object that raises [ValidationError] for an incorrect value (Example 19); it is assigned to a field via its parameter [validators];
  • lines 42–44: a validator written as a simple function. [bcrypt] considers only the first 72 bytes of a password (the security layer, discussed above): the limit applies to bytes, not characters ([encode()]: an accented letter takes up two bytes in [UTF-8]);
  • lines 51–54: a username is always in lowercase. A custom field, a child of [CharField], redefines [to_python], the method that converts the input into a Python value: it is called before the validators, which therefore check the input after it has already been converted. [super().to_python(value)] first performs the standard processing of [CharField] (removing spaces surrounding the input);
  • Lines 59–69: a function that creates a password field. [strip=False]: spaces are not removed; they can be part of a password. [min_length]: the minimum length, which [Django] checks itself; its message contains [%(limit_value)d], the parameter that [Django] places there. The [PasswordInput] widget is never redrawn; the HTML attribute [maxlength] prevents users from typing more than 72 characters; [autocomplete="new-password"] instructs the browser to prompt for a new password, rather than filling the field with the saved password;
  • lines 78–90: the parent class of our forms (Example 18). Its constructor assigns each input field the appropriate subclass of CSS ([form-select] for a list, [form-control] for the others). The [signaler] method adds the [is-invalid] class (a red border) to fields with input errors and to those flagged by a business rule error (a username that is already in use): [set(a) | set(b)] is the union of two sets. It returns the form itself: the views call it when passing the form to the template;
  • lines 93–102: the title, a list ([ChoiceField], example 18); the first and last names, 20 characters maximum, the column widths SQL (the [maxlength] field in the input area is added by [Django] itself). Each error message is replaced with our own ([error_messages], example 19). [invalid_choice] is the message for a value not included in the list (a manually crafted query). The spaces surrounding an entry are removed by [CharField];
  • lines 106–109: the validated input ([cleaned_data]), converted to [DonneesPersonne] for the business layer: the business layer is not familiar with forms. [d.get(clé)] returns [None] for a field that the form does not have; [x or None] converts an empty string to [None] (unchanged, or the default value);
  • lines 114–131: the administrator’s form. The parameter [creation], which we have created, distinguishes between creation and modification; it is placed after [*args]: it is a required parameter ([PersonneForm(request.POST, creation=False)]). The fields specific to this form are added by the builder in the [self.fields] dictionary: their options depend on [creation] (the tooltips differ: “by default, the name is in lowercase,” “leave blank to keep it unchanged”). The username and password are optional ([required=False]): a validator applies only to an entered value, so an empty field is accepted. Only the “modify” field has the hidden “version” field (the optimistic lock, business layer);
  • lines 139–163: the password and its confirmation, which are common to both registration and the patient’s account. The two fields are compared using the form’s [clean] method (Example 19), which is called after each field is validated. [add_error] attaches the message to the confirmation field, unless that field already contains an error (“Confirm the password.”): only one message per field. The minimum length requirement applies only to a password chosen by a patient (6 characters);
  • lines 167–170: creating a customer account: login, password, and confirmation are required;
  • lines 175–186: “Manage My Account”: the new password is optional (blank: unchanged), the current password is required. It is not validated by the form, but by the view: an incorrect password must be counted by the attempt limiter as a failed login. [autocomplete="current-password"]: Here, the browser may suggest the saved password.

# =========================================================================
# web/modeles_vues.py: “view models”: objects constructed
# all at once by a view, which the template simply reads. This rule is followed by
# all pages: no logic in the templates. The views prepare
# formatted data ("Ms. Marie PELISSIER", "8:00 - 8:20",
# selection = True...) and already filtered according to the user’s role; the
# templates simply place them in the HTML.
# =========================================================================

from dataclasses import dataclass


# an option from a drop-down list (doctor, patient)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class OptionVue:
    id: int
    libelle: str
    selectionne: bool


# a row in the displayed calendar (a time slot)
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LigneAgenda:
    id_creneau: int
    horaire: str            # "8:00 - 8:20"
    libre: bool
     # displayed name for a booked slot; None = “Reserved”
    patient: str | None
    moi: bool               # the logged-in patient’s appointment
    reservable: bool        # Display the "Book" button?
    url_reserver: str
     # filled in only if the "Cancel" button is displayed
    id_rv: int | None


# Calendar displayed: doctor, day, rows
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AgendaVue:
    medecin: str            # "Ms. Marie PELISSIER"
    jour: str               # "Wednesday, September 23, 2026"
    lignes: list[LigneAgenda]


# the time slot booking window
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReservationVue:
    id_creneau: int
    horaire: str
     # ADMIN / DOCTOR: patients to choose from
    clients: list[OptionVue]
     # USER: the patient is the patient themselves
    patient: str | None


# An upcoming appointment in the patient’s account
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RendezVousVue:
    id: int
    jour: str               # "Wednesday, September 23, 2026"
    horaire: str            # "8:00 - 8:20"
    medecin: str            # "Ms. Marie PELISSIER"
    url_agenda: str         # the doctor’s schedule for that day

The file [web/modeles_vues.py] contains the view templates: objects constructed by a view, which the template simply reads. The rule, followed by all pages: no logic in the templates. The views prepare data that is already formatted (“Ms. Marie PELISSIER,” “8:00 – 8:20”) and already filtered according to the user’s role; the templates place them in the HTML. These are fixed data classes ([frozen=True], example 08): once constructed, a view template never changes.

  • Lines 14–18: An option from a drop-down list: the ID, the label, and whether the option is selected?
  • Lines 22–33: A calendar entry: a time slot, and what the logged-in user is authorized to view and do with it. [patient] is populated only if the user is authorized to see the patient’s name; [reservable] indicates whether to display the “Book” button; [id_rv] indicates whether to display the “Cancel” button;
  • lines 37–52: the displayed calendar and the booking window: for the administrator and doctors, the list of patients to choose from; for a patient, their own name;
  • lines 56–62: an upcoming appointment in the patient’s section.
