docs.title: 5.1.1. The configuration: config/settings.py
docs.text:
# config/settings.py: the configuration for Example 22

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-e%uqntr!nz5i2w(d^_-cwr6w=w^2z^mx6vpvpgsg91qvp)bnzl"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

# the default language and the languages supported by the application
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
LANGUAGES = [
    ("fr", "Français"),
    ("en", "English"),
]
# the application's DICTIONNAIRES folders (.po files, compiled into .mo files)
LOCALE_PATHS = [BASE_DIR / "locale"]
# the cookie that stores the selected language (this is also the default name)
LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME = "django_language"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "pages",
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
     # LocaleMiddleware: the language of each request, read from the language cookie,
     # otherwise from the browser’s Accept-Language header, or otherwise LANGUAGE_CODE
    "django.middleware.locale.LocaleMiddleware",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "OPTIONS": {
            "context_processors": [
                "django.template.context_processors.request",
                 # the variable LANGUAGE_CODE: the language of the request
                "django.template.context_processors.i18n",
            ],
        },
    },
]

STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / "static",
    BASE_DIR.parent / "commun" / "static",
]
  • Line 14: the application’s default language, which is used for requests that do not specify a language (Example 08). This is also the language of the template texts; therefore, French does not require a dictionary;
  • Lines 15–18: the languages supported by the application;
  • Line 20: [LOCALE_PATHS], the folders where [Django] searches for the application's dictionaries, in addition to the [locale] folders for each application (including those for [Django] itself). Each dictionary is stored in a [<langue>/LC_MESSAGES] folder, under the name [django.po] (and [django.mo]): this is the organization required by [gettext];
  • line 22: the name of the cookie that stores the selected language. [django_language] is the default value; we include it here so it is visible;
  • lines 29–33: the [LocaleMiddleware] middleware from [Django] replaces our [FixerLangue] middleware from Example 16. For each request, it selects the language from among those specified in the [LANGUAGES] setting: the language specified in the language cookie, if one exists; otherwise, the browser’s preferred language, based on the [Accept-Language] header (Example 12); otherwise, [LANGUAGE_CODE]. It activates it ([translation.activate], Example 16), and stores it in [request.LANGUAGE_CODE]. Finally, it adds the header [Content-Language] (the page’s language) to the response, along with the header [Vary: Accept-Language], which notifies caches that the response depends on this header;
  • line 43: the context processor [i18n] adds the variables [LANGUAGE_CODE] (the language of the request), [LANGUAGES], and [LANGUAGE_BIDI] (true for a language written from right to left) to the templates.

docs.title: 5.1.2. The dictionary: locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po
docs.text:
# locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po: the English dictionary from Example 22.
# msgid: the original text, as written in the templates (in French);
# msgstr: its translation. This file is compiled into django.mo (the file read by
# Django) using the command: python manage.py compilemessages
msgid ""
msgstr ""
"Language: en\n"
"MIME-Version: 1.0\n"
"Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8\n"
"Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit\n"
"Plural-Forms: nplurals=2; plural=(n != 1);\n"

#: templates/fragments/navbar.html:6
msgid "Accueil"
msgstr "Home"

#: templates/fragments/navbar.html:7
msgid "Produits"
msgstr "Products"

#: templates/pages/accueil.html:4 templates/pages/accueil.html:7
msgid "Bienvenue"
msgstr "Welcome"

#: templates/pages/accueil.html:9
#, python-format
msgid "Bonjour %(nom)s !"
msgstr "Hello %(nom)s!"

#: templates/pages/accueil.html:11
#, python-format
msgid "Nous sommes le %(date)s."
msgstr "Today is %(date)s."

#: templates/pages/produits.html:4 templates/pages/produits.html:7
msgid "Nos produits"
msgstr "Our products"

#: templates/pages/produits.html:9
msgid "Produit"
msgstr "Product"

#: templates/pages/produits.html:9
msgid "Prix"
msgstr "Price"

#: templates/pages/produits.html:21
#, python-format
msgid "%(n)s produit au catalogue."
msgid_plural "%(n)s produits au catalogue."
msgstr[0] "%(n)s product in the catalogue."
msgstr[1] "%(n)s products in the catalogue."

A [.po] file is a sequence of entries, separated by blank lines:

  • lines 1–4: a comment;
  • lines 5–11: the header entry: an empty string ([msgid ""]), whose “translation” ([msgstr]) contains the dictionary information: the language, the character set, and the language’s plural rule ([Plural-Forms]: in English, two forms, the second for any number other than 1);
  • lines 13–15: a standard entry: [msgid] is the source text, as written in the template; [msgstr] is its translation. The line [#:] indicates where the text was found (a template and a line): this is a comment for the translator;
  • lines 25–28: text containing a variable. In the dictionary, a variable is written as [%(nom)s] (the syntax for format strings from [Python], example 10); the line [#, python-format] flags this to the tools. The translation may reposition the variable or change the punctuation surrounding it (the exclamation point is not preceded by a space in English);
  • lines 47–52: a plural form: [msgid] is the singular form, [msgid_plural] is the plural form, and each form in the translation is numbered ([msgstr[0]], [msgstr[1]]), in the order specified by the rule [Plural-Forms]. In French, 0 and 1 are singular, whereas in English 0 is plural (“0 products”): [gettext] knows this, thanks to this rule. This is an improvement over the “product(s)” used in previous versions of the case study.

This file is not written by hand. The command:

python manage.py makemessages -l en

scans the project’s templates and the [Python] code, extracts all text marked “to be translated,” and creates or updates the [locale/en/LC_MESSAGES/django.po] file: new text is added to it with an empty translation, and existing translations are preserved. All that remains is to write the translations, either in a text editor or in specialized software ([Poedit], for example). The command:

python manage.py compilemessages

It then compiles each [.po] file into a [.mo] file—a binary file that is quick to read—which is the one used by [Django]. You must restart the server after a compilation: the dictionaries are loaded once and for all. These two commands use the programs from [gettext] ([xgettext], [msgfmt]...), which must be installed (for [Linux], the [gettext] package; for [Windows], for example, the binaries distributed on the mlocati.github.io website). Since the [django.mo] file is provided with the example, it is not necessary to install these packages to run it.

docs.title: 5.1.3. Language selection: routes and views
docs.text:
# config/urls.py: the main routing table

from django.urls import path, re_path

from pages import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("", views.accueil, name="accueil"),
    path("produits", views.produits, name="produits"),
     # re_path: a route described by a regular expression; another language
     # neither "fr" nor "en" matches the route (404)
    re_path(r"^langue/(?P<code>fr|en)$", views.changer_langue, name="langue"),
]
  • Line 12: [re_path] describes a route using a regular expression, rather than the syntax of [path] (Example 02). [^] and [$] mark the start and end of the path; [(?P<code>fr|en)] is a named group: the text it recognizes—[fr] or [en] (the vertical bar means “or”)—is passed to the view in the [code] parameter. Another language does not match any route: [/langue/de] returns a 404 error.
# pages/views.py: Views are not aware of the language; they provide
# data; the templates translate and format it

from datetime import date

from django.conf import settings
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.utils.http import url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import Produit


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return render(request, "pages/accueil.html", {"nom": "Marie", "aujourdhui": date(2026, 9, 23)})


@require_GET
def produits(request):
    return render(request, "pages/produits.html", {"produits": [
        Produit("Clavier", 2500),
        Produit("Souris", 1250),
        Produit("Écran", 114900),
    ]})


# GET /language/en: saves the language selection in a cookie, then returns to the
# previous page
@require_GET
def changer_langue(request, code):
    reponse = redirect(page_d_origine(request))
     # the cookie: valid for one year, unreadable by the JavaScript on the page (httponly),
     # never sent with a request POST originating from another site (SameSite Lax)
    reponse.set_cookie(settings.LANGUAGE_COOKIE_NAME, code, max_age=365 * 24 * 3600,
                       httponly=True, samesite="Lax")
    return reponse


# the page from which the user came (Referer header); if it belongs to the CE site: redirect
# to any address in the request would allow sending
# the user to another site (“open redirect” vulnerability)
def page_d_origine(request):
    referer = request.headers.get("Referer", "")
     # url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme: true for a relative address or an
     # absolute URL where the machine is the one making the request
    if url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(referer, allowed_hosts={request.get_host()}):
        return referer
    return "/"
  • Lines 14–25: The home and product views do not know the language; they provide raw data (a name, a date, amounts in cents). Translation and formatting are handled by the templates. The class [Produit] has a name and a price in cents; the library [formats] is the one from Example 16: its filter [date_longue] writes a date in the “full” format of the active language (“Wednesday, September 23, 2026,” “Wednesday, September 23, 2026”), and its filter [monnaie] displays an amount;
  • lines 30–37: the language-change view responds by redirecting the user back to the page they came from; the user is returned to their original page in the new language;
  • lines 35–36: The response includes a cookie, which the browser will send back with every request. [set_cookie] receives its name, value, and options: [max_age], its lifetime in seconds (one year); [httponly=True] makes it invisible to the [JavaScript] on the page; [samesite="Lax"] prevents the browser from sending it with a POST request originating from another site. It is added to the response as a [Set-Cookie] header;
  • lines 43–49: the original page is specified by the [Referer] header in the request (the misspelled version, with a single [r], is that of the HTTP standard), which the browser populates with the URL from the page that contained the link. But this header comes from the client, which can put anything in it. Blindly redirecting to this address would turn our application into an open redirect: a malicious link bearing our domain name could send the user to a malicious site. The function [url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme] in [Django] ([django.utils.http]) checks whether an address is relative or whether it points to one of the allowed machines (in this case, the one from the request: [request.get_host()]); otherwise, the user is redirected to the home page.

[Django] also provides a ready-made view for changing the language, [django.views.i18n.set_language], which performs the same task using a form (POST); we wrote our own to demonstrate it and to allow language switching via a simple link.

docs.title: 5.1.4. Translating in Templates
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{% load static %}
{# LANGUAGE_CODE: the language of the request, "fr" or "en" #}
<html lang="{{ LANGUAGE_CODE }}">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# the title: the [titre] block of the page, already translated #}
  <title>{% block titre %}{% endblock %}</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css' %}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'css/styles.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {% include "fragments/navbar.html" %}
    <main>
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • line 4: the page’s [lang] attribute indicates its language to browsers, search engines, and screen readers; [LANGUAGE_CODE] is the language of the request, provided by the context processor [i18n];
  • Line 9: The page title is provided by the page itself, already translated (block [titre]).
{# i18n: the translation tag library #}
{% load i18n %}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <div class="navbar-nav me-auto">
    {# translate: the translation of a text into the request language #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'accueil' %}">{% translate "Accueil" %}</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'produits' %}">{% translate "Produits" %}</a>
  </div>
  {# get_available_languages: the languages in the LANGUAGES setting, as (code, name) pairs #}
  {% get_available_languages as langues %}
  <div class="btn-group btn-group-sm">
    {% for code, nom in langues %}
      {# the current language is highlighted #}
      <a class="btn {% if code == LANGUAGE_CODE %}btn-primary{% else %}btn-outline-primary{% endif %}"
         href="{% url 'langue' code %}" title="{{ nom }}">{{ code|upper }}</a>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
</nav>
  • line 2: the translation tags are in the [i18n] library, which each template must load (example 16);
  • lines 6–7: The [{% translate %}] tag returns the translation of a text into the language of the request (or the text itself, if it has no translation);
  • lines 10–17: The [{% get_available_languages %}] tag stores the languages from the [LANGUAGES] setting—pairs of (code, name)—in a variable, which the loop then parses ([for code, nom in langues]). One button per language, which links to the [/langue/<code>] view. The current language is highlighted ([btn-primary], solid button).
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load i18n formats %}

{% block titre %}{% translate "Bienvenue" %}{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>{% translate "Bienvenue" %}</h1>
  {# blocktranslate: text containing variables {{ name }} #}
  <p>{% blocktranslate %}Bonjour {{ nom }} !{% endblocktranslate %}</p>
  {# with: the date, formatted first (filter date_longue, see Example 16), then inserted into the text #}
  <p>{% blocktranslate with date=aujourdhui|date_longue %}Nous sommes le {{ date }}.{% endblocktranslate %}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 4: the [titre] block, translated, for the parent template;
  • line 9: the [{% blocktranslate %}] tag translates text containing variables: [{{ nom }}] becomes [%(nom)s] in the dictionary. Only simple variables are allowed here (no filters or periods);
  • line 11: a calculated variable can therefore only be included in the text via [with]: the date, formatted in the query language by the filter [date_longue], is stored in the variable [date] in the text.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load i18n formats %}

{% block titre %}{% translate "Nos produits" %}{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>{% translate "Nos produits" %}</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>{% translate "Produit" %}</th><th class="text-end">{% translate "Prix" %}</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>
      {% for produit in produits %}
        <tr>
          <td>{{ produit.nom }}</td>
          {# the currency filter from Example 16: the format depends on the language #}
          <td class="text-end">{{ produit.prix_centimes|monnaie }}</td>
        </tr>
      {% endfor %}
    </tbody>
  </table>
  {# plural: `count` selects the form based on the number `n`; `plural` separates the forms #}
  <p>{% blocktranslate count n=produits|length %}{{ n }} produit au catalogue.{% plural %}{{ n }} produits au catalogue.{% endblocktranslate %}</p>
{% endblock %}
  • line 15: the filter [monnaie], whose result depends on the language;
  • line 21: the plural. [count n=produits|length] returns the number that determines the form ([length], example 14); the [{% plural %}] tag separates the singular form from the plural form, written in the source language. Product names, however, are not translated: they are data that, in a real-world application, would come from a database.

Outside of templates, translation is handled by the functions of the [django.utils.translation] module: [gettext("Accueil")] (often imported under the short name [_]: [_("Accueil")]), [ngettext] for the plural, and [gettext_lazy], a “lazy” translation performed only when the text is used: this is the one to use for text defined when a module is loaded (the label of a form field, for example), when the language of the request is not yet known. The case study uses it.

docs.title: 5.1.5. Execution
docs.text:
The home page, in French (the default language), then in English after clicking the “EN” button:

The products page, in both languages. The amounts follow the conventions of each language:

The language switch, as seen with [curl]. The option [-H] provides the header [Referer] that the browser would send:

curl -i -H "Referer: http://localhost:8000/produits" http://localhost:8000/language/en

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: http://localhost:8000/languages/en
Vary: Accept-Language
Content-Language: fr
Set-Cookie: django_language=en; expires=Mon, 27 Sep 2027 17:37:43 GMT; HttpOnly; Max-Age=31536000; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

The redirect takes you back to the original page, and the cookie is set to last for one year. The response itself is still in French ([Content-Language: fr]): the language was only selected when the request arrived, before the cookie existed. A [Referer] that points to another site does not allow you to be redirected there:

curl -i -H "Referer: https://pirate.example/piege" http://localhost:8000/language/en

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /
...

The user returns to the home page and remains on our site. Finally, the home page, requested with the cookie [django_language=en] (option [-b] of [curl]):

curl -b "django_language=en" http://localhost:8000/

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Welcome</title>
...
    <a class="nav-link" href="/">Home</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="/produits">Products</a>
...
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>Hello Marie!</p>
  <p>Today is Wednesday, September 23, 2026.</p>
...

The cookie is not signed: it is transmitted in plain text, and the user can modify it. This is not a problem: it contains no confidential information, and [LocaleMiddleware] only accepts the languages specified in the [LANGUAGES] setting. The following example illustrates the level of trust that can be placed in a cookie. Without a cookie, [LocaleMiddleware] reads the browser’s [Accept-Language] header: [curl -H "Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9" http://localhost:8000/] renders the page in English. The two mechanisms thus combine naturally: the browser’s language on the first visit, followed by the language the user has chosen. A third, common approach places the language in the URL ([/en/produits]): the [i18n_patterns] function of [Django] then prefixes the routes with the language, and [LocaleMiddleware] reads it from the path. This case study focuses on the cookie.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
The document’s PDF is |HERE|.

The document’s codes are |HERE|.

This document is a product of Anthropic’s IA Claude. It follows the document “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Symfony] Web Framework” (2026), which itself followed the documents “Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Laravel] Web Framework,” "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Flask] Web Framework," "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [Spring MVC] Web Framework," "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [ASP.NET Core MVC] Web Framework," and "Step-by-Step Introduction to the [NestJS] Web Framework" (2026). This document leaves the [PHP] world to return to the [Python] language, that of the [Flask] course, but with a framework of a completely different scale:

  • the [Symfony] framework is replaced by the [Django] 6.1 framework, using the [Python] language (version 3.12 or later);
  • the [Twig] views are replaced by the [Django] templates, written in its template language, DTL (Django Template Language);
  • The Form and Validator components of [Symfony] are replaced by the forms from [Django] (the [django.forms] module), which describe both the fields of a HTML form, their conversion, and their validation;
  • the Security component of [Symfony] (firewall, authenticators, roles) is replaced by middleware and decorators written specifically for this purpose, using the [PyJWT] library for JWT tokens and the [bcrypt] library for passwords;
  • the event listeners in [Symfony] are replaced by the middleware in [Django], which wraps the processing of each request, and by its signals;
  • ORM is replaced by ORM from [Django], still based on [MySQL].

The document closely follows the structure of the [Symfony] course: first, numerous small projects, each focused on a single concept, followed by a comprehensive case study—a web application for scheduling appointments at a medical practice—with all files fully commented. The examples have the same numbers and cover the same topics as in courses [Symfony], [Laravel], [Flask], [Spring MVC], and [ASP.NET Core MVC]: a reader familiar with one of these courses can compare the frameworks on a case-by-case basis. However, this is not necessary: this document stands on its own and assumes no prior knowledge of these frameworks. The only prerequisites are a basic understanding of web programming (the HTTP protocol, the HTML language) and the fundamentals of the [Python] language (variables, lists, dictionaries, functions, classes, modules). The less common features of [Python] used in the examples (decorators, data classes, type annotations, context managers, generators, etc.) are explained when they first appear.

docs.title: 1.1. Django’s Role in a Web Application
docs.text:
A web application is often built in layers, with each layer communicating only with its immediate neighbors:

  • the web layer receives requests HTTP from the browser and returns pages HTML to it. This is the layer that [Django] helps us write;
  • the business layer contains the application’s business rules (e.g., “a patient can have only one upcoming appointment”). It knows nothing about the web: it could just as easily serve a command-line application;
  • the data access layer (DAO layer, for Data Access Object) reads from and writes to the database. We will use the ORM (Object Relational Mapper) from [Django], which maps table rows to [Python] objects.

The web layer itself follows the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern. This is where you need to pay attention to the terminology, because [Django] does not use the terms from MVC in their usual sense. The documentation for [Django] refers to the MTV architecture (Model–Template–View):

  • what MVC calls the controller (C), [Django] calls a view: it is a [Python] function (or a class) that processes a type of request (for example, [GET /agenda]). A view reads the request parameters, invokes the business layer, and then selects the page to display. In the [Symfony] course, this was an action of a controller;
  • what MVC calls the view (V), [Django] calls a template: a file HTML that contains expressions [{{ ... }}] and instructions [{% if %}], [{% for %}]..., which the template engine replaces with data. In the [Symfony] course, it was a view ([Twig]);
  • what MVC calls the model (M)—the set of data passed to the page—[Django] calls the template context: a dictionary [Python];
  • finally, what [Django] calls a model is a class [Python] that represents a database table (the file [models.py]): what [Symfony] used to call an entity.

This document uses the terminology from [Django], since that is the terminology used in its documentation, error messages, and file names ([views.py], [templates], [models.py]): here, a view is therefore always the function [Python] that processes a request, and a template is the file HTML that generates the page. The term “model” has two meanings, which the context always distinguishes: in Chapter 2, a view’s model refers to the data it receives from the request, described by a class; starting in Chapter 7, a model of [Django] is a class of ORM. Finally, the term “page template” (or “layout”) refers to the common template from which other pages inherit (Example 15).

The processing of a request follows the numbered steps in the diagram:

  • 1: The browser sends a request, such as HTTP;
  • 2: The web server receives the request and passes it to the [Django] application via the [application] object in the [config/wsgi.py] file. During development, this server is the one that includes [Django], launched by the command [python manage.py runserver]; in production, it will be a [Python] server, such as [gunicorn] or [waitress], often placed behind a web server such as [nginx]. [Django] routes the request through a series of middleware components, classes from [Django], and the application that intervene before and after the view (session management, anti-CSRF protection, language settings, security, etc.), and compares the requested path to the application’s routes—described in the [urls.py] files—to select the view responsible for handling this request: this is routing;
  • 3: The view requests the data it needs from the business layer; the business layer, if necessary, contacts the DAO layer, which queries the [MySQL] database in SQL, via ORM;
  • 4: The view builds the context (the M model) and instructs the template engine to generate the page (function [render]);
  • 5: The page HTML generated by the template is the view’s response, which [Django] returns to the browser after passing it back through the middleware.

[Django] is, along with [Flask], one of the two major web frameworks in the [Python] world. Free and open-source, it was created in 2003 by Adrian Holovaty and Simon Willison at the Lawrence Journal-World, a newspaper in Kansas, and released in 2005. It is named after the jazz guitarist Django Reinhardt. It is now developed by a community under the auspices of the Django Software Foundation and runs wherever [Python] ([Windows], [Linux], [macOS]) runs. High-traffic websites use it ([Instagram], [Pinterest], [Mozilla]...). Its motto, “the web framework for perfectionists in a hurry,” clearly reflects its approach: whereas [Flask] provides only a core that is supplemented by extensions, [Django] comes “batteries included”: routing, templates, forms and validation, ORM, and database migrations, sessions, messages, translations, caching, protection against common attacks (CSRF, injection SQL, click hijacking), and even an automatically generated data administration interface. All of this forms a cohesive package, documented in one place, and designed to work together. Compared to [Symfony], [Django] makes different choices: no service container or dependency injection, but [Python] modules that are imported; configuration written in [Python], in a single file ([settings.py]), rather than in [YAML]; views that are simple functions. [Django] also follows a regular release schedule: one release approximately every eight months, and a “long-term support” release ” (LTS) every two years (5.2 in 2025, 6.2 in 2027), and deprecation notices that always precede the removal of a feature by two versions. [Django] can create servers that return JSON to a [JavaScript] client ([Angular], [React], [Vue.js], [Flutter]...), often with the extension [Django REST framework], unlike traditional web applications, where the server generates the HTML pages and the browser simply displays them. This document examines this second use case.

One key difference with [PHP] explains a great deal about [Django]: the application is loaded once, when the server starts up, and then remains in memory to process all subsequent requests (Example 01). What is built at startup (the configuration, the routing table, the objects stored in module variables) is shared by all requests. This is the opposite of [Symfony], which rebuilt the application with each request: we will return to this point frequently, particularly in the chapter on data scopes.

docs.title: 1.2. Tools Used
docs.text:
The examples were written and tested using the following tools (their installation is described in the appendix):

  • [Python] 3.13 (any version 3.12 or later is suitable: this is the minimum requirement for [Django] 6.1);
  • [pip], the library manager for [Python], and the [venv] module, which creates virtual environments (both included with [Python]);
  • the [Visual Studio Code] editor, along with the Microsoft extensions [Python] and [Pylance] (code analysis, execution, debugging) and an extension for [Django] templates (syntax highlighting);
  • a modern browser ([Chrome], [Firefox], [Edge]);
  • the command-line tool [curl], which displays raw HTTP responses (it is included with [Windows] 10 and 11);
  • SGBD [MySQL] 8.4 or later (or [MariaDB] 10.11 or later), for example, the one from [Laragon] under [Windows], starting with the chapter on data access, and for the case study.

[Django] and the other libraries are not part of [Python]: [pip] downloads them from the PyPI repository (Python Package Index) during installation (so you must be connected to the Internet on that day), and installs them in a virtual environment, a project-specific folder (see below). Each project describes its libraries in a [requirements.txt] file. The following table lists the main ones, along with the versions used:

LibraryRoleVersion[Django]The framework: development server, routing, views, middleware, templates, forms, sessions, messages, translations, cache, ORM; It installs the two libraries it needs: [asgiref] (the link between synchronous and asynchronous code) and [sqlparse] (formatting of displayed SQL orders)6.1.1[Babel]Formatting of numbers, amounts, and dates according to the language (example 16)2.18.0[PyJWT]JWT tokens (chapter on authentication)2.15.0[mysqlclient]The [MySQL] driver used by [Django] (Example 28 and Case Study)2.3.0[bcrypt]Password hashing (case study)5.0.0

[Django] is typically installed by [pip], after which a project is created using the [django-admin startproject] command, which is installed by [Django] (see appendices):

pip install django
django-admin startproject mon_projet

This command creates a folder named [mon_projet] that contains a file named [manage.py] and a package named [mon_projet] consisting of five files ([settings.py], [urls.py], [wsgi.py], [asgi.py], [__init__.py]). Applications are then added using the [python manage.py startapp nom] command, which creates a folder containing seven files. This is how you start a real project. For learning purposes, this method has one drawback: the generated file [settings.py] already contains about a hundred lines of code, which activate about ten applications and seven middleware components—the purpose of which is not yet clear. The examples in this document therefore start from the other end: Example 01 is the smallest possible [Django] application, and each example adds only the files and settings it needs, written and commented on by hand. The case study at the end follows the structure of a standard [Django] application.

docs.title: 1.3.1. Installing Laragon
docs.text:
The case study requires the SGBD [MySQL]. Laragon can provide this and more. As of September 2026, Laragon is available at URL and [Download Laragon – Fast & Modern Dev Environment]. Laragon includes tools that allow you to install a web server and the SGBD and [MySQL]:

  • in [1], an Apache web server;
  • into [2], the SGBD [MySQL];
  • to [3], a messaging tool that we will not be using;
  • [4] starts all services (Apache, [MySQL], MailPit);
  • [5] displays the web page for URL and [http://localhost]. By default, this URL refers to the <laragon-install>\www folder, where <laragon-install> is the Laragon installation folder;
  • in [6], launches the HeidiSQL tool, which allows you to manage MySQL databases. We will use this tool to create the database used in the case study;
  • In [7], open a terminal where all the binaries needed for Laragon are located in PATH;
  • in [8], opens a Windows Explorer window in the folder associated with URL and [http://localhost];

The Laragon installation folder contains the following items:

In [1], the [bin] folder contains numerous applications:

  • In [1], the Apache web server;
  • in [2], a command-line terminal;
  • in [3], a [git] client that allows you to manage different versions of a project;
  • in [4], a database manager;
  • [5], an email manager;
  • in [6], the SGBD and [MySQL];
  • [7], another web server;
  • in [8], [node.js] to run JavaScript scripts;
  • [9], a text editor;
  • [10], the PHP interpreter;
  • [11], the [Python] interpreter;
  • [12], a cache server;

Laragon comes with a comprehensive development environment. In this course, we will use only SGBD, [MySQL], [6], and the [heidisql] tool to manage it graphically. Laragon’s [Python] [11] interpreter may not be recent enough for [Django] 6.1 (you need version 3.12 or later): Instead, we will install [Python] from its official website (see appendices), checking the box in the installer that adds [python] to the machine’s existing PATH.

The README mentioned in the case study indicates that you must enter the following commands in a terminal window opened in the application’s folder:

python -m venv .venv

to create a virtual environment named [Python] and a folder named [.venv], where the application libraries will be installed;

.venv\Scripts\activate

to activate this environment in the terminal (under [Linux] and [macOS]: [source .venv/bin/activate]). The terminal prompt then begins with [(.venv)];

pip install -r requirements.txt

to install the [Python] libraries required for the case study ([Django], [mysqlclient], [PyJWT], [bcrypt]) ;

python manage.py runserver 8081

to run the case study. If you use a [PowerShell] terminal in VSCode, [PowerShell] may refuse to run the activation script, displaying a message stating that “script execution is disabled on this system.” To enable this, for your user account only, enter the following once in a [PowerShell] terminal:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser

You will need to restart VSCode for this change to take effect. Alternatively, in VSCode, you can select a terminal named [Command Prompt] instead of [PowerShell], where the script [activate] runs without this authorization.

To create the [MySQL] database required for the case study, proceed as follows:

  • In [1], all services must be started;
  • in [2], the [Database] option allows you to manage the database;

The option [Database] launches a utility called HeidiSQL:

  • In [1], you can select various SGBD options. The default value provided is SGBD MySQL. This is acceptable;
  • in [2], you log in to HeidiSQL;

  • In [1-2], run the file SQL, then select the file [dbrdvmedecins2.sql], which you’ll find in the folder [django-sept-2026/rdvmedecins2-django/database]:

Running the [3] file will create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database used by the case study. To view it, run F5 within HeidiSQL to refresh the display.

Note: The following screenshots show a database named [dbrdvmedecins], whereas the case study database is named [dbrdvmedecins2]. The two databases are virtually identical, so we determined it was unnecessary to take new screenshots.

The database [dbrdvmedecins] has been created. Here is its content:

  • in [1-3], the table [clients];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the row’s version number. This number increments each time the row is modified;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • in [1-3], the table [medecins];
    • [id] is the primary key of the table;
    • [version] is the version number of the row;
    • [titre, nom, prenom] identifies the person;

  • In [1-3], the table of doctors’ appointment time slots:
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: row version number;
    • [id_medecin]: foreign key referencing the doctor’s primary key;
    • [hdebut, mdebut]: hour and minutes of the appointment start time. Thus, [8,20] means 8:20 a.m.
    • [hfin, mfin]: hour and minutes of the end of the consultation.

  • In [1-3], the [rv] table of scheduled appointments;
    • [id]: primary key;
    • [version]: version number;
    • [jour]: appointment date;
    • [id_creneau]: foreign key referencing the primary key of the appointment time slot. Since a time slot is linked to a doctor, we know which doctor is handling this appointment;
    • [id_client]: foreign key to the number (primary key) of the customer making the inquiry;

  • in [1-3], the table [users], which lists the users authorized to use the application;
    • [id, version]: primary key, version number;
    • [login, password]: user credentials;
    • [nom]: user name;
    • [role]: the user’s role. [ADMIN] has full access; [MEDECIN] views their own calendar; [PATIENT] (a client of the firm) schedules and cancels their own appointments;

docs.title: 1.3.2. Performing the Case Study
docs.text:
Reviewer’s note: I advise the reader to carry out the case study immediately as described below. Once you fully understand the role of this appointment application, ask your favorite IA to modify the application as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own consultation slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons;

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. Ask IA to provide you with the new application code and the SQL script to create the new database. To do this, you’ll need to provide them with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database.

Also, I haven’t reviewed the course created by Claude. He had already produced the courses [NestJS], [ASP.NET Core MVC], [Spring MVC], and [Flask], all of which were perfect. I assumed the same was true for this one. If you run into a problem understanding something, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand. Claude, for example, is very good at this. You may need to “upload” the example you don’t understand to him.

End of note.

The case study at the end of this document is a complete application. Readers will likely want to see it in action before delving into the details of the framework: here’s how to run it. It’s located in the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder, next to the [exemples] folder:

django-sept-2026/
├── exemples/
└── rdvmedecins2-django/

You must have installed [Python] (version 3.12 or later), [Visual Studio Code], and [MySQL] (see appendices). Then:

  • Create the [dbrdvmedecins2] database by running the [rdvmedecins2-django/database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql] script. Using [Laragon], open the [HeidiSQL] tool (Database button), then run the script via the File / Run SQL menu (see above). At the command line, from the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder:
mysql -u root < database/dbrdvmedecins2.sql
  • Open the [rdvmedecins2-django] folder in [Visual Studio Code] (File menu / Open Folder), then open a terminal (Terminal menu / New Terminal);
  • create the application’s virtual environment, activate it, and then install its libraries: [pip] reads the file [requirements.txt], downloads [Django] and the other libraries, and places them in the application’s [.venv] folder (takes a few tens of seconds). Under [Windows]:
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
  • Under [Linux] and [macOS], the second command is [source .venv/bin/activate]. [Visual Studio Code] displays a window asking if you want to use this environment for the folder: accept; any terminals opened afterward will activate it automatically;
  • verify the connection to the database. The application connects to [MySQL] on [127.0.0.1], port 3306, using the user [root] without a password (the default settings for [Laragon]). If your [root] account has a password, enter it in the application’s [.env] file, on the [DB_PASSWORD=] line;
  • run the application:
python manage.py runserver 8081
  • [Django] displays:
Watching for file changes with StatReloader
Performing system checks...

System check identified no issues (0 silenced).
September 27, 2026 - 19:30:12
Django version 6.1.1, using settings 'config.settings'
Starting development server at http://127.0.0.1:8081/
Quit the server with CTRL-BREAK.

The development server is listening on port 8081 of the machine ([127.0.0.1], i.e., [localhost]). Each request received will be logged in the console, along with the SQL commands sent to the database;

  • Open the URL [http://localhost:8081] in a browser:

  • Log in with one of the demo accounts, whose password is the same as the username: [admin] (administrator), [pelissier], [tatou], [dupont] (doctors), [martin], [durand], [bistrou], [german] (patients). You must also enter the characters from the image, in uppercase or lowercase.

Upon startup, the command [runserver] verifies the project and, along with [MySQL], connects to the database for this purpose: if the database is inaccessible, the server does not start, and the console displays the error at the end of a long call stack. If the message is [(2002, "Can't connect to server on '127.0.0.1' (10061)")], it means that [MySQL] has not started; with [(1045, "Access denied for user 'root'@'localhost' (using password: NO)")], it means the password is incorrect; with [(1049, "Unknown database 'dbrdvmedecins2'")], it means the script SQL was not executed. If the [python manage.py runserver] command fails with the message [ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'], it means the virtual environment is not enabled (or that [pip install] has not been executed); if the error message is [Error: That port is already in use.], it means that port 8081 is already in use (by another version of the application, for example). The application’s [README.md] file describes other scenarios. Stop the application using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal ([Ctrl-Pause] under [Windows], as stated in the message from [Django], but [Ctrl-C] also works).

Once the reader fully understands the purpose of this appointment application, they can ask their favorite IA to modify it as follows: from now on, each doctor will be able to:

  • set their own appointment slots between two dates. This will allow them to adjust their schedule as needed;
  • remove certain time slots from the calendar for a given day—for example, if they are unavailable for personal reasons.

The modification is not straightforward because it involves a change to the database structure. You must request the new application code and the SQL script—which creates the new database—from the IA, providing them with the ZIP file containing the complete project as well as the SQL script for the old database. Similarly, if you encounter a point in this document that you don’t understand, the solution is always the same: ask your favorite IA to explain what you don’t understand, providing the relevant example if necessary.

The case study at the end of the document demonstrates how to use the application and then explains each of its files.

docs.title: 1.4. Examples
docs.text:
The examples are stored in the [exemples] folder, with one subfolder per example:

exemples/
├── 01-structure/
├── 02-routage/
├── ...
├── 28-couches/
├── commun/
│   ├── static/
│   │   └── bootstrap/
│   └── README.md
└── requirements.txt

Each example is a small application ([Django]) that runs on its own. All examples use the same libraries, described in the file [exemples/requirements.txt]:

# the example libraries, installed once and for all in the
# virtual environment in the examples folder: pip install -r requirements.txt
Django==6.1.1
mysqlclient==2.3.0
PyJWT==2.15.0
Babel==2.18.0
  • lines 1–2: comments; in [Python], as in this file, a comment extends from [#] to the end of the line;
  • Lines 3–6: the libraries, one per line, with their exact versions: [Django] itself, [mysqlclient] (access to [MySQL], Example 28), [PyJWT] (the JWT tokens, example 25), and [Babel] (language-specific formatting of numbers and dates, example 16). The [==] operator enforces the version; [>=6.1,<6.2] would accept all 6.1.x versions. The two libraries required by [Django] ([asgiref], [sqlparse]) are not listed: [pip] installs them automatically, since [Django] declares them.

[Python] recognizes only one library folder per interpreter. To ensure that each project has its own libraries in the appropriate versions, a virtual environment is created: a folder containing a lightweight copy of the interpreter and its own library folder ([Lib/site-packages] under [Windows], [lib/python3.13/site-packages] elsewhere). To run the examples, create a virtual environment and install their libraries there once and for all in a terminal opened to the [exemples] folder:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

[python -m venv .venv] executes the [venv] module from [Python], which creates the environment in the [.venv] folder. The script [activate] (under [Linux] and [macOS]: [source .venv/bin/activate]) modifies the terminal’s PATH: the commands [python] and [pip] then refer to those in the environment, and the prompt begins with [(.venv)]. [pip install -r requirements.txt] installs the file’s libraries. The [exemples/.venv] environment is shared by all 28 examples: it is activated in each terminal where you want to run one. The command [pip list] displays the installed libraries, and [deactivate] deactivates the environment. The [commun] folder contains the CSS [Bootstrap] ([commun/static/bootstrap]) framework, shared by the examples that format their pages (starting with Example 15).

Almost all of the examples have the same structure—that of a standard [Django] project, stripped down to the essentials. For example, the structure of Example 13:

13-premiere-vue/
├── config/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── wsgi.py
├── pages/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── modeles.py
│   ├── urls.py
│   └── views.py
├── templates/
│   └── pages/
│       ├── inconnu.html
│       └── index.html
└── manage.py
  • [manage.py]: the project’s command-line tool, which specifically launches the development server (Example 01);
  • [config]: the project’s configuration package: its settings ([settings.py]), its routes ([urls.py], Example 02), and its entry point for a web server ([wsgi.py]). A project created by [django-admin startproject] gives this package the project’s name; we refer to it as [config] in all examples to clarify its role;
  • [pages]: an application [Django]: a package [Python] that groups together views ([views.py]), their routes ([urls.py]), and the classes they require. A project is a collection of applications, which the [INSTALLED_APPS] setting lists (example 02);
  • [templates]: the templates (from the chapter on templates).

To run an example, open a terminal in its folder (in [Visual Studio Code]: right-click the example folder, then select "Open in the built-in terminal"), activate the virtual environment for the examples ([..\.venv\Scripts\activate] under [Windows], [source ../.venv/bin/activate] elsewhere), and type:

python manage.py runserver

All examples listen on port 8000: you can only run one at a time (or you must change the port: [python manage.py runserver 8001]). Stop the server using [Ctrl-C] in the terminal. You don’t need to restart the server after modifying a [Python] file or a template: the development server monitors the project files and restarts automatically when any of them change (example 01).

When you open the [exemples] folder in [Visual Studio Code], you must specify the virtual environment’s interpreter for the [Python] extension (Python command: Select Interpreter from the command palette, [Ctrl-Maj-P], then [.venv\Scripts\python.exe]): The [Pylance] extension then analyzes all files using the environment’s libraries, including [Django]: In each file, you can take advantage of code completion, navigation to the definition of a class or function ([F12] key), and error reporting. Since all examples include a [config] package, the analysis may confuse the packages of two examples; this has no impact on execution, since each example is run separately from its own folder. To avoid this confusion, simply open the example’s folder directly.

docs.title: 1.5. Document Contents
docs.text:
The document is organized as follows:

Each example introduces only a few new concepts, and the chapters build on one another: it is best to read them in order. The case study, on the other hand, draws on all the concepts from the previous chapters: whenever relevant, its commentary refers to the example where the concept was introduced. docs.title: 9. Layered Architecture and Data Access
docs.text:
The previous examples kept their data in memory. A real application stores it in a database and is organized into layers (see the diagram in the introduction):

  • the web layer (views, forms, templates): read the request, call the business layer, select the template;
  • the business layer: business rules;
  • the DAO layer (Data Access Object): database queries.

Each layer is aware only of the layer below it, and as few details about it as possible: the web layer is unaware of the queries, and the business layer is unaware of the HTML. This separation makes each layer easier to understand, test, and evolve. Example 28 applies this to managing a list of people: it is, on a smaller scale, the management of doctors and clients from the case study.

In [Python], database access is organized across several layers:

  • the DB-API 2.0 standard (PEP 249) of [Python] defines a common interface for all SGBD: open a connection, obtain a cursor, execute a SQL command, and read rows. Each SGBD has its own driver: for [MySQL] (and [MariaDB]), [Django] recommends [mysqlclient], a library written in C, installed by the [requirements.txt] example file;
  • ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) from [Django] maps classes (models) to database tables and converts the read rows into objects. It manages connections and transactions, generates the SQL commands itself—tailored to each SGBD—and translates errors from each driver into common exceptions (a uniqueness constraint violation becomes a [IntegrityError], regardless of the SGBD). It follows the so-called Active Record pattern: each object knows how to save itself ([personne.save()]) and delete itself ([personne.delete()]), and each class has a handler ([Personne.objects]) from which requests are sent. This is the model for [Eloquent], the ORM of [Laravel]; [Doctrine], the ORM derived from [Symfony], on the other hand, followed the Data Mapper pattern, where a separate object reads and saves the entities.

ORM, derived from [Django], is part of [Django] and is one of its key components: the administration interface, the authentication application, database sessions, and generic views all rely on it. It is the equivalent of [JPA] and [Hibernate] in [Java], [Entity Framework Core] to [C#], or [SQLAlchemy] (used with [Flask]) to [Python]. Note a consequence of how [Django] works: by default, each request opens its own connection to the database (upon its first SQL request) and closes it upon termination (upon the [request_finished] signal, example 24). The [CONN_MAX_AGE] setting allows connections to remain open from one request to the next (persistent connections), and [Django] 5.1 added a true connection pool for [PostgreSQL]. Opening a connection to [MySQL] on the same machine takes only a few milliseconds.

This example requires a running [MySQL] 8.4 or later server (or [MariaDB] 10.11 or later; the minimum versions are [Django] 6.1): The appendix explains how to install one using [Laragon].

docs.title: 9.1.1. The database
docs.text:
The [dbpersonnes] database is created by the SQL script. Using [Laragon], you can run it, for example, in the [HeidiSQL] tool (File menu / Run a SQL file), or from the command line, from the example folder:

mysql -u root < database/dbpersonnes.sql

The [database/dbpersonnes.sql] file:

-- Example 28 database: a single table, [personnes]
-- The script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbpersonnes;
CREATE DATABASE dbpersonnes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_unicode_ci;
USE dbpersonnes;

CREATE TABLE personnes (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
   -- row version, incremented with each modification (see layer DAO)
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  prenom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  nom VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  age INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
   -- No two people can have the same first and last names
  CONSTRAINT unq_personnes_prenom_nom UNIQUE (prenom, nom)
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO personnes (prenom, nom, age) VALUES
  ('Marie', 'Pélissier', 42),
  ('Jacques', 'Bromard', 35),
  ('Philippe', 'Jandot', 58);
  • Line 3: The script is written in [UTF-8]; this is specified to the server so that the accents in the data ([Pélissier]) remain intact;
  • line 5: the character set [utf8mb4] accepts all characters (accents, emojis, etc.). The [utf8mb4_unicode_ci] collation compares strings without distinguishing between uppercase and lowercase letters or accents: for [MySQL], [pelissier], and [Pélissier] are equal;
  • line 11: a version number, incremented each time the line is modified (see “optimistic lock,” below);
  • line 17: a named uniqueness constraint: the database does not allow two people with the same first and last names.

[Django] can also create the tables itself, based on the schemas, using migrations: [Python] files that describe, step by step, the creation and modifications of each table. The [python manage.py makemigrations] command writes these files by comparing the schemas to the state described by the previous migrations; [python manage.py migrate] applies them to the database. This is the standard way of working with [Django]. We maintain a script, SQL, which is common to all versions of the case study and shows exactly what the database contains. Conversely, the command [python manage.py inspectdb] writes the schemas for an existing database: a good starting point, worth reviewing.

  • lines 32–42: the [DATABASES] configuration describes the application’s databases: in this case, a single one, the [default] database. [ENGINE] refers to the engine of [Django] for [MySQL] (which uses the driver [mysqlclient]); followed by the database name, the username, and the password (left blank with the [Laragon] settings: if your server has a password, enter it here), the hostname, and the port. [OPTIONS] passes the character set for communication with the server—the database’s character set—to the driver;
  • lines 44–55: the templates, with [APP_DIRS] for the form templates (example 18) and the message context processor (example 20);

It follows the format of the [logging.config] module: destinations ([handlers]: in this case, the console, via a [StreamHandler], which writes to the error output), and logs ([loggers]), identified by their names. The log [django.db.backends] receives, in debug mode only, every SQL command sent to the database, along with its duration: we send this to the console at level [DEBUG] (the most detailed). [disable_existing_loggers: False] stores the logs that [Django] configures itself.

There is nothing else to configure: the modules in the three layers import each other (the web layer imports the business layer, which imports the DAO layer), and the ORM layer establishes the connection to the database itself when it needs to.

docs.title: 9.1.3. The Person model: people/models.py
docs.text:
# people/models.py: a row in the [personnes] table, a MODÈLE Django

from django.db import models


# a Django model: a class that inherits from models.Model; each class attribute
#, which is a CHAMP (models.XxxField), corresponds to a column in the table
class Personne(models.Model):
     # the primary key, generated by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT)
    id = models.AutoField(primary_key=True)
     # the VERSION for the row, incremented with each modification (see the DAO layer)
    version = models.IntegerField(default=0)
     # the columns VARCHAR(30) and INT
    prenom = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    nom = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    age = models.IntegerField()

     # Meta: information about the model itself
    class Meta:
         # the table name (default: personnes_personne, application_modèle)
        db_table = "personnes"
         # the table already exists (script database/dbpersonnes.sql): Django does not create it
        managed = False
         # the order of the rows when the query does not specify one
        ordering = ["nom", "prenom"]

     # the text representing the object (in the console, messages, etc.)
    def __str__(self):
        return f"{self.prenom} {self.nom}"

The file is named [models.py]: this is where [Django] looks for the models of an application declared in [INSTALLED_APPS].

  • Line 8: A template is a class that inherits from [models.Model];
  • Line 10: The primary key, generated by the database ([AutoField]: the [AUTO_INCREMENT] of [MySQL]). [Django] would add it automatically if it were not declared (a field [id], of the type chosen by the setting [DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD]); we include it here for clarity. It is equal to [None] until the object has been inserted;
  • line 12: the row version. The ORM from [Django] does not have a built-in optimistic lock: it is written by the DAO layer (see below);
  • lines 14–16: the columns. Each class attribute that is a field in the model ([models.XxxField]) corresponds to the column of the same name; the column type is inferred from the field type ([CharField]: [VARCHAR], of length [max_length]; [IntegerField]: [INT]). As in a form (example 08), the fields are declared as attributes of the class, but they are not the same fields: those in [django.db.models] describe columns, while those in [django.forms] describe form fields;
  • lines 19–25: the inner class [Meta] provides information about the template itself. [db_table]: the table name (otherwise, [Django] would take the application name followed by the model name, [personnes_personne]). [managed = False]: The table already exists, and [Django] does not manage it: [makemigrations] will not generate any creation or modification migrations for it. [ordering]: the order of rows when a query does not specify one;
  • lines 28–29: the method [__str__] (Example 12) returns the text representing the object: [str(p)], or [{p}] in an f-string, returns [Marie Pélissier].

A model is an ordinary class to which methods and properties can be added. The ORM, on the other hand, populates the attributes based on the lines read and generates the commands SQL from the attributes.

docs.title: 9.1.4. The DAO layer: people/dao.py
docs.text:
# people/dao.py: the DAO layer, requests, no handling rules

from django.db.models import F

from .models import Personne


# SELECT ... FROM people ORDER BY last name, first name. objects: the GESTIONNAIRE of the model,
# from which all queries originate; all() returns a QuerySet, a query that is
# executed only when its results are read (here, via `list`)
def lister() -> list[Personne]:
    return list(Personne.objects.all())


# SELECT ... FROM people WHERE id = ?; None if the person does not exist
def lire(id: int) -> Personne | None:
    return Personne.objects.filter(id=id).first()


# a person with the same first and last name, other than [sauf_id]. filter: the conditions
# WHERE ; exclude: the conditions WHERE NOT
def homonyme(prenom: str, nom: str, sauf_id: int = 0) -> Personne | None:
    return Personne.objects.filter(prenom=prenom, nom=nom).exclude(id=sauf_id).first()


# INSERT INTO people ...: create constructs the object and saves it
def inserer(prenom: str, nom: str, age: int) -> Personne:
    return Personne.objects.create(prenom=prenom, nom=nom, age=age)


# UPDATE people SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?: the
# row is modified only if its version has not changed since it was read (VERROU
# OPTIMISTE). F("version") refers to the column itself, in the order SQL. update
# returns the number of modified rows: 0 if the version has changed
def modifier(id: int, version: int, prenom: str, nom: str, age: int) -> bool:
    lignes = Personne.objects.filter(id=id, version=version).update(
        prenom=prenom, nom=nom, age=age, version=F("version") + 1)
    return lignes == 1


# DELETE FROM people WHERE id = ?
def supprimer(personne: Personne) -> None:
    personne.delete()

The DAO layer contains only queries, with no business rules. Each function begins with [Personne.objects], the model manager, from which all queries originate.

  • Lines 11–12: [all()] returns a [QuerySet]: an object that describes a query without executing it. The query is sent to the database only when its results are needed (here, when [list] iterates through them): a [QuerySet] is said to be lazy. It can thus be populated before execution ([filter], [exclude], [order_by]...), with each method returning a new [QuerySet]. The order is that of [Meta.ordering];
  • Lines 16–17: [filter(id=id)] adds the condition [WHERE id = ...]; [first()] executes the query, limited to one row ([LIMIT 1]), and returns the first object, or [None]. ([Personne.objects.get(id=id)] would return the object, but would throw the exception [Personne.DoesNotExist] if it did not exist, and the shortcut [get_object_or_404], example 03, would return a 404 error);
  • Lines 22–23: Several conditions in [filter] are combined by [AND]; [exclude] adds a condition [NOT]. The named parameters refer to the fields ([prenom=...]); suffixes specify the comparison: [age__gte=18] ([>=]), [nom__startswith="P"], [nom__iexact=...] (case-insensitive)... The values are transmitted to the database separately and are never copied into the text of the order SQL, which makes injection impossible SQL;
  • lines 27–28: [create] constructs the object and saves it ([INSERT]); after insertion, ORM stores the ID generated by the database in the object. This is equivalent to [p = Personne(prenom=..., ...)] followed by [p.save()];
  • lines 35–38: the update, with its optimistic lock. [update] updates all rows specified by [QuerySet] in a single operation using a single [UPDATE] command, and returns the number of updated rows. The filter has two conditions: the ID and the read version. If another query has modified the row in the meantime—causing its version to change—[UPDATE] does not modify any rows, and the function returns [False]. This is the principle of optimistic locking: nothing is locked, but concurrent modifications are detected. The expression [F("version") + 1] refers to the column itself, in the order SQL ([version = version + 1]): the calculation is performed by the database, not in [Python] based on a value read earlier;
  • Lines 42–43: the deletion: [delete()] sends the [DELETE] from the object’s line.

Unlike [Doctrine], ORM from [Django] does not have a handler that compares each read object to its original state in order to save only the modified columns: [save()] rewrites all columns of the object (or those of its parameter [update_fields]). This is simpler and more predictable; [update] allows you to write exactly in the desired order.

docs.title: 9.1.5. The business layer: people/metier.py
docs.text:
# people/metier.py: the MÉTIER layer, the business rules, and only those.
# Every write operation is a TRANSACTION: validated (COMMIT) if the function
# completes normally, or canceled (ROLLBACK) if an exception occurs

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django.db import IntegrityError, transaction

from . import dao
from .models import Personne

HOMONYME = "Une personne porte déjà ces prénom et nom."
MODIFIEE = "Cette fiche a été modifiée entre-temps : rechargez-la."
INCONNUE = "Cette personne n'existe pas (ou plus)."


# a business rule rejects the operation; the message is intended for the user
class MetierErreur(Exception):
    pass


# a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DonneesPersonne:
    prenom: str
    nom: str
    age: int


def lister() -> list[Personne]:
    return dao.lister()


def lire(id: int) -> Personne:
    personne = dao.lire(id)
    if personne is None:
        raise MetierErreur(INCONNUE)
    return personne


# with transaction.atomic(): the block is executed within a transaction. The
# database uniqueness constraint (two simultaneous inserts) triggers IntegrityError, which becomes a
# business error
def ajouter(donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
             # Rule 1: No two people can have the same first and last names
            if dao.homonyme(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom):
                raise MetierErreur(HOMONYME)
            return dao.inserer(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, donnees.age)
    except IntegrityError as e:
        raise MetierErreur(HOMONYME) from e


def modifier(id: int, version: int, donnees: DonneesPersonne) -> Personne:
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
            personne = lire(id)
             # Rule 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else
            if personne.version != version:
                raise MetierErreur(MODIFIEE)
            if dao.homonyme(donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, id):
                raise MetierErreur(HOMONYME)
             # the UPDATE ... WHERE version = ... does not modify anything if another request has
             # modified the row since we read it
            if not dao.modifier(id, version, donnees.prenom, donnees.nom, donnees.age):
                raise MetierErreur(MODIFIEE)
            return lire(id)
    except IntegrityError as e:
        raise MetierErreur(HOMONYME) from e


def supprimer(id: int) -> Personne:
    with transaction.atomic():
        personne = lire(id)
        dao.supprimer(personne)
        return personne
  • lines 12–14: messages from business rules;
  • lines 18–19: an exception class specific to the business layer: a business rule rejects the operation, and the exception message is intended for the user. It inherits from [Exception] without adding anything to it; only its name matters;
  • lines 23–27: a person’s data, as transmitted by the web layer to the business layer: a simple object, unrelated to [Django];
  • lines 34–38: a nonexistent person is a business error;
  • lines 44–52: Rule No. 1: No two people may have the same first and last names. The rule is verified before writing to the database, and a [MetierErreur] exception is thrown if it is not followed. But this verification is not sufficient: two simultaneous requests could both verify that there is no namesake, and then both proceed to insert the record. The database’s uniqueness constraint then rejects the second [INSERT], and the ORM raises a [IntegrityError], which is transformed into the same [MetierErreur]. The database is the last line of defense. [raise ... from e] links the original exception to the new one: the log will show both;
  • lines 55–70: Rule No. 2: Do not modify a record that has been modified in the meantime by someone else. The update form carries the version of the record that was read (in a hidden field); if it differs from the current version, the record has changed since it was displayed. There remains the case where the concurrent modification occurs between reading line 58 and saving line 66: this is detected by the optimistic lock in layer DAO. The function then re-reads the person record to return the new version;
  • lines 73–77: the deletion sets the person to “deleted” for the confirmation message.

Every operation that writes data is executed within a transaction: [transaction.atomic()], used by [with] (a context manager, example 20), opens a transaction ([BEGIN]) at the beginning of the block; if the block ends normally (even with a [return]), the transaction is committed ([COMMIT]); if an exception occurs within the block, the transaction is rolled back ([ROLLBACK]): none of the changes made within the block are retained, and the exception continues on its path. [transaction.atomic] can also be used as a decorator for an entire function ([@transaction.atomic]). The business layer thus determines the scope of transactions: one business operation equals one transaction. Outside a [atomic] block, ORM operates in “autocommit” mode: each SQL command is committed immediately. A [IntegrityError] is intercepted outside the [with] block: inside the block, the transaction would no longer be usable after the error. Other exceptions (such as a database failure or a programming error) are not business errors: they continue to be processed.

docs.title: 9.1.6. The Web Layer
docs.text:
The data entry is described by a form (Example 19):

# people/forms.py: a person’s form (see examples 18 and 19)

from django import forms

from .metier import DonneesPersonne


class PersonneForm(forms.Form):
    prenom = forms.CharField(label="Prénom", max_length=30, error_messages={
        "required": "Le prénom est obligatoire.", "max_length": "30 caractères au plus."})
    nom = forms.CharField(label="Nom", max_length=30, error_messages={
        "required": "Le nom est obligatoire.", "max_length": "30 caractères au plus."})
    age = forms.IntegerField(label="Âge", min_value=0, max_value=150, error_messages={
        "required": "L'âge est obligatoire.",
        "invalid": "L'âge doit être un nombre entier.",
        "min_value": "L'âge doit être compris entre 0 et 150.",
        "max_value": "L'âge doit être compris entre 0 et 150."})

     # modification=True: the edit form, which has one additional field
    def __init__(self, *args, modification=False, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for champ in self.fields.values():
            champ.widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"
         # Version: a hidden field, in the edit form only
        if modification:
            self.fields["version"] = forms.IntegerField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)

     # validated data for the business layer; CharField has already removed the
     # leading and trailing spaces from the input (strip option, true by default)
    def donnees(self) -> DonneesPersonne:
        d = self.cleaned_data
        return DonneesPersonne(d["prenom"], d["nom"], d["age"])
  • lines 9–17: the fields and their constraints, with messages in French;
  • lines 20–26: an additional parameter for the constructor, [modification], specified by name ([PersonneForm(request.POST, modification=True)]): a parameter written after [*args] can only be passed by name. The update form receives one additional field, “version,” in a hidden field: [self.fields] is a dictionary to which a field can be added;
  • Lines 30–32: the validated data, in the format expected by the business layer.

[Django] can also generate a form from a template (the [forms.ModelForm] class): its fields and their constraints are derived from the columns, and its [save()] method saves the object. This is very common. However, the form would then modify the model before the business layer has verified its rules. A separate form keeps the layers distinct: the web layer transmits only validated data to the business layer.

# persons/views.py: the WEB layer; it only recognizes the business layer

from django.contrib import messages
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.urls import reverse
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods

from . import metier
from .forms import PersonneForm
from .metier import MetierErreur


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return redirect("personnes_liste")


@require_GET
def liste(request):
    return render(request, "personnes/liste.html", {"personnes": metier.lister()})


# GET: the empty form; POST: the submitted form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def ajout(request):
    titre = "Ajouter une personne"
    action = reverse("personnes_ajout")
    if request.method == "GET":
        return page_formulaire(request, titre, PersonneForm(), action)
    formulaire = PersonneForm(request.POST)
    if not formulaire.is_valid():
        return page_formulaire(request, titre, formulaire, action, statut=422)
    try:
        p = metier.ajouter(formulaire.donnees())
    except MetierErreur as e:
         # a business rule rejects it: the form is redisplayed, with the data entered, and
         # the message at the bottom of the page
        return page_formulaire(request, titre, formulaire, action, erreur=str(e))
    messages.success(request, f"{p} a été ajouté(e).")
    return redirect("personnes_liste")


# GET: the edit form, pre-filled
@require_GET
def modification(request, id):
    try:
        p = metier.lire(id)
    except MetierErreur as e:
        messages.error(request, str(e))
        return redirect("personnes_liste")
    formulaire = PersonneForm(modification=True, initial={
        "prenom": p.prenom, "nom": p.nom, "age": p.age, "version": p.version})
    return page_formulaire(request, "Modifier une personne", formulaire,
                           reverse("personnes_personne", args=[id]), methode="PUT")


# PUT: the update form is submitted; DELETE: the deletion
@require_http_methods(["PUT", "DELETE"])
def personne(request, id):
    if request.method == "DELETE":
        try:
            p = metier.supprimer(id)
            messages.success(request, f"{p} a été supprimé(e).")
        except MetierErreur as e:
             # no form to redisplay: the error is also displayed in a flash message
            messages.error(request, str(e))
        return redirect("personnes_liste")
    titre = "Modifier une personne"
    action = reverse("personnes_personne", args=[id])
    formulaire = PersonneForm(request.POST, modification=True)
    if not formulaire.is_valid():
        return page_formulaire(request, titre, formulaire, action, methode="PUT", statut=422)
    try:
        p = metier.modifier(id, formulaire.cleaned_data["version"], formulaire.donnees())
    except MetierErreur as e:
        return page_formulaire(request, titre, formulaire, action, methode="PUT", erreur=str(e))
    messages.success(request, f"{p} a été modifié(e).")
    return redirect("personnes_liste")


# the form page; a business error: code 422, as with a form
# invalid (see example 19)
def page_formulaire(request, titre, formulaire, action, methode=None, erreur=None, statut=200):
    return render(request, "personnes/formulaire.html", {
        "titre": titre, "formulaire": formulaire, "action": action, "methode": methode,
        "erreur": erreur}, status=422 if erreur else statut)
  • line 8: the business layer, the only layer known to the web layer;
  • lines 25–40: the addition, in three steps: form validation (input errors, example 19); the call to the business layer (business rules); then the PRG schema, with a success flash message (example 20). A [MetierErreur] re-displays the form, along with the entered data and the exception message ([str(e)]), which the template will display at the bottom of the page. Input errors and business logic errors are thus handled in the same way;
  • lines 44–54: the edit form, pre-filled with the retrieved person (parameter [initial], example 18). If the person does not exist, the form redirects to the list with a flash error message ([messages.error]). The form is submitted using method PUT (the hidden field [_method], Example 21), to URL [/personnes/<id>] ([reverse], with the route parameters in [args]);
  • lines 58–78: the view from [/personnes/<id>], for the methods PUT (update, following the same pattern as the add operation) and DELETE (delete, protected by the anti-CSRF token, Example 21). For deletion, there is no form to redisplay: any error is also conveyed in a flash message;
  • lines 83–86: the form page. A business error is returned with code 422, as for an invalid form.

The web layer contains neither SQL nor any business rules: it translates the request into a call to the business layer and the result into a page. The routes ([personnes/urls.py]): [/personnes] (the list), [/personnes/ajout], [/personnes/<id>/modification], and [/personnes/<id>] (PUT and DELETE).

The templates:

<!doctype html>

  • line 20: the footer block, where pages display their errors (example 19);
