docs.title: 9.1.8. The SQL commands
docs.text:
Let’s track the SQL commands for a modification in the console (the server was restarted, and the database was recreated). The display of the modification form for person #1:

(0.000)
                SELECT VERSION(),
                       @@sql_mode,
                       @@default_storage_engine,
                       @@sql_auto_is_null,
                       @@lower_case_table_names,
                       CONVERT_TZ('2001-01-01 01:00:00', 'UTC', 'UTC') IS NOT NULL
            ; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `personnes`.`id`, `personnes`.`version`, `personnes`.`prenom`, `personnes`.`nom`, `personnes`.`age` FROM `personnes` WHERE `personnes`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `personnes`.`nom` ASC, `personnes`.`prenom` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "GET /personnes/1/modification HTTP/1.1" 200 2450

Each line shows the command’s duration (in seconds), the command SQL, its parameters ([args]), and the database name ([alias]). The first two commands are used to establish the connection: [Django] queries the server (its version, its settings), then sets the transaction isolation level ([READ COMMITTED]: a transaction sees the changes committed by others). Next comes the read by primary key, with its [ORDER BY] (corresponding to [Meta.ordering]) and its [LIMIT 1] (corresponding to [first()]). In the log, the parameters are copied in order so that they can be read; originally, they are sent separately ([args]). There is no transaction: an isolated read does not require one. The master record is saved with a new age:

(0.000) BEGIN; args=None; alias=default
(0.001) SELECT `personnes`.`id`, `personnes`.`version`, `personnes`.`prenom`, `personnes`.`nom`, `personnes`.`age` FROM `personnes` WHERE `personnes`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `personnes`.`nom` ASC, `personnes`.`prenom` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.001) SELECT `personnes`.`id`, `personnes`.`version`, `personnes`.`prenom`, `personnes`.`nom`, `personnes`.`age` FROM `personnes` WHERE (`personnes`.`nom` = 'Pélissier' AND `personnes`.`prenom` = 'Marie' AND NOT (`personnes`.`id` = 1)) ORDER BY `personnes`.`nom` ASC, `personnes`.`prenom` ASC LIMIT 1; args=('Pélissier', 'Marie', 1); alias=default
(0.000) UPDATE `personnes` SET `prenom` = 'Marie', `nom` = 'Pélissier', `age` = 43, `version` = (`personnes`.`version` + 1) WHERE (`personnes`.`id` = 1 AND `personnes`.`version` = 0); args=('Marie', 'Pélissier', 43, 1, 1, 0); alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `personnes`.`id`, `personnes`.`version`, `personnes`.`prenom`, `personnes`.`nom`, `personnes`.`age` FROM `personnes` WHERE `personnes`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `personnes`.`nom` ASC, `personnes`.`prenom` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.001) COMMIT; args=None; alias=default
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "POST /personnes/1 HTTP/1.1" 302 0

(the connection was opened, as in the previous request). Within a single transaction ([BEGIN] ... [COMMIT]), we can see: the read of the record, the search for a namesake, the [UPDATE], and then the re-read of the record. The [UPDATE] increments the version ([version + 1]) and sets the optimistic lock condition ([AND version = 0]). The development server logs the request as a POST: this is how it arrived, before the middleware converted it to a PUT. Now let’s submit the same form a second time, still using the old version:

(0.000) BEGIN; args=None; alias=default
(0.000) SELECT `personnes`.`id`, `personnes`.`version`, `personnes`.`prenom`, `personnes`.`nom`, `personnes`.`age` FROM `personnes` WHERE `personnes`.`id` = 1 ORDER BY `personnes`.`nom` ASC, `personnes`.`prenom` ASC LIMIT 1; args=(1,); alias=default
(0.000) ROLLBACK; args=None; alias=default
Unprocessable Content: /personnes/1
[27/Sep/2026 19:45:19] "POST /personnes/1 HTTP/1.1" 422 2661

The version being read is not the one from the form: the business layer raised a [MetierErreur], which rolled back the transaction ([ROLLBACK]), and the page displays “This record has been modified in the meantime: please reload it.” Similarly, adding a namesake stops after the namesake search, without a [INSERT].

docs.title: 4. Templates and Forms
docs.text:
Until now, views generated their own responses: text, JSON, and a few HTML tags written as a string. In a MVC application, generating the page is the role of Part V, which [Django] calls a template: a file that describes the page, with placesholders for the data passed to it by the view—the template context (the M model of MVC; see introduction).

[Django] has its own template engine and its own template language, DTL (Django Template Language). It can also use other engines, such as [Jinja2], the one used by [Flask] (setting [TEMPLATES]); this document focuses on DTL, which all [Django] applications use. A template is a text file, in this case HTML (given the extension [.html]), stored in a folder named [templates], in which three types of tags are interpreted on the server:

  • [{{ variable }}]: the value of a context variable, inserted into the page;
  • [{% balise %}]: a tag that controls the engine: condition ([{% if %}]), loop ([{% for %}]), template inheritance ([{% extends %}], [{% block %}]), inclusion ([{% include %}]), creation of a URL ([{% url %}])...;
  • [{# commentaire #}]: a comment that does not appear on the generated page. It fits on a single line; a multi-line comment is written between the [{% comment %}] and [{% endcomment %}] tags.

Everything else is copied verbatim. The expressions are not written in [Python], but in the deliberately limited language of DTL: [modele.titre] refers to the key [titre] in a dictionary, or the attribute [titre] of an object, or the element [titre] in a list ([Django] tries them in that order), and, if it is a method, [Django] calls it without any parameters; filters transform a value ([nom|upper] capitalizes a name); tags perform actions. That’s it: DTL has no arithmetic operators, no function calls with parameters, and no assignments. This is by design: the creators of [Django] wanted templates to be written by graphic designers, without the risk of application logic creeping into the pages. A calculation is therefore performed in [Python]—either in the view or in a method of a context object—and the template simply displays the result. The languages of [Twig] ([Symfony]) and [Jinja2] ([Flask]), which were inspired by it, are more permissive: they perform calculations ([total / nombre]) and call functions with parameters. Finally, a template is not re-parsed with every request: upon its first use, [Django] parses it and transforms it into a list of nodes—a [Python] object—which it keeps in memory and reuses thereafter (in debug mode, it re-parses it if it has been modified). We’ll see what this list looks like.

docs.title: 4.1.1. The configuration: config/settings.py
docs.text:
The template engine is configured via the setting [TEMPLATES]:

# config/settings.py: the configuration for Example 13

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-_ph!-_ox*o_&n8o2i=ykjwic(j9!mwf!cc2(()%nzdrs9ssai_"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "pages",
]

# the MOTEURS, DE, and GABARITS: here, only one—the Django one (DTL, Django Template
# Language), which looks for templates in the project’s `templates` folder
TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
    },
]
  • Lines 19–24: [TEMPLATES] is a list of template engines, each described by a dictionary. Here, there is only one: [BACKEND] refers to the engine [Django] (DTL); [DIRS] is the list of folders where it searches for templates: the [templates] folder of the project. The configuration can also instruct the engine to look for templates in the [templates] folder of each application within the [INSTALLED_APPS] configuration ([APP_DIRS: True], example 18): this is how a reusable application provides its own templates.

The templates are stored in a subfolder named [pages], which is named after the application: this is standard practice, which prevents two applications from each having a [index.html] template and one from overwriting the other.

docs.title: 4.1.2. The template context: pages/modeles.py
docs.text:
# pages/modeles.py: the view model, the data that the Python view passes to the template

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PageModele:
    titre: str
    message: str
    heure: str

A template’s context is a dictionary named [Python]. Here, it will have only one entry, [modele], an immutable object of the class [PageModele] (see Example 03), which contains the three pieces of information that the template will display. There is no requirement to define a template’s context using a class: one could pass three separate variables to the template. However, a class documents what the template expects and allows the editor to verify the view’s code. This is the approach that the case study will follow, where each important page has its own template class.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Views: pages/views.py
docs.text:
# pages/views.py: views that render a page generated by a GABARIT

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.utils import timezone
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import PageModele


# render: the template engine renders the page from the template
# templates/pages/index.html and CONTEXTE, a dictionary of the variables set
# available to the template (in this case, a single one, “modele”); the resulting page is the body
# of the response
@require_GET
def index(request):
    modele = PageModele(
        "Mon premier gabarit",
        "Cette page a été fabriquée par Django, sur le serveur.",
         # the time, in the application’s time zone (setting TIME_ZONE)
        timezone.localtime().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render(request, "pages/index.html", {"modele": modele})


# the same template with a different model; or a different template, with code 404
@require_GET
def bonjour(request, nom):
    if nom == "inconnu":
         # status: the response code
        return render(request, "pages/inconnu.html", {"nom": nom}, status=404)
    modele = PageModele(
        f"Bonjour {nom}",
        "Cette fois, le titre de la page vient de l'URL.",
        timezone.localtime().strftime("%H:%M:%S"))
    return render(request, "pages/index.html", {"modele": modele})
  • Lines 16–20: The view constructs the model. [timezone.localtime()], from the [django.utils.timezone] module, returns the current time in the application’s time zone (settings [TIME_ZONE], [Europe/Paris]); [strftime] formats it: [%H] for hours, [%M] for minutes, [%S] for seconds;
  • Line 21: The shortcut [render] (from the [django.shortcuts] module, example 04) causes the template engine to generate the page. It receives the request, the template name (the file path, relative to one of the template folders), and the context: a dictionary, where each key becomes a template variable—in this case, a single one: [modele]. [render] returns a [HttpResponse] object, whose body is the rendered page (of type [text/html]);
  • lines 27–29: another template, with a different variable ([nom]). The parameter [status] of [render] specifies the response code: in this case, 404, for a custom error page;
  • lines 30–34: the same template as the view [index], with a different model. This is the benefit of separating views from templates: a single template can be used for multiple views.

The routes ([pages/urls.py]) associate [/] with the view [index], and [/bonjour/<str:nom>] with the view [bonjour].

docs.title: 4.1.4. The template: templates/pages/index.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  {# {{ ... }}: the value of a variable, inserted into the page #}
  <title>{{ modele.titre }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ modele.titre }}</h1>
  <p>{{ modele.message }}</p>
  <p>Page fabriquée à {{ modele.heure }}.</p>
</body>
</html>
  • line 5: a comment from DTL;
  • line 6: [{{ modele.titre }}] inserts the value of the [titre] attribute of the [modele] variable. The dot is the access operator for DTL, whereas [Python] would write [modele.titre] or [modele["titre"]], as appropriate.

Everything inserted by [{{ }}] is escaped: the characters [<], [>], [&], ["], and ['] are replaced by their entities HTML. This is the role that function [format_html] played in Example 09, but this time it is automatic: a template therefore cannot inadvertently insert the HTML provided by a user into the page.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The template: templates/pages/inconnu.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Inconnu</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Personne ne s'appelle [{{ nom }}] ici.</h1>
</body>

A template does not have to accept an object: the variable [nom] is a string.

docs.title: 4.1.6. Execution
docs.text:
The time displayed is that of the application's time zone. The raw response shows how the engine works: the [{{ }}] tags have been replaced with their values, and the comment has disappeared (leaving behind an empty line with its indentation).

curl -i http://localhost:8000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">

  <title>Mon premier gabarit</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Mon premier gabarit</h1>
  <p>Cette page a été fabriquée par Django, sur le serveur.</p>
  <p>Page fabriquée à 19:28:44.</p>
</body>
</html>

The “custom” error page, followed by a name containing HTML and an apostrophe ([<b>martin'], encoded as URL):

curl -i http://localhost:8000/hello/unknown
curl "http://localhost:8000/bonjour/%3Cb%3Emartin'"

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Inconnu</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Personne ne s'appelle [inconnu] ici.</h1>
</body>
</html>
<!doctype html>
...
  <title>Bonjour <b>martin'</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Bonjour <b>martin'</h1>
  <p>Cette fois, le titre de la page vient de l'URL.</p>
...

The tag [<b>] was escaped, without the view or the template having to do anything (the apostrophe was also escaped: [']; the one in the message is escaped as well, which does not affect its display). Here, finally, is the template as [Django] stores it in memory. The command [python manage.py shell] opens a console [Python] where [Django] is ready; the option [-c] causes it to execute a few instructions:

python manage.py shell -c "from django.template.loader import get_template; print(*get_template('pages/index.html').template.nodelist, sep='\n')"

<TextNode: '<!doctype html>\n<html lan'>
<TextNode: '\n  <title>'>
<Variable Node: modele.titre>
<TextNode: '</title>\n</head>\n<body>\n '>
<Variable Node: modele.titre>
<TextNode: '</h1>\n  <p>'>
<Variable Node: modele.message>
<TextNode: '</p>\n  <p>Page fabriquée '>
<Variable Node: modele.heure>
<TextNode: '.</p>\n</body>\n</html>\n'>

The template has become a list of nodes: pieces of text ([TextNode], whose display is truncated), copied as-is, and variables ([VariableNode]), whose values are looked up in the context and then escaped. The comment left no nodes. Generating the page involves iterating through this list and reassembling the text fragments. A template is therefore simply a safer and more readable way to write a function [Python] that generates HTML.

docs.title: 4.2. Example 14: The Template Language
docs.text: This example combines the main constructs of DTL into a single template.

docs.title: 4.2.1. The Model and the View
docs.text:
The template model is described by three immutable data classes:

# bases/modeles.py: the template for Example 14

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Adresse:
    rue: str
    ville: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Produit:
    nom: str
    prix: float
    en_stock: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BasesModele:
    titre: str
    nom: str
     # str | None: a string, or None
    surnom: str | None
    html: str
    connecte: bool
    devise: str
    produits: list[Produit]
    panier: list[Produit]
    adresse: Adresse

     # @property: a method that is read as an attribute (modele.total). The
     # template language cannot perform calculations: calculations are done in Python
    @property
    def total(self) -> float:
        return sum(p.prix for p in self.produits)

    @property
    def prix_moyen(self) -> float:
        return self.total / len(self.produits)
  • line 24: [str | None]: a string, or [None] (example 06);
  • lines 28–29: lists of [Produit] objects;
  • lines 34–40: Since DTL cannot perform calculations, the calculations required by the template (total price, average price) are methods of the model. The decorator [@property] turns a method into a property: it is read as an attribute, without parentheses ([modele.total]), and this is how DTL will see it. For simplicity, the prices here are of type [float] (Example 06 showed why we prefer whole cents).

The model contains values of various types: strings, [None], Booleans, lists of objects, empty lists, and objects containing other objects.

# bases/views.py: a template that uses the main constructs of the Django template language

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import Adresse, BasesModele, Produit


@require_GET
def index(request):
     # arguments NOMMÉS: each value is associated with an attribute by its name
    modele = BasesModele(
        titre="Les bases des gabarits",
        nom="Martin",
        surnom=None,
        html="<b>ceci est du HTML</b>",
        connecte=True,
        devise="€",
        produits=[
            Produit("Clavier", 25, True),
            Produit("Souris", 12.5, False),
            Produit("Écran", 149, True),
        ],
        panier=[],
        adresse=Adresse("12 rue des Lilas", "Angers"))
    return render(request, "bases/index.html", {"modele": modele})

The view constructs the model using named parameters (see Example 02): each value is preceded by the name of the attribute it is intended for, which makes the call readable despite the number of parameters.

docs.text:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>{{ modele.titre }}</title>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>{{ modele.titre }}</h1>
  {% comment %}
    1. afficher une valeur du modèle ; None s'affiche... None ; le filtre default
    remplace une valeur vide (None, "", 0, liste vide...). Un commentaire {# #} holds
    sur une seule ligne ; celui-ci, sur plusieurs, s'écrit entre comment et endcomment
  {% endcomment %}
  <p>1. Nom : {{ modele.nom }} - surnom : [{{ modele.surnom }}] [{{ modele.surnom|default:"aucun" }}]</p>
  {# 2. {{ }} escapes the HTML; the safe filter inserts it as-is #}
  <p>2a. {{ modele.html }}</p>
  <p>2b. {{ modele.html|safe }}</p>
  {# 3. a condition #}
  {% if modele.connecte %}
    <p>3. Vous êtes connecté.</p>
  {% else %}
    <p>3. Vous n'êtes pas connecté.</p>
  {% endif %}
  {# 4. a loop: the `forloop` variable describes the state of the loop #}
  <p>4. Nos produits :</p>
  <ul>
    {% for produit in modele.produits %}
      <li>n° {{ forloop.counter0 }} : {{ produit.nom }}, {{ produit.prix }} {{ modele.devise }}
        {{ produit.en_stock|yesno:"(en stock),(épuisé)" }}
        {% if forloop.first %} - le premier{% endif %}
        {% if forloop.last %} - le dernier, vu par {{ modele.nom }}{% endif %}
      </li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {# 5. the empty list: the `empty` block of a `for` loop #}
  <p>5. Votre panier :
    {% for p in modele.panier %}<span>{{ p.nom }}</span>{% empty %} il est vide.{% endfor %}
  </p>
  {% comment %}
    6. with : une variable du gabarit ; le filtre length compte les produits ;
    floatformat arrondit, et écrit le nombre selon la langue (réglage LANGUAGE_CODE)
  {% endcomment %}
  {% with nombre=modele.produits|length %}
    <p>6. {{ nombre }} produits, pour un total de {{ modele.total }} {{ modele.devise }} ;
      prix moyen : {{ modele.prix_moyen|floatformat:2 }} {{ modele.devise }}</p>
  {% endwith %}
  {# 7. an object inside an object, and a filter that capitalizes text #}
  <p>7. Adresse : {{ modele.adresse.rue }}, {{ modele.adresse.ville|upper }}</p>
  {# 8. verbatim: text that Django copies verbatim without interpreting it #}
  <p>8. Des accolades affichées telles quelles : {% verbatim %}{{ modele.nom }}{% endverbatim %}</p>
</body>
</html>
  • Lines 9–13: a multi-line comment;
  • line 14: a value [None] is displayed... [None]: this is the text representation of [None]. The filter [default] replaces an “empty” value ([None], empty string, 0, empty list...) with a default value. A filter is applied using a vertical bar and may take an optional parameter following a colon: [valeur|filtre:"paramètre"]. A variable that does not exist at all in the context ([modele.inconnu]) would be displayed as an empty string, without an error;
  • lines 16–17: [{{ }}] escapes HTML (2a); the filter [safe], on the other hand, inserts the value as-is, without escaping (2b). [safe] is reserved for HTML generated by the application itself, never for user input. The [{% autoescape off %}] tag disables escaping for an entire section of the template;
  • lines 19–23: a condition: [{% if %}], [{% elif %}], [{% else %}], [{% endif %}]. Each block is closed by a [{% end... %}] tag. A condition can use the operators [==], [!=], [<], [>], [<=], [>=], [in], [not], [and], [or];
  • lines 27–33: a loop [{% for ... in ... %}] ... [{% endfor %}]. Within the loop, the special variable [forloop] describes the loop’s state: [forloop.counter0] (the iteration number, starting at 0), [forloop.counter] (starting at 1), [forloop.first], [forloop.last] (true on the first and last iterations), [forloop.revcounter] (the number of remaining iterations). The variables outside the loop ([modele.nom], [modele.devise]) remain accessible;
  • Line 29: The [yesno] filter selects a text based on whether a value is true or false: its two texts (a third, optional text would be used for [None]) are separated by a comma. This is the equivalent, in DTL, of a conditional expression;
  • line 37: a [for] loop can have a [{% empty %}] block, which is executed if the list is empty. This is simpler than a [{% if %}] that would test the length of the list;
  • Lines 43–46: the [{% with %}] tag creates a variable that is valid until [{% endwith %}]: in this case, the number of products, calculated by the [length] filter (the number of elements in a list or characters in a string);
  • Lines 44–45: the calculated properties of the model. The filter [floatformat] rounds a number—[floatformat:2]—to two decimal places. It formats the number according to the conventions of the application’s language ([LANGUAGE_CODE]): the decimal point is formatted for French. All numbers inserted into a page are formatted this way: [Django] formats numbers and dates according to the active language ([12.5] becomes [12,5]);
  • line 48: the period passes through objects ([modele.adresse.ville]), and the filter [upper] capitalizes a string (while correctly handling accented characters);
  • line 50: the [{% verbatim %}] tag copies its content without interpreting it: this is useful when a page contains curly braces intended for a [JavaScript] framework.

The DTL has about sixty filters ([lower], [capfirst], [title], [truncatechars], [join], [slice], [first], [last], [date], [time], [linebreaks], [urlize], [pluralize], [add], [divisibleby], [escape], [json_script]...) and about thirty tags ([if], [for], [with], [url], [now], [cycle], [firstof], [include], [extends], [block], [load], [csrf_token], [spaceless]...); The applications for [Django] add more ([static], [translate]...), and the application can write its own (Example 16).

docs.title: 4.3. Example 15: Parent template, fragments, static files
docs.text:
The pages of a website usually share the same structure: a header, a navigation bar, a footer, and the same style sheets. Rather than repeating this structure in every template, it is written once in a parent template (also called a layout), which the pages extend. This example also uses [Bootstrap], the most widely used CSS framework, for the layout.

15-gabarit/
├── config/
│   ├── contextes.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── pages/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── modeles.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── css/
│       └── styles.css
├── templates/
│   ├── fragments/
│   │   └── navbar.html
│   ├── pages/
│   │   ├── accueil.html
│   │   ├── brute.html
│   │   └── equipe.html
│   ├── layout.html
│   └── macros.html
└── manage.py

docs.title: 4.3.1. Static Files
docs.text:
A HTML page references other files: style sheets, [JavaScript] scripts, and images. These files, which the server sends as-is, are called static files. With [Django], they are stored in [static] folders (the project folder and the application folders), and the [django.contrib.staticfiles] application manages them. The configuration:

# config/settings.py: the configuration for Example 15

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-u0g1t-=6%v^*y#i*czmc@ge#-yk6m!jj13lte=0yw_pa6y+2m4"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
     # the Django application that manages the STATIQUES files (style sheets,
     # images, scripts): the {% static %} tag, and their serving via runserver
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
    "pages",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
        "OPTIONS": {
             # the PROCESSEURS, DE, and CONTEXTE: functions that add variables to the
             # context of TOUS templates; request: the current request
            "context_processors": [
                "django.template.context_processors.request",
                "config.contextes.site",
            ],
        },
    },
]

# for static files: {% static 'css/styles.css' %} -> /static/css/styles.css
STATIC_URL = "static/"
# the directories where Django looks for static files: the one in the example, and
# the one for Bootstrap, shared by examples 15 through 28
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / "static",
    BASE_DIR.parent / "commun" / "static",
]
  • lines 14–19: the [django.contrib.staticfiles] application, one of the applications included with [Django];
  • lines 21–34: the template engine, with two context processors, described later;
  • line 37: [STATIC_URL], the prefix for the URL static files: the file [css/styles.css] will be available in URL and [/static/css/styles.css];
  • Lines 40–43: [STATICFILES_DIRS], the list of static file folders for the project (in addition to the [static] folders for the applications). The first one is the one from the example. The second is the [exemples/commun/static] folder, which contains [Bootstrap]: rather than including a copy in each example, examples 15 through 28 share it (see introduction). [Django] searches for a file in all these folders, in order, and returns the first one found.

In debug mode, the development server serves the static files itself, using the [staticfiles] application: a URL that begins with [/static/] is not handled by the application’s routes, but by the static file handler. In production ([DEBUG = False]), it no longer does this: that is not the role of a [Python] application. The command [python manage.py collectstatic] then copies all static files from the project and applications into a single folder (the setting [STATIC_ROOT]), which the web server ([nginx], [Apache]...) serves directly, or that is served by a library such as [WhiteNoise] (see case study).

A few additional CSS rules in addition to [Bootstrap]: a light gray background, the footer style, and the style for an error area that will be used in the following examples.

docs.title: 4.3.2. The parent template: templates/layout.html
docs.text:
<!doctype html>
{# the PARENT page template: the pages use the ÉTENDENT template and fill its blocks #}
{% load static %}
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  {# block: a placeholder that the page can fill; here with default content #}
  <title>{% block titre %}Accueil{% endblock %} - {{ nom_site }}</title>
  {# static: the URL of a static file #}
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css' %}">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="{% static 'css/styles.css' %}">
</head>
<body>
  <div class="container py-3">
    {# insertion of the fragments/navbar.html template #}
    {% include "fragments/navbar.html" %}
    <main>
      {# The content of the page requested by the view is inserted here #}
      {% block contenu %}{% endblock %}
    </main>
    {# request: the current request; nom_site: a global variable (see config/contextes.py) #}
    <footer class="pied">Page [{{ request.path }}] - © {% now "Y" %} {{ nom_site }}</footer>
  </div>
</body>
</html>
  • Line 3: [{% load static %}] loads a tag library: that of the [staticfiles] application, which provides the [{% static %}] tag. Tags and filters that are not part of the core of DTL are stored in libraries, which a template must load before using them;
  • line 7: the [viewport] tag instructs mobile browsers to display the page at the screen’s width, which is what [Bootstrap] expects;
  • line 9: the [{% block %}] tag marks a named slot, which pages that extend the template can fill by defining a block with the same name. The content written between [{% block titre %}] and [{% endblock %}] is the default content for the placeholder, used by a page that does not define this block. [nom_site] is a global variable present in all templates (see [config/contextes.py], below);
  • Lines 11–12: [{% static 'chemin' %}] generates URL from a static file: [STATIC_URL] followed by the path. Writing the URL files by hand ([/static/css/styles.css]) would also work, but [{% static %}] adapts if you change [STATIC_URL] (to serve the files from another site, for example), or if you add a hash of their content to the filenames for caching purposes (case study);
  • line 17: [{% include %}] inserts the content of another template, in this case the navigation bar. The included template sees the variables from the template that includes it;
  • line 20: the placeholder that each page fills with its own content;
  • line 23: the variable [request] is the current request ([request.path]: the path of the requested URL). It is present in all templates thanks to the context processor [request] (see below). The tag [{% now "Y" %}] writes the current date in the following format: [Y], with the year as four digits.

The [container] class of [Bootstrap] centers the content and limits its width; [py-3] adds vertical padding: [Bootstrap] provides hundreds of classes of this type, which are combined in the [class] attribute.

docs.title: 4.3.3. Global variables: config/contextes.py
docs.text:
# config/contextes.py: a context processor

# Django calls it for every template rendered with the request (render(request, ...));
# the dictionary it returns is added to the context: nom_site is a variable GLOBALE,
# present in all templates
def site(request):
    return {"nom_site": "Mon site"}

A context processor is a function that receives the request and returns a dictionary of variables to be added to the context of all templates. [Django] calls the processors from the [context_processors] setting (lines 28–31 of the file [config/settings.py]) every time a template is generated using the request (as is the case with [render(request, ...)]). The [django.template.context_processors.request] processor, included with [Django], adds the variable [request]; ours adds [nom_site]. Other applications of [Django] provide their own: messages (example 20), language (example 22)... A processor is called for each template generated: it must be fast.

docs.title: 4.3.4. The navigation bar: templates/fragments/navbar.html
docs.text:
{# a fragment: a section of a page, inserted via an #} include
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">{{ nom_site }}</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# URL: the URL of a route, designated by its name #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'accueil' %}">Accueil</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'equipe' %}">Équipe</a>
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'brute' %}">Page sans gabarit parent</a>
  </div>
</nav>

A fragment: a piece of a page that has no meaning on its own. The classes [navbar], [navbar-brand], and [nav-link] are those of the navigation bar in [Bootstrap]. The links are generated by the [{% url %}] tag (line 6), based on the route names (example 04): [{% url 'equipe' %}] yields [/equipe]. The route parameters follow the name: [{% url 'contacts_fiche' contact.id %}] (example 21).

docs.title: 4.3.5. Named fragments: templates/macros.html
docs.text:
{# FRAGMENTS NOMMÉS (partialdef): reusable page fragments, stored in a single file #}

{# a Bootstrap card, with a name and a function #}
{% partialdef carte %}
  <div class="card">
    <div class="card-body">
      <h5 class="card-title">{{ nom }}</h5>
      <p class="card-text">{{ fonction }}</p>
    </div>
  </div>
{% endpartialdef %}
  • lines 4–11: The [{% partialdef %}] tag, introduced with [Django] 6.0, defines a named fragment (partial): a portion of a template, in this case a map ([card]) from [Bootstrap]. A file can contain several of these. Defined in this way, the fragment is not displayed where it is written: it is displayed elsewhere, using [{% include "macros.html#carte" %}] (the file name, a hash symbol, the fragment name), or, within the same file, using [{% partial carte %}]. The fragment displays two variables, [nom] and [fonction], which will be provided to it upon inclusion.

Students of the [Symfony] course will recognize how this course used the macros from [Twig]. There is one difference: a macro from [Twig] could only see its own parameters; an included fragment can see all the variables in the template that includes it, in addition to the ones passed to it. The keyword [only] ([{% include "..." with nom="..." only %}]) restricts it to the latter. For a more complex component that requires [Python] code, an inclusion tag is written (Example 16).

docs.title: 4.3.6. The pages
docs.text:
{# this page, ÉTEND, is the parent template: it provides only the content of its blocks #}
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>Bienvenue</h1>
  <p>Cette page ne contient que son propre contenu : l'entête, la barre de
    navigation et le pied de page viennent du gabarit parent <code>layout.html</code>.</p>
  {# the fragment [carte] from the file macros.html, with two variables defined in place #}
  {% include "macros.html#carte" with nom="Un fragment" fonction="inclus avec des variables écrites sur place" %}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 2: The page extends the parent template: [Django] generates the parent page, replacing its blocks with those defined by the page. [{% extends %}] must be the first tag in the template (only a comment [{# #}] may precede it). In a template that extends another template, all content must be within blocks: text written outside of blocks does not appear in the generated page;
  • lines 4–10: the [contenu] block, which fills the slot of the same name. The page does not define the [titre] block: the slot retains its default content, “Home”;
  • line 9: the inclusion of the fragment [carte], with two variables specified after the keyword [with]. The HTML in the fragment is not escaped a second time: [Django] knows it is already safe HTML (the variables, however, were escaped within the fragment).
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block titre %}Notre équipe{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>Notre équipe</h1>
  <div class="row g-3">
    {% for membre in membres %}
      <div class="col-md-4">
        {# the variables in the fragment are arbitrary expressions #}
        {% include "macros.html#carte" with nom=membre.nom fonction=membre.fonction %}
      </div>
    {% endfor %}
  </div>
{% endblock %}
  • line 3: the block [titre], on a single line;
  • lines 7–14: one map per team member, in a grid of [Bootstrap] ([row], [col-md-4]: three columns on a medium or large screen, one column on a narrow screen);
  • line 11: the variables passed to the fragment can be any expressions.

A block in the parent can also be supplemented rather than replaced: [{{ block.super }}], written in the page block, inserts the content that the block had in the parent. A template can extend a template that itself extends another: inheritance has as many levels as needed. The view contains no new features:

# pages/views.py: three pages

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import Membre


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return render(request, "pages/accueil.html")


@require_GET
def equipe(request):
    membres = [
        Membre("Marie Pélissier", "Directrice"),
        Membre("Jacques Bromard", "Développeur"),
        Membre("Philippe Jandot", "Graphiste"),
    ]
    return render(request, "pages/equipe.html", {"membres": membres})


@require_GET
def brute(request):
    return render(request, "pages/brute.html")

Finally, the third page does not use the parent template:

<!doctype html>
{# this template does not extend the parent template: it is a complete page #}
<html lang="fr">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Page brute</title>
</head>
<body>
  <p>Cette page n'utilise pas le gabarit parent : ni Bootstrap, ni barre de navigation.</p>
  <p><a href="{% url 'accueil' %}">Retour à l'accueil</a></p>
</body>
</html>

The browser received a complete page: the parent template, the navigation bar fragment, the page, and the cards were assembled on the server. The URL style sheets were calculated by [{% static %}]: these are URL specific to the site. You can verify that the style sheets are being served correctly (the [-I] option of [curl] displays only the response headers when sending a HEAD request):

curl -I http://localhost:8000/static/bootstrap/css/bootstrap.min.css
curl -I http://localhost:8000/static/css/styles.css

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/css
Content-Length: 232111
Content-Disposition: inline; filename="bootstrap.min.css"
Last-Modified: Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:41:12 GMT

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/css
Content-Length: 422
Content-Disposition: inline; filename="styles.css"
Last-Modified: Sun, 27 Sep 2026 16:42:11 GMT

The first file comes from the [commun/static] folder, the second from the [static] folder in the example: to the browser, there is no difference between them. The content type was inferred from the file extension ([text/css]): a browser will reject a stylesheet that is declared as something else. Finally, an attempt to access the static file folders:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://localhost:8000/static/..%2F..%2Fconfig%2Fsettings.py"

500

(the [-s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"] options display only the response code; under [Windows], it displays [-o NUL]). The URL option requests the [config/settings.py] file from the example, moving up two folders (the [/] files are encoded as [%2F], so that neither [curl] nor the browser simplifies the path on its own). [Django] failed: the console displays the exception [SuspiciousFileOperation], with the message “The joined path (...) is located outside of the base path component.” Code 500 indicates an unhandled exception; the key point is that the file was not sent.

docs.title: 4.4. Example 16: Extending the template language
docs.text:
A template often needs to format values: an amount with its currency, a date written out in full, or text in uppercase. This code does not belong in the view (which does not handle presentation), and DTL does not allow it to be written in the template (see the introduction to this chapter). Instead, it is written in [Python], in a library of tags and filters: a module that adds its own filters and tags to the template language. Components that generate pieces of HTML from data—the inclusion tags—are also written in [Python].

│   ├── middleware.py

│   └── ...

docs.title: 4.4.1. The library: pages/templatetags/formats.py
docs.text:
A tag library is a module contained in an application’s [templatetags] package (which must be declared in [INSTALLED_APPS]); the module name ([formats]) is the name that a template will assign to [{% load formats %}]:

# pages/templatetags/formats.py: a BIBLIOTHÈQUE set of language extensions for the
# templates, loaded by {% load formats %}: two filters and two tags

from babel.dates import format_date
from babel.numbers import format_currency
from django import template
from django.utils.translation import get_language

# the object that stores the filters and tags from the library
register = template.Library()


# a FILTRE: {{ produit.prix_centimes|currency }} or {{ ...|currency:"USD" }}. An
# amount in cents, in a currency, in the format of the active language:
# 114990 -> "1,149.90 €" in French, "€1,149.90" in English. The library
# Babel library knows the conventions for each country
@register.filter
def monnaie(centimes, devise="EUR"):
    return format_currency(centimes / 100, devise, locale=get_language())


# a date written out in full, in the active language: "Sunday, September 27, 2026"
@register.filter
def date_longue(jour):
    return format_date(jour, format="full", locale=get_language())


# a BALISE D'INCLUSION: {% link 'products' '/products' 'Products' %} displays the
# the "labels" template (lien.html), with the context returned by the function.
# takes_context: the function also receives the context of the template that calls it
@register.inclusion_tag("etiquettes/lien.html", takes_context=True)
def lien(context, route, chemin, texte):
     # a link in the navigation bar, which receives the class [active] if the
     # is located under the path [chemin]
    actif = context["request"].path.startswith(chemin)
    return {"route": route, "texte": texte, "actif": actif}


# a Bootstrap badge: green if the product is in stock, red otherwise
@register.inclusion_tag("etiquettes/badge.html")
def badge(stock):
    return {"stock": stock}
  • lines 4–5: two functions from the [Babel] library (see introduction), which knows the conventions for writing numbers, amounts, and dates for all countries (it uses data from the Unicode project CLDR);
  • line 7: [get_language] sets the active language for the current query ([fr], [en]); we’ll see who sets it;
  • line 10: the object [register], a [template.Library], stores the module’s filters and tags. The variable name is hard-coded: this is where [Django] looks for them;
  • Lines 17–19: A filter is a function, registered by the decorator [@register.filter] under its own name, [monnaie]. Its first parameter is the filtered value; the second, optional parameter is the filter’s parameter in the template ([prix|monnaie:"USD"]): here, the currency, designated by its international code ([EUR], [USD]). The filter formats an amount received in cents (see example 06). The formatting depends on the language: in French, [1 149,90 €] (space to separate thousands, decimal comma, currency symbol after the amount); in English, [€1,149.90];
  • lines 23–25: date formatting: the format [full] writes the date in full, including the day of the week ([dimanche 27 septembre 2026]);
  • lines 31–36: an inclusion tag, defined by [@register.inclusion_tag]: a function that calculates a context, and a template (here, [etiquettes/lien.html]) that displays it. In a template, [{% lien 'produits' '/produits' 'Produits' %}] calls the function with these three parameters, then inserts the template, built using the dictionary it returned. With [takes_context=True], the function receives the context of the calling template as its first parameter: it finds the query there and determines whether the link points to the current page ([startswith] checks the beginning of a string);
  • lines 40–42: a second inclusion tag, without the context: a badge.

A library can also provide “simple” tags ([@register.simple_tag]), which return a value, and complete tags, which parse their own content (such as [{% if %}]): this is less common. The templates for the two inclusion tags:

<a class="nav-link{% if actif %} active{% endif %}" href="{% url route %}">{{ texte }}</a>

{% if stock > 0 %}<span class="badge text-bg-success">{{ stock }} en stock</span>{% else %}<span class="badge text-bg-danger">épuisé</span>{% endif %}

The link for the current page is assigned the class [active] by [Bootstrap], which highlights it. [{% url route %}] generates the URL for a route whose name is stored in a variable. The badge is green ([text-bg-success]) or red ([text-bg-danger]) depending on inventory. The package [templatetags] also has its file [__init__.py]; without it, it would not be a package.

docs.title: 4.4.2. The language of each request: config/middleware.py
docs.text:
# config/middleware.py: the language of each request

from django.utils import translation


class FixerLangue:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

     # the ?lang=en parameter from URL; otherwise, French
    def __call__(self, request):
        langue = "en" if request.GET.get("lang") == "en" else "fr"
         # activate: the language ACTIVE, which Django uses to format
         # numbers and dates, and to translate its messages
        translation.activate(langue)
        return self.get_response(request)

Each request has an active language, which, by default, is the same as the one specified in the [LANGUAGE_CODE] setting. Here, the [?lang=en] parameter of URL selects English; French is the default language. A middleware component (example 03) sets it before each view using the [translation.activate] function: This is the language that [get_language] will return—the language in which [Django] formats numbers and dates and translates its own messages (such as form error messages). The active language is specific to the execution thread handling the request: two simultaneous requests may have different languages. It is not reset from one request to the next; this is why the middleware sets it for each request, even for French. The chapter on internationalization will replace this middleware with that of [Django] and [LocaleMiddleware], and will use this same language to translate the text.

docs.title: 4.4.4. The view: pages/views.py
docs.text:
# pages/views.py: two pages

from datetime import date

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import Produit


@require_GET
def accueil(request):
    return render(request, "pages/accueil.html", {"aujourdhui": date.today()})


@require_GET
def produits(request):
    liste = [
        Produit("clavier", 2500, 12),
        Produit("souris", 1250, 0),
        Produit("écran", 114990, 3),
    ]
     # The calculation is performed here, in Python: the template simply displays the result
    total = sum(p.prix_centimes * p.stock for p in liste)
    return render(request, "pages/produits.html", {"produits": liste, "total_stock": total})

Views pass raw values to templates: a date ([date.today()], today’s date) and amounts in cents. Formatting is handled by the templates. The total inventory, however, is a calculation: it is calculated in [Python] (line 24), since DTL cannot perform calculations. The [Produit] class combines a name, a price (in cents; see example 06), and a stock quantity.

docs.title: 4.4.5. The templates
docs.text:
{% load formats %}
<nav class="navbar navbar-expand bg-light rounded mb-3 px-3">
  <span class="navbar-brand">Extensions</span>
  <div class="navbar-nav">
    {# 1. a condition written in the template; resolver_match: the path of the current request #}
    <a class="nav-link{% if request.resolver_match.url_name == 'accueil' %} active{% endif %}" href="{% url 'accueil' %}">Accueil</a>
    {# 2. our tag [lien] #}
    {% lien 'produits' '/produits' 'Produits' %}
    {# 3. The URL constructs the route path; the parameters for URL are added manually #}
    <a class="nav-link" href="{% url 'produits' %}?lang=en">Products (en)</a>
  </div>
</nav>
  • line 1: the fragment loads the library it needs on its own: [{% load %}] libraries are not passed on to included templates or to templates that extend a parent. Each template loads its own libraries;
  • line 6: the same as with the [lien] tag, written directly in the template, with a condition. [request.resolver_match] describes the result of routing the current request: [url_name] is the name of the route. The tag avoids having to repeat the condition for each link;
  • line 8: the tag call, with its three parameters, separated by spaces;
  • line 10: [{% url %}] only generates the path: the parameters for URL are added manually ([?lang=en]).
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load i18n formats %}
{% block titre %}Accueil{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>Accueil</h1>
  {# our filter date_longue #}
  <p>Nous sommes le {{ aujourdhui|date_longue }}.</p>
  {# the active language, set by the FixerLangue middleware #}
  {% get_current_language as langue %}
  <p>Langue de formatage : {{ langue }}
    (<a href="{% url 'accueil' %}?lang=en">en anglais</a>, <a href="{% url 'accueil' %}">en français</a>)</p>
{% endblock %}
  • Line 2: The page loads two libraries: [i18n], the internationalization library for [Django], and our own;
  • line 8: our filter [date_longue];
  • Lines 10–11: The [{% get_current_language as langue %}] tag, from the [i18n] library, stores the active language in a template variable.
{% extends "layout.html" %}
{% load formats %}
{% block titre %}Produits{% endblock %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1>Produits</h1>
  <table class="table table-sm w-auto">
    <thead><tr><th>Produit</th><th>Prix</th><th>Prix en dollars</th><th>Stock</th></tr></thead>
    <tbody>

The parent template [layout.html] is a simplified version of the one in Example 15; its attribute [lang] receives the active language ([<html lang="{{ langue }}">], after [{% get_current_language as langue %}]).

docs.title: 4.5. Example 17: a GET form
docs.text:
A HTML form sends its fields to the server in one of two ways, depending on its [method] attribute:

  • [method="get"]: The fields are added to the URL as parameters ([/recherche?mot_cle=le&genre=roman]). This is the method used by a form that performs a query: a search or a filter. The URL containing the results can be bookmarked, shared, or reloaded safely;
  • [method="post"]: The fields are included in the request body (see Example 11). This is the method used by a form that modifies data: a registration, an addition, or a deletion.

This first form is a book search. It is hand-coded in HTML within the template: the following examples will use the [Django] form templates.

docs.title: 4.5.1. The template: books/modeles.py
docs.text:
# books/modeles.py: a book, and the search template model

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Livre:
    titre: str
    auteur: str
    genre: str


# the template: the search field (to redisplay it), categories, results
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RechercheModele:
    mot_cle: str
    genre: str
    genres: list[str]
    resultats: list[Livre]
  • Lines 14–19: The template contains the user’s input, which the form will display, the list of suggested genres, and the results.

docs.title: 4.5.2. The view: books/views.py
docs.text:
# books/views.py: a search form, submitted by GET

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .modeles import Livre, RechercheModele

# from the CONSTANTES module: data written in the code for the example
GENRES = ["roman", "poésie", "théâtre"]
LIVRES = [
    Livre("Le Rouge et le Noir", "Stendhal", "roman"),
    Livre("Les Fleurs du mal", "Baudelaire", "poésie"),
    Livre("Madame Bovary", "Flaubert", "roman"),
    Livre("Alcools", "Apollinaire", "poésie"),
    Livre("Le Cid", "Corneille", "théâtre"),
]


# GET / and GET /search?mot_cle=...&genre=... : the ET form and its results
@require_GET
def recherche(request):
    mot_cle = request.GET.get("mot_cle", "")
    genre = request.GET.get("genre", "")
    mot = mot_cle.lower()
     # a list in COMPRÉHENSION: the books that meet the condition
    resultats = [livre for livre in LIVRES
                 if (mot == "" or mot in livre.titre.lower() or mot in livre.auteur.lower())
                 and (genre == "" or livre.genre == genre)]
    return render(request, "livres/recherche.html", {
        "modele": RechercheModele(mot_cle, genre, GENRES, resultats),
    })
  • lines 9–16: two module constants: the list of genres and the list of books. In a real application, these would come from a database;
  • lines 20–21: a single view referenced by two routes ([config/urls.py]: [""] and ["recherche"], named [livres_accueil] and [livres_recherche]). On the first visit ([/]), there are no parameters, and all books are displayed;
  • lines 22–23: the form fields are read as parameters for URL (example 07), with an empty string as the default value;
  • lines 24–28: filtering, using a list comprehension with a condition ([if]): a book is selected if the keyword is empty or appears in its title or author (in lowercase on both sides: [lower()] correctly handles accented characters), and if the genre is empty or matches the book’s genre. A condition can span multiple lines, enclosed in parentheses;
  • lines 29–31: the template.

docs.title: 4.5.3. The template: templates/books/recherche.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Recherche de livres</h1>
  {# method="get": the fields are sent in the URL (?mot_cle=...&genre=...) #}
  <form method="get" action="{% url 'livres_recherche' %}" class="row g-2 align-items-end mb-3">
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="mot_cle">Titre ou auteur</label>
      {# value: the field displays the entered value (escaped by {{ }}) #}
      <input class="form-control" id="mot_cle" name="mot_cle" value="{{ modele.mot_cle }}">
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <label class="form-label" for="genre">Genre</label>
      <select class="form-select" id="genre" name="genre">
        <option value="">(tous)</option>
        {% for genre in modele.genres %}
          {# the boolean "selected" attribute, set if the condition is true, omitted otherwise #}
          <option value="{{ genre }}"{% if genre == modele.genre %} selected{% endif %}>{{ genre }}</option>
        {% endfor %}
      </select>
    </div>
    <div class="col-auto">
      <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Rechercher</button>
    </div>
  </form>
  <p>{{ modele.resultats|length }} livre(s) trouvé(s).</p>
  <ul>
    {% for livre in modele.resultats %}
      <li><i>{{ livre.titre }}</i>, {{ livre.auteur }} ({{ livre.genre }})</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}
  • line 6: the [<form>] tag. The [action] attribute is the URL to which the form is submitted; [method="get"] places the fields in the URL. The classes of [Bootstrap] arrange the fields on a single line;
  • line 8: a label. Its [for] attribute specifies the identifier ([id]) of the field it describes: clicking the label places the cursor in the field, and screen readers read the label along with the field;
  • line 10: an input field. Its attribute [name] is the name of the parameter sent to the server: this is the link between the form and the view ([request.GET.get("mot_cle", "")]). The attribute [value] is the displayed value: the previous entry, redisplayed (and escaped by [{{ }}], which is essential in an attribute: an entry containing a quotation mark ["] would otherwise close the attribute);
  • lines 14–20: a drop-down list. Each [<option>] has a value ([value]), sent to the server, and text, displayed. The first option, with an empty value, means “all genres”;
  • line 18: the option selected in the previous request is assigned the attribute [selected]. This is a Boolean attribute: its presence alone is sufficient; it has no value. The condition sets it if true, and sets nothing otherwise;
  • line 23: the submit button;
  • line 26: the number of results.

docs.title: 4.6. Example 18: Form fields
docs.text:
This example shows all the field types in a HTML form, which was sent this time by POST. It demonstrates how to redisplay each field type along with its current value, how the browser sends the values for each field, and how the server verifies that a received value is indeed one of the available options. Writing all of this by hand, as in Example 17, would be time-consuming and repetitive. The forms from [Django], which we used in the previous chapter to validate parameters, can also be displayed: each field has a widget—an object that creates its input field in HTML, along with the current value—and the form redisplays the input and any errors. This is the complete version of what the [Symfony] course delegated to its Form component, and what the [Flask] course delegated to [WTForms].
