The form’s dropdown lists (titles, countries, hobbies, languages) are constants in a module: in a real application, they would come from a database. Each list consists of (value, text) pairs: the value is what is sent to the server, and the text is what is displayed (example 08). A pair is written in parentheses: it is a tuple, a sequence of values that cannot be modified.

docs.title: 4.6.2. The form: formulaire/forms.py
docs.text:
# form/forms.py: the form’s DESCRIPTION: its fields, their types, and their widgets

from django import forms

from . import listes


# a parent class for our forms: it assigns the
# the appropriate Bootstrap class CSS
class FormulaireBootstrap(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
         # fields: the form fields, in a dictionary {name: field}
        for champ in self.fields.values():
            widget = champ.widget
            if isinstance(widget, (forms.RadioSelect, forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)):
                classe = "form-check-input"
            elif isinstance(widget, forms.Select):
                classe = "form-select"
            else:
                classe = "form-control"
             # attrs: the HTML attributes of the input field
            widget.attrs["class"] = classe


# the form fields, in the order they are displayed. The CHAMP (forms.XxxField)
# converts and validates the value; the WIDGET (forms.XxxInput...) renders the input field
class Formulaire(FormulaireBootstrap):
     # radio buttons: a list of options, rendered by the RadioSelect widget;
     # error_messages: the "required field" error message
    titre = forms.ChoiceField(choices=listes.TITRES, widget=forms.RadioSelect,
                              error_messages={"required": "Le titre est obligatoire."})
     # an input field; required=False: the field is not required
    nom = forms.CharField(required=False)
     # a password: never displayed again on the page
    mot_de_passe = forms.CharField(label="Mot de passe", required=False, widget=forms.PasswordInput)
     # a date: an <input type="date"> field; the value is a Python date
    naissance = forms.DateField(label="Date de naissance", required=False,
                                widget=forms.DateInput(attrs={"type": "date"}))
     # checkboxes: a list of options MULTIPLES
    loisirs = forms.MultipleChoiceField(choices=listes.LOISIRS, required=False,
                                        widget=forms.CheckboxSelectMultiple)
     # drop-down list: the default widget for a ChoiceField
    pays = forms.ChoiceField(choices=listes.PAYS)
     # multiple-select list, displayed on four lines
    langues = forms.MultipleChoiceField(label="Langues parlées", choices=listes.LANGUES,
                                        required=False,
                                        widget=forms.SelectMultiple(attrs={"size": 4}))
    commentaire = forms.CharField(required=False, widget=forms.Textarea(attrs={"rows": 2}))
     # a hidden field
    jeton = forms.CharField(widget=forms.HiddenInput)
  • Lines 10–23: A parent class for our forms, which assigns each input field the appropriate class (CSS derived from [Bootstrap]). It redefines the constructor ([__init__]), which receives the same parameters as that of [forms.Form] ([*args], [**kwargs], example 08), and begins by calling it ([super().__init__(...)]). The form’s [fields] attribute is then a dictionary of its fields; each field has its own widget ([champ.widget]), whose dictionary [attrs] contains the attributes HTML of the input field. [isinstance] accepts a tuple of classes: is the widget of one of these classes? Radio buttons and checkboxes take the class [form-check-input], lists take [form-select], and others take [form-control];
  • Lines 28–51: the fields, in the order they are displayed. Two objects must be distinguished: the field ([forms.XxxField]) converts and validates the value, as in the previous chapter; its widget ([forms.XxxInput], [forms.Select]...) draws the input field. Each field has a default widget, which is replaced by the parameter [widget]. By default, a field’s label is its name, formatted ([mot_de_passe] would become “Password,” [nom] “Name”); the parameter [label] selects it;
  • Lines 31–32: A [ChoiceField] is a drop-down list. With the [RadioSelect] widget, it becomes a group of radio buttons (a single selection). The [error_messages] parameter (example 09) displays the “required field” error message;
  • line 34: a [CharField] (default widget: [TextInput], a [<input type="text">]), optional. A required field ([required=True], the default) generates the attribute HTML [required], which the browser checks (example 19);
  • line 36: a password (widget [PasswordInput], a [<input type="password">]), which is never returned to the page: its field is always empty when displayed;
  • lines 38–39: a date ([DateField]), whose value will be an object [date] of type [Python]. The [DateInput] widget receives the [type="date"] attribute: a [<input type="date">] field, for which the browser displays a calendar. Such a field exchanges its value with the server in the [aaaa-mm-jj] format, regardless of the format in which the browser displays it ([DateField] accepts this format);
  • lines 41–42: a [MultipleChoiceField] (example 10), drawn by the [CheckboxSelectMultiple] widget: checkboxes;
  • Line 44: a [ChoiceField] with its default widget, [Select]: a drop-down list;
  • Lines 46–48: a [MultipleChoiceField] with its default widget, [SelectMultiple]: a multi-select list, displayed across four lines (the HTML [size] attribute, specified by [attrs]);
  • line 49: a text box ([Textarea]), spanning two lines;
  • line 51: a hidden field ([HiddenInput]).

[Django] also provides [EmailField] (example 19), [IntegerField], [DecimalField], [URLField], [BooleanField] (a single checkbox), [FileField], [ImageField], [SlugField], [UUIDField], [JSONField]... and other widgets: [EmailInput], [NumberInput], [CheckboxInput], [ClearableFileInput], [SelectDateWidget] (three lists: day, month, year)...

docs.title: 4.6.3. Field layout: config/rendu.py and form templates
docs.text:
A [Django] form is automatically generated using templates: one template for the entire form, one for each complete field (label, input field, tooltip, error messages), and one for each type of widget. [Django] provides all these templates in the [django.forms] application, with a neutral layout. To achieve the layout of [Bootstrap], we replace a few of them. First, [Django] must search for the form templates, just like the others, in the folders defined by the [TEMPLATES] configuration: this is the role of a form renderer:

# config/rendu.py: the form rendering engine

from django.forms.renderers import TemplatesSetting


# TemplatesSetting: a rendering engine that searches for its templates just like the others
# project templates (TEMPLATES setting): a template from the project’s templates folder
# can therefore replace Django’s
class RenduBootstrap(TemplatesSetting):
     # the template for a complete field: label, input field, tooltip, error messages
    field_template_name = "formulaires/champ.html"
  • line 9: [TemplatesSetting] is the form renderer that searches for its templates using the project’s template engine: a template from the project’s [templates] folder can therefore replace a template from [Django] with the same name. Our class inherits this behavior;
  • Line 11: The [field_template_name] attribute specifies the template for a complete field: ours, [formulaires/champ.html].

The configuration:

# config/settings.py: the configuration for Example 18

from pathlib import Path

BASE_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
DEBUG = True
SECRET_KEY = "django-insecure-b13ls-fk@*cj%i9(=5e1aa_eg(j0&*2cs)oc=j+qo&(!v06l^y"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = []
LANGUAGE_CODE = "fr"
TIME_ZONE = "Europe/Paris"
ROOT_URLCONF = "config.urls"
WSGI_APPLICATION = "config.wsgi.application"

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    "django.contrib.staticfiles",
     # Django form templates (one template per field type)
    "django.forms",
    "formulaire",
]

MIDDLEWARE = [
     # TOUTES's anti-CSRF protection for POST requests (see below)
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
]

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        "BACKEND": "django.template.backends.django.DjangoTemplates",
        "DIRS": [BASE_DIR / "templates"],
         # APP_DIRS: Django also looks for templates in the "templates" folder of
         # each application, including django.forms
        "APP_DIRS": True,
    },
]

# the MOTEUR DE RENDU forms: ours, which renders the fields using the
# Bootstrap 5 classes (see config/rendu.py)
FORM_RENDERER = "config.rendu.RenduBootstrap"

STATIC_URL = "static/"
STATICFILES_DIRS = [
    BASE_DIR / "static",
    BASE_DIR.parent / "commun" / "static",
]
  • line 17: the application [django.forms], which provides the form templates from [Django], in its folder [templates];
  • Lines 21–24: the anti-CSRF protection middleware (see below);
  • line 32: [APP_DIRS: True]: [Django] also searches for templates in the [templates] folder of each declared application, including [django.forms]. The [DIRS] folders are checked first: our templates take precedence over those in [Django];
  • line 38: the [FORM_RENDERER] setting specifies our rendering engine.

The template for a complete field:

{# a complete field, with Bootstrap classes; field: the field to render #}
{% if field.use_fieldset %}
  {# a group of radio buttons or checkboxes: a fieldset and its label #}
  <fieldset class="mb-3">
    <legend class="form-label fs-6 mb-1">{{ field.label }}</legend>
    {{ field }}
{% else %}
  <div class="mb-3">
    <label class="form-label" for="{{ field.id_for_label }}">{{ field.label }}</label>
    {{ field }}
{% endif %}
    {% if field.help_text %}<div class="form-text" id="{{ field.auto_id }}_helptext">{{ field.help_text }}</div>{% endif %}
    {% if field.errors %}<div class="invalid-feedback d-block" id="{{ field.auto_id }}_error">{% for erreur in field.errors %}{{ erreur }}{% if not forloop.last %}<br>{% endif %}{% endfor %}</div>{% endif %}
{% if field.use_fieldset %}</fieldset>{% else %}</div>{% endif %}

The template receives the field to be rendered, [field] (a [BoundField] object: the field, linked to the form, and therefore to its value and errors):

  • Lines 2–6: A group of radio buttons or checkboxes ([field.use_fieldset] applies to these widgets) is surrounded by a [<fieldset>], whose caption ([<legend>]) is the group label: this is what screen readers expect;
  • lines 8–10: another field has a [<label>], linked to the input field by its identifier ([id_for_label]: [id_nom], by default [id_] followed by the field name). [{{ field }}] defines the input field using its widget’s template;
  • line 12: the field’s help text (parameter [help_text] for a field), if it has one;
  • line 13: the field’s errors ([field.errors]), using the classes from [Bootstrap] ([invalid-feedback]: red text, [d-block]: always visible). Its identifier, [id_nom_error], is the one specified by [Django] in the [aria-describedby] attribute of the input field, so that screen readers read the message along with the field;
  • Line 14: the closing tag for the tag opened in the first part.

Finally, two widget templates from [Django] are replaced so that the radio buttons and checkboxes are displayed in the same way as in [Bootstrap], side by side:

{# replaces the Django template: a group of radio buttons or checkboxes, side by side #}
<div id="{{ widget.attrs.id }}">{% for group, options, index in widget.optgroups %}{% for option in options %}
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">{% include option.template_name with widget=option %}</div>{% endfor %}{% endfor %}
</div>

{# Replaces the Django template: UN radio button or UNE checkbox, followed by its label #}
{% include "django/forms/widgets/input.html" %}
<label class="form-check-label" for="{{ widget.attrs.id }}">{{ widget.label }}</label>

They have exactly the same names and paths as the templates in [Django] that they replace ([django/forms/widgets/...], found in the [django/forms/templates] folder of the library):

  • [multiple_input.html] draws the group: for each option ([widget.optgroups]: the options, grouped together; we have no subgroups), a [<div class="form-check form-check-inline">] that contains the option, drawn using its own template ([option.template_name]);
  • [input_option.html] renders an option: the input field ([<input type="radio">] or [<input type="checkbox">], using the template from [Django] and [input.html]), followed by its label.

All of this needs to be written only once: Examples 19, 21, and 28, as well as the case study, use these files. Ready-made libraries, such as [django-crispy-forms] and its package [crispy-bootstrap5], or [django-bootstrap5], do the same; we preferred to demonstrate the mechanism.

docs.title: 4.6.4. The view: form/views.py
docs.text:
# form/views.py: a form that uses all types of fields

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods

from .forms import Formulaire

# the initial values (one per field, a list for a multi-select field)
INITIALES = {"titre": "Mme", "pays": "fr", "langues": ["français"], "jeton": "A7X2"}


# GET: the form, with initial values; POST: the submitted fields are
# read, validated, and then redisplayed by the same form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def formulaire(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
         # initial: the values displayed until something is submitted
        return render(request, "formulaire/formulaire.html",
                      {"formulaire": Formulaire(initial=INITIALES)})
     # a form LIÉ for the submitted data: it converts and validates them
    formulaire = Formulaire(request.POST)
    valide = formulaire.is_valid()
    donnees = None
    if valide:
         # cleaned_data: the values converted by each field; a list (for fields
         # multiple) is written as text, with its values separated by commas
        donnees = {cle: ", ".join(valeur) if isinstance(valeur, list) else valeur
                   for cle, valeur in formulaire.cleaned_data.items()}
     # what the browser actually sent, field by field; lists(): the
     # pairs (name, list of all the field’s values)
    recu = "\n".join(f"{nom} = [{', '.join(valeurs)}]" for nom, valeurs in request.POST.lists())
    return render(request, "formulaire/formulaire.html", {
        "formulaire": formulaire,
        "recu": recu,
        "valide": valide,
        "donnees": donnees,
    })
  • line 9: the form’s initial values: a dictionary, one value per field (a list for a multi-value field);
  • line 14: a single view for both methods: GET displays the form, POST processes it;
  • lines 16–19: in GET, an unbound form (without data), with its initial values (parameter [initial]): it is not validated and does not display any errors;
  • lines 21–22: in POST, a form linked to the submitted fields ([request.POST]), then validated ([is_valid], previous chapter): each field converts its value (the date, the lists, etc.), verifies that a selection is among those that were offered, and applies its constraints;
  • lines 24–28: if the form is valid, its data is converted ([cleaned_data]) into a human-readable dictionary (using the [{clé: valeur for ...}] syntax): a list is written as text, with its elements separated by commas ([", ".join(...)]);
  • Line 31: For this example, what the browser actually sent. The method [lists()] of a [QueryDict] (Example 10) iterates through the pairs (name, list of all values). The string [\n] is a line break;
  • lines 32–37: the linked form is passed to the template, which will display it, along with the user’s input and any errors.

docs.title: 4.6.5. The template: templates/form/formulaire.html
docs.text:
{% extends "layout.html" %}

{% block contenu %}
  <h1 class="h3">Un formulaire complet</h1>
  <form method="post" action="{% url 'formulaire' %}" style="max-width: 40rem">
    {# the anti-CSRF token: a hidden field that the middleware CsrfViewMiddleware verifies #}
    {% csrf_token %}
    {# as_field_group: a complete field (label, input field, error messages) #}
    {{ formulaire.titre.as_field_group }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ formulaire.nom.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ formulaire.mot_de_passe.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ formulaire.naissance.as_field_group }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ formulaire.loisirs.as_field_group }}
    <div class="row g-2">
      <div class="col">{{ formulaire.pays.as_field_group }}</div>
      <div class="col">{{ formulaire.langues.as_field_group }}</div>
    </div>
    {{ formulaire.commentaire.as_field_group }}
    {# a hidden field: the input field alone, without a label #}
    {{ formulaire.jeton }}
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Envoyer</button>
  </form>
  {# received: present in the context if the form was submitted #}
  {% if recu %}
    <h2 class="h5 mt-3">Ce que le serveur a reçu</h2>
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">{{ recu }}</pre>
    <p>Formulaire valide : {{ valide|yesno:"oui,non" }}</p>
    <ul>
      {# errors: a dictionary {field: list of errors}; items: its key-value pairs #}
      {% for champ, erreurs in formulaire.errors.items %}
        {% for erreur in erreurs %}<li>{{ champ }} : {{ erreur }}</li>{% endfor %}
      {% endfor %}
    </ul>
    {% if valide %}
      <p>Les données du formulaire :</p>
      <ul>
        {% for cle, valeur in donnees.items %}
          <li>{{ cle }} : {{ valeur }}</li>
        {% endfor %}
      </ul>
    {% endif %}
  {% endif %}
{% endblock %}
  • Line 5: The [<form>] tag, entered manually: the [Django] form does not generate it;
  • line 7: the [{% csrf_token %}] tag creates a hidden field containing the anti-CSRF token (see below);
  • line 9: [{{ formulaire.titre }}] refers to the [titre] field in the form (a [BoundField]); its method [as_field_group] renders it in full using the template [formulaires/champ.html]: label, input field (with its current value), and error messages;
  • lines 10–20: the other fields, arranged according to the grid classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 22: the hidden field, of which only the input field is rendered;
  • line 26: the variable [recu] exists only after a submission; a missing variable is “false”;
  • lines 32–34: the errors. [formulaire.errors] is a dictionary, which is iterated over using [items] (without parentheses, as in DTL): for each field, the list of its errors;
  • lines 39–41: a loop over a dictionary that iterates through both the keys and the values.

We could have written the entire form in a single line: [{{ formulaire }}], which renders all the fields in order using the form template (rendering engine setting [form_template_name]). By processing the fields one by one, you can arrange them as you like.

docs.title: 4.6.6. CSRF Protection
docs.text:
A CSRF attack (Cross-Site Request Forgery) involves a malicious site tricking the victim’s browser into sending a form to our application. The browser includes our application’s cookies in the request—and thus the logged-in user’s session—so the request appears legitimate. The solution: every form in our application contains a random token that the malicious site cannot know.

[Django] applies this to the entire application via a middleware component, [CsrfViewMiddleware] (line 23 of the file [config/settings.py]). When a page is generated, the [{% csrf_token %}] tag writes to the hidden field [csrfmiddlewaretoken], and the middleware sends, along with the response, a cookie named [csrftoken], which contains a secret. For any request that modifies (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), before rendering the view, the middleware verifies that the token sent (in the [csrfmiddlewaretoken] field, or in the [X-CSRFToken] header, for a request sent via [JavaScript]) matches the cookie’s secret. A malicious site cannot read our site’s cookie or view our pages: it cannot generate a valid token. If the verification fails, the view is not called: [Django] responds with a 403 error on its own. This is a significant difference from [Symfony], whose Form component verified the token for each form and let the action decide what to do next: With [Django], all POST requests are protected, and a view cannot forget to be protected. The [@csrf_exempt] decorator exempts a view from this verification (for a API called by other servers, for example).

docs.title: 4.6.7. Execution
docs.text:
The initial values are visible: the “Mrs.” radio button, the country “France,” and the language “French.” The HTML generates (excerpts):

<form method="post" action="/formulaire" style="max-width: 40rem">
    <input type="hidden" name="csrfmiddlewaretoken" value="nz41EEOJgdJJDxCYFtTWLl9AEEBdxQmnR6Rs8F8f0Xvr10ayE7RJproG7YEWvhWi">
    <fieldset class="mb-3">
    <legend class="form-label fs-6 mb-1">Titre</legend>
    <div id="id_titre">
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
<input type="radio" name="titre" value="Mr" class="form-check-input" required id="id_titre_0">
<label class="form-check-label" for="id_titre_0">Mr</label>
</div>
  <div class="form-check form-check-inline">
<input type="radio" name="titre" value="Mme" class="form-check-input" required id="id_titre_1" checked>
<label class="form-check-label" for="id_titre_1">Mme</label>
</div>
...
<input type="checkbox" name="loisirs" value="lecture" class="form-check-input" id="id_loisirs_0">
...
    <select name="langues" size="4" class="form-select" id="id_langues" multiple>
  <option value="français" selected>français</option>
  <option value="anglais">anglais</option>
...
    <input type="hidden" name="jeton" value="A7X2" class="form-control" id="id_jeton">
    <button class="btn btn-primary" type="submit">Envoyer</button>
  </form>

[Django] has written everything: the identifiers ([id_titre_1]), the labels associated with their fields, the field names (the checkboxes all have the name [loisirs]: the browser will send a repeated parameter, e.g., 10), the attributes [checked] and [selected] for current values, the attribute [required] for required fields, and the classes of [Bootstrap]. The first hidden field contains the anti-CSRF token; it is different on every page (it is “masked” by a random number, so that a network eavesdropper cannot guess the secret by comparing multiple pages). Let’s fill out the form and submit it:

The page shows what the server received: one parameter per field, with multiple values for the checkboxes and the dropdown list; the password was sent but is not displayed again in its field. The browser displayed the date according to its own settings, but sent it in the format [aaaa-mm-jj]; the template formatted it in the French style, [14 mai 1990], just like any date it displays. The hidden field [jeton] was sent back exactly as is: this is how information that the user cannot see is sent back and forth (the case study uses this for a record’s version number). However, a hidden field is not a protected field: the user can modify it using their browser’s developer tools, and the server must validate it just like any other field. The anti-CSRF token is also included among the received fields; it is not part of the form data.

Now let's submit a form using [curl], without a token, and with a country that wasn't listed:

curl -i -d "nom=Martin&pays=xx" http://localhost:8000/form

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
...
  <title>403 Forbidden</title>
...

The request did not proceed beyond the middleware: the view was not called, and the server console indicates this:

Forbidden (CSRF cookie not set.): /formulaire
[27/Sep/2026 19:30:21] "POST /formulaire HTTP/1.1" 403 2567

In a browser, the error page for [Django] explains the reason for the rejection (in debug mode):

For the token to be accepted, [curl] must behave like a browser: first request the form, retaining the [csrftoken] cookie (option [-c], which saves received cookies to a file), then resend the cookie (option [-b]) and the token read from the page:

curl -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/form
curl -b cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=VHhabRgR...GKF&nom=Martin&pays=xx&jeton=A7X2" http://localhost:8000/form

...
    <pre class="bg-light p-2 border">csrfmiddlewaretoken = [VHhabRgRYFWR4Y5STU7Cto4curX1DysB8tDcThyhCVZZbHeGwk3l3pjeMmAGHVKF]
nom = [Martin]
pays = [xx]
jeton = [A7X2]</pre>
    <p>Formulaire valide : non</p>
    <ul>


        <li>titre : Le titre est obligatoire.</li>

        <li>pays : Sélectionnez un choix valide. xx n’en fait pas partie.</li>

    </ul>
...

(the token is the one from the page received by the first request). This time, the view was called, and the form is invalid for two reasons: no title was sent, and the country [xx] is not among the options. This final check is performed by the [ChoiceField] field itself, without us having requested it: a malicious user could send anything, not just what the page suggested. Here, the view returns the invalid form with a 200 status code; the following example will choose a more appropriate status code.

docs.title: 4.7. Example 19: Form Validation
docs.text:
A registration form, in which each field has its own constraints. If an error occurs, the form is redisplayed with the user’s input and a message below each invalid field. We add a rule that applies to two fields: the password and its confirmation must match.

19-validation-formulaire/
├── config/
│   ├── rendu.py
│   ├── settings.py
│   └── ...
├── inscription/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── forms.py
│   └── views.py
├── static/
│   └── ...
├── templates/
│   ├── formulaires/
│   │   └── champ.html
│   ├── inscription/
│   │   ├── bienvenue.html
│   │   └── inscription.html
│   └── layout.html
└── manage.py

The files [config/settings.py], [config/rendu.py], and [templates/formulaires/champ.html] are the same as those in Example 18.

docs.title: 4.7.1. The form: registration/forms.py
docs.text:
# registration/forms.py: the registration form, its fields, and their constraints

from django import forms


# the parent class from Example 18: Bootstrap’s CSS classes
class FormulaireBootstrap(forms.Form):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        for champ in self.fields.values():
            champ.widget.attrs["class"] = "form-control"


class InscriptionForm(FormulaireBootstrap):
     # max_length: a constraint validated by the server, which Django also writes to
     # the page (the `maxlength` attribute) for the browser
    nom = forms.CharField(max_length=20, error_messages={
        "required": "Le nom est obligatoire.",
        "max_length": "Le nom ne doit pas dépasser 20 caractères."})
     # EmailField: a valid address with a fully qualified domain name (exemple.fr, not “example”)
    email = forms.EmailField(label="Adresse électronique", error_messages={
        "required": "L'adresse électronique est obligatoire.",
        "invalid": "Adresse électronique invalide."})
     # IntegerField: an integer; an entry that is not an integer results in an "invalid" error
    age = forms.IntegerField(label="Âge", min_value=18, max_value=120, error_messages={
        "required": "L'âge est obligatoire.",
        "invalid": "Un nombre entier est attendu.",
        "min_value": "L'âge doit être compris entre 18 et 120 ans.",
        "max_value": "L'âge doit être compris entre 18 et 120 ans."})
    mot_de_passe = forms.CharField(label="Mot de passe", min_length=6, widget=forms.PasswordInput,
                                   error_messages={
                                       "required": "Le mot de passe est obligatoire.",
                                       "min_length": "Le mot de passe doit comporter au moins 6 caractères."})
    confirmation = forms.CharField(label="Confirmation", widget=forms.PasswordInput,
                                   error_messages={"required": "La confirmation est obligatoire."})

     # clean: validation of the form ENTIER, after each field has been validated. It is
     # where two fields are compared
    def clean(self):
        donnees = super().clean()
        mot_de_passe = donnees.get("mot_de_passe")
        confirmation = donnees.get("confirmation")
         # Both fields passed their own validation checks but differ
        if mot_de_passe and confirmation and mot_de_passe != confirmation:
             # add_error: an error associated with the confirmation field
            self.add_error("confirmation", "La confirmation ne correspond pas au mot de passe.")
        return donnees
  • lines 7–11: the parent class from Example 18, simplified: all fields are input fields;
  • lines 17–19: the name is required and must not exceed 20 characters. Each error is assigned a message in French based on its code (e.g., 09). The parameter [max_length] has two effects: the field checks the length (on the server), and its widget sets the attribute HTML [maxlength], which limits the input in the browser ([min_length] does the same, with the attribute [minlength]);
  • lines 21–23: a [EmailField] verifies that an address is valid and requires a fully qualified domain name ([exemple.fr], not [exemple]). Its widget, [EmailInput], generates a [<input type="email">], which the browser can validate;
  • lines 25–29: a [IntegerField] produces a [<input type="number">], with the attributes [min] and [max] derived from [min_value] and [max_value], and converts the input to an integer. An entry that is not an integer produces the error [invalid];
  • lines 30–35: the password (at least 6 characters) and its confirmation, two [CharField] fields using the [PasswordInput] widget. A parameter can span multiple lines;
  • lines 39–47: the method [clean] validates the entire form after validating each field (and its methods [clean_<champ>], example 12). [super().clean()] returns [cleaned_data], which contains only the valid fields: [donnees.get("mot_de_passe")] equals [None] if the password has already been rejected (too short). The comparison is performed only if both fields are valid; if they differ, [add_error] attaches an error to the [confirmation] field ([add_error(None, "...")] would attach it to the form itself: a “general” error, which is returned by [non_field_errors()]). This is the way to validate a rule that applies to multiple fields.

docs.text:
# registration/views.py: a form validated by the server

from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods

from .forms import InscriptionForm


# GET /registration: the form; ?html5=true: the browser is allowed to validate it
# before submission. POST /registration: the submitted form
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def inscription(request):
    html5 = request.GET.get("html5") == "true"
    if request.method == "POST":
        formulaire = InscriptionForm(request.POST)
         # is_valid: each field was successfully converted and meets its constraints, and
         # the `clean` method did not report any errors
        if formulaire.is_valid():
            return render(request, "inscription/bienvenue.html",
                          {"inscription": formulaire.cleaned_data})
         # an invalid form, redisplayed with the input and errors, with the
         # code 422 (Unprocessable Content)
        return render(request, "inscription/inscription.html",
                      {"formulaire": formulaire, "html5": html5}, status=422)
     # the initial display: an empty form
    return render(request, "inscription/inscription.html",
                  {"formulaire": InscriptionForm(), "html5": html5})
  • Line 13: The parameter [?html5=true] enables browser validation (see below);
  • lines 15–20: a form linked to the submitted fields. If it is valid, the welcome page receives its data (the following example will show that it is better to redirect after a successful POST);
  • lines 23–24: otherwise, the form is redisplayed, showing the input and any errors, along with code 422 (Unprocessable Content: “the request is well-formed, but its content is invalid”);
  • lines 26–27: on the first display, an empty, unbound form.

The invalid form is therefore redisplayed by the POST view itself, which retains the input and errors: this is the standard approach used by [Django], as well as by [Symfony]. Other frameworks, such as [Laravel], instead respond by redirecting to the form page, while preserving the input and errors in the session for the next request.

docs.title: 4.7.4. Execution
docs.text:
Let’s submit a form full of errors: a name consisting of spaces, an address without a full domain, an age of 12, a password that’s too short, and a different confirmation:

The input was retained (except for the passwords), and each error is flagged below its corresponding field. The name consisting of spaces is flagged as missing: a ***[CharField] removes the spaces surrounding each entry (parameter ***[strip]***, example 08), and redisplays the cleaned-up value. The confirmation, however, contains no errors, even though it differs from the password: since the password was rejected, the [clean] method did not compare them. URL is the form’s token, [/inscription]*: the page was displayed by the view in response to POST. With [curl], by providing the anti-CSRF token as in Example 18, you can also send something a browser would not send—a non-numeric age:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=...&nom=Martin&email=jean.martin@exemple.fr&age=abc&mot_de_passe=secret123&confirmation=secret123" http://localhost:8000/registration

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
...
    <label class="form-label" for="id_age">Âge</label>
    <input type="number" name="age" value="abc" min="18" max="120" class="form-control" required aria-invalid="true" aria-describedby="id_age_error" id="id_age">
    <div class="invalid-feedback d-block" id="id_age_error">Un nombre entier est attendu.</div>
...

We see the input redisplayed, the attributes HTML5 ([required], [min], [max]), the error message [invalid], and the attributes [aria-invalid] and [aria-describedby]—which [Django] automatically adds to a field with an error—and which link the field to its message for screen readers.

docs.title: 4.7.5. Browser validation
docs.text:
Let's remove the [novalidate] attribute by clicking the "Enable" link (parameter [?html5=true]). The browser then checks the attributes [required], [type="email"], [min], [max], [maxlength]... before submitting the form, and displays its own messages in a tooltip below the first field with an error (“Please fill in this field,” “The value must be greater than or equal to 18,” etc.): the form is not submitted as long as there is an error. [Django] generated these attributes automatically based on the fields: [required] for any required field, [maxlength] and [minlength] based on [max_length] and [min_length], [min] and [max] based on [min_value] and [max_value], [type="email"] and [type="number"] based on the widgets. They therefore always comply with the server’s constraints. Only the rule for the [clean] method (confirmation) is not handled by the browser.

This validation is convenient for the user: it’s immediate, with no back-and-forth with the server. But it does not replace the server’s validation: a user can disable it, and a program like [curl] ignores it completely. The rule is absolute: the server always validates; browser validation is merely an added convenience.

A correct entry, at last. The name, entered with spaces on either side, was cleaned up by the form:

docs.title: 4.8. Example 20: The Post/Redirect/Get Pattern
docs.text:
When a POST view responds with a page, that page is the result of a POST. If the user reloads it (presses [F5]), the browser sends the POST, after a warning that few people read: the command is sent twice, and the message is posted twice. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern (PRG) avoids this problem: a successful POST view does not render a page; it responds with a redirect (example 04) to a page GET, which the browser requests immediately. Reloading this page simply re-executes the GET.

One problem remains: the GET page would like to display a message (“the task has been added”), but it is the POST view that knows this message, and it cannot pass a variable to a request that has not yet occurred. The solution: a flash message, posted by the POST view, which is retained until it is read, displayed, and then discarded. [Django] provides these through its [django.contrib.messages] application.

docs.title: 4.8.2. The service: tasks/service.py
docs.text:
# tasks/service.py: the list of tasks, shared by all users

import threading

# The server process remains in memory from one request to the next: a variable of the
# MODULE lives as long as the server. The list is therefore shared by all
# requests from all users (and is lost when the server shuts down)
_taches = ["Lire le chapitre 3"]

# the server processes multiple requests EN MÊME TEMPS, in multiple threads
# (threads): a lock ensures that only one thread at a time modifies the list
_verrou = threading.Lock()


def liste() -> list[str]:
     # a copy: the caller cannot modify the service’s list
    with _verrou:
        return list(_taches)


def ajouter(libelle: str) -> None:
     # with: the lock is acquired here and released upon exiting the block, even after an exception
    with _verrou:
        _taches.append(libelle)

The task list is shared by all users and must persist from one request to the next. We saw this in Examples 01 and 06: in [Python], the server remains in memory from one request to the next. A simple module variable is therefore sufficient. Readers of the [Symfony] course will recall that, in [PHP], the list had to be stored in a cache or a file.

  • Line 8: the list, a module variable. It exists for as long as the server process runs: it is lost when the server shuts down or restarts (after a code change, during development). And if the production server runs multiple processes (which is standard practice: one per processor, for example), each will have its own list. A real-world application would therefore store the list in a database (Chapter 7);
  • Line 12: The development server processes multiple requests at the same time, each in its own thread. Two simultaneous updates could conflict. A lock ([threading.Lock]) ensures that only one thread at a time executes the code it protects;
  • lines 15–18: The function returns a copy of the list, created under the protection of the lock;
  • lines 21–24: The statement [with] acquires the lock, executes the block, and then releases the lock—in all cases, even if an exception interrupts the block. An object that can be used by [with] is called a context manager; files are another example ([with open(...) as f:] closes the file at the end of the block).

The service is a module, not a class: its functions are called by [service.liste()] and [service.ajouter(...)]. This is the simplest way, in [Python], to have a single object shared by the entire application (Example 06).

docs.title: 4.8.3. Views: tasks/views.py
docs.text:
# tasks/views.py: the Post/Redirect/Get pattern

from django.contrib import messages
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_http_methods, require_POST

from . import service


# GET /tasks: the list and the form for adding tasks; POST /tasks: adding a task, according to the
# Post/Redirect/Get pattern
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST"])
def taches(request):
    if request.method == "GET":
        return render(request, "taches/taches.html", {"taches": service.liste()})
    libelle = request.POST.get("libelle", "").strip()
    if libelle == "" or len(libelle) > 40:
         # Invalid input: the page is reloaded without redirection
        return render(request, "taches/taches.html", {
            "taches": service.liste(),
            "libelle": libelle,
            "erreur": "Le libellé doit comporter de 1 à 40 caractères."})
    service.ajouter(libelle)
     # a "flash" message: it will survive the redirection for the request SUIVANTE
    messages.success(request, f"La tâche [{libelle}] a été ajoutée.")
     # No page: a redirect to the page GET
    return redirect("taches")


# POST /tasks/no-program: the counterexample (a page in response to POST)
@require_POST
def ajouter_sans_prg(request):
    service.ajouter(request.POST.get("libelle", "").strip() or "(sans titre)")
    return render(request, "taches/taches.html", {"taches": service.liste(), "sans_prg": True})
  • lines 16–22: The input is validated manually to keep the example concise ([strip] removes the surrounding spaces). An invalid entry is redisplayed without redirection: there is nothing to protect against a duplicate submission, since nothing has been modified;
  • line 25: [messages.success] displays a “success” level flash message " (there are also [debug], [info], [warning], and [error]: the level allows messages to be displayed differently);
  • line 27: the redirect to the page GET, named [taches] (example 04);
  • lines 31–34: the counterexample: a page in response to POST. The operator [or] returns its left operand if it is “true” (here, a non-empty string), and the right operand otherwise.

docs.title: 4.8.5. Where are flash messages stored?
docs.text:
Between the POST request and the subsequent GET request, the message must be stored somewhere. We chose a cookie. Let’s examine it using [curl], by saving the cookies to a file (options [-c] and [-b], Example 18), after requesting the page to obtain the anti-CSRF token:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -d "csrfmiddlewaretoken=...&libelle=Faire%20les%20exercices" http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Location: /taches
Set-Cookie: messages=.eJyLjlaKj88qzs-Lz00tLk5MT1XSMdAxMtVR8klUKIkpNTBINUrOSFWIdkvMLEpVyEktVkitSC1KzkxOLY5VSFQAq7CEKLRUSMzKL4WyU_WUdJSUYmMB-SAezw:1xAsin:eyFszHLnZB1gbIkSumQ9Au2Fcc-M4jZeI-3gHV-o6uI; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax

The response to POST is a redirect (status code 302, header [Location]), accompanied by the cookie [messages]. This cookie is [HttpOnly] (the [JavaScript] on the page cannot read it) and [SameSite=Lax] (the browser does not send it with a POST request originating from another site). Its value consists of three parts, separated by colons: the data, a date (encoded in base 62), and a signature. The data is the list of messages, in JSON, compressed and then base-64-encoded (the leading period indicates compression). When decoded, they yield:

[["__json_message",0,25,"La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée.",""]]

It shows the message level (25: success) and its text. The cookie’s content is therefore not secret: anyone can decode it. But it is signed: the signature is calculated based on the data and the application’s secret key ([SECRET_KEY], example 01). If the browser sends back a modified cookie, the signature no longer matches, and [Django] ignores it: a user cannot fabricate fake messages. Let’s follow the redirect by sending back the cookie:

curl -i -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8000/tasks

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Vary: Cookie
Set-Cookie: messages=""; expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=0; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
...
      <div class="alert alert-success" role="status">La tâche [Faire les exercices] a été ajoutée.</div>
...
      <li>Lire le chapitre 3</li>

      <li>Faire les exercices</li>
...

The message is displayed; the middleware, seeing that it has been read, deletes the cookie (an empty cookie that expired in 1970). A new request, GET, would no longer display the message. The [Vary: Cookie] header alerts caches that the response depends on the request’s cookies. The task list, meanwhile, is stored in the server’s memory.

docs.text:
Adding a task: the browser followed the redirect; the URL header corresponds to the GET page, which can be safely reloaded.

An invalid entry, redisplayed with its error message:

The counterexample: the page is the response to POST, and its URL is [/taches/sans-prg]. If you click on [F5], the browser asks if you want to resubmit the form; if you agree, the task is added a second time.

docs.title: 4.9. Example 21: Links, Buttons, and Confirmation
docs.text:
A principle of the HTTP protocol: a GET request does not change anything. Browsers, search engines, and tools that preload pages freely follow links without asking the user for permission. A “delete” link ([<a href="/contacts/2/supprimer">]) would therefore be dangerous: a bot crawling the site would delete everything. In a web application:

  • viewing is done via a link ([<a href>]), which sends a GET request;
  • editing (save, duplicate, delete) is done via a button placed in a form, protected by an anti-CSRF token.

This example manages a contact list and displays a confirmation window before each deletion.

docs.title: 4.9.1. Method simulation: config/middleware.py
docs.text:
A HTML form can only send GET and POST requests. However, the HTTP protocol supports other methods: DELETE for deletion, and PUT and PATCH for updates. Many frameworks work around this limitation: a POST form that contains a hidden field [_method], with a value of [DELETE] (or [PUT], [PATCH]), is treated as a request for that method. This is known as method spoofing. [Symfony] offered this as an option; [Django] does not. Let’s implement it as middleware:

# config/middleware.py: a form’s HTTP method, replaced by its _method field

# A HTML form can only send GET and POST. A POST form that contains a
# hidden field _method (DELETE, PUT, PATCH) is treated as a request for this method
class MethodeSurchargee:
    METHODES = {"DELETE", "PUT", "PATCH"}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

     # process_view: Django calls this APRÈS during routing, just before the view (and after the
     # process_view of the middleware preceding it, including the one that checks the
     # anti-CSRF token of a POST). Return None: the request continues on its way
    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
        if request.method == "POST":
            methode = request.POST.get("_method", "").upper()
            if methode in self.METHODES:
                request.method = methode
        return None
  • line 6: a class attribute: the set ([set], enclosed in curly braces) of accepted methods;
  • lines 11–12: [__call__] passes the request on without doing anything;
  • lines 17–22: the method [process_view]: [Django] calls it after routing, just before calling the view, with the selected view and its parameters (the chapter on the lifecycle will cover this in detail). If the request is a POST whose [_method] field points to one of the accepted methods, the middleware replaces the method in the request. Returning [None] allows the request to continue on its path.

Why [process_view], and not [__call__]? Because of anti-CSRF protection. The [CsrfViewMiddleware] middleware performs its validation within its own method, [process_view], which is called before ours, since it precedes it in the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration. The token is therefore validated on the POST request, before we transform it into DELETE. This is what the comment in the [config/settings.py] file states:

# contacts/service.py: contacts, shared by all, in memory (see example 20)

import threading

from .modeles import Contact

_contacts = [
    Contact(1, "Marie Durand", "01 23 45 67 89"),
    Contact(2, "Paul Martin", "06 12 34 56 78"),
    Contact(3, "Philippe Jandot", "02 98 76 54 32"),
]
_dernier_id = 3
_verrou = threading.Lock()


def liste() -> list[Contact]:
    with _verrou:
        return list(_contacts)


# the contact, or None if it does not exist
def lire(id: int) -> Contact | None:
    with _verrou:
        return next((c for c in _contacts if c.id == id), None)


def modifier(id: int, nom: str, telephone: str) -> Contact | None:
    with _verrou:
         # enumerate: the (position, element) tuples in the list
        for i, contact in enumerate(_contacts):
            if contact.id == id:
                 # a contact is immutable (frozen): a new one is created, which
                 # replaces the old one in the list
                _contacts[i] = Contact(id, nom, telephone)
                return _contacts[i]
        return None


def ajouter(nom: str, telephone: str) -> Contact:
     # global: the function modifies the module’s variable _dernier_id (without this keyword,
     # the assignment would create a local variable)
    global _dernier_id
    with _verrou:
        _dernier_id += 1
        contact = Contact(_dernier_id, nom, telephone)
        _contacts.append(contact)
        return contact


def supprimer(id: int) -> Contact | None:
    with _verrou:
        for i, contact in enumerate(_contacts):
            if contact.id == id:
                 # pop removes element i from the list and returns it
                return _contacts.pop(i)
        return None

Contacts are stored in memory, just like the tasks in Example 20. Each contact is an immutable object [Contact] (an ID, a name, a phone number, file [contacts/modeles.py]). A few points about [Python]:

  • line 12: the last assigned identifier;
  • lines 27–36: a contact is immutable; we create a new one, which replaces the old one in the list. [enumerate] iterates through a list in pairs (position, element);
  • lines 39–47: a function that assigns a value to a module variable must declare it using [global] (line 42): without this keyword, the assignment [_dernier_id += 1] would create a local variable for the function (and would fail here, since it reads its value before assigning it). Reading a module variable, or modifying the list it refers to ([_contacts.append(...)]), does not require anything of the sort;
  • line 55: [pop(i)] removes the element at position [i] from the list and returns it;
  • The functions return [None] for a nonexistent contact: it is up to the view to decide on the response.

# contacts/views.py: links (GET) and buttons (POST, DELETE)

from django.contrib import messages
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import redirect, render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET, require_http_methods

from . import service
from .forms import ContactForm


# the contact, or a 404 error if it does not exist
def contact_ou_404(contact):
    if contact is None:
        raise Http404("contact inconnu")
    return contact


# a LIEN (<a href>): a GET request, which does not modify anything
@require_GET
def liste(request):
    return render(request, "contacts/liste.html", {"contacts": service.liste()})


# GET /contacts/2: the profile; POST /contacts/2: one of its two buttons;
# DELETE /contacts/2: deletion (a POST and its field _method)
@require_http_methods(["GET", "POST", "DELETE"])
def contact(request, id):
    if request.method == "DELETE":
        return supprimer(request, id)
    contact = contact_ou_404(service.lire(id))
    if request.method == "GET":
        formulaire = ContactForm(initial={"nom": contact.nom, "telephone": contact.telephone})
        return render(request, "contacts/fiche.html", {"contact": contact, "formulaire": formulaire})
    formulaire = ContactForm(request.POST)
    if not formulaire.is_valid():
        return render(request, "contacts/fiche.html", {"contact": contact, "formulaire": formulaire})
    nom = formulaire.cleaned_data["nom"]
    telephone = formulaire.cleaned_data["telephone"]
     # the clicked button is the only one to send its name: "duplicate" in request.POST
     # is true if this button submitted the form
    if "dupliquer" in request.POST:
        copie = service.ajouter(f"{nom} (copie)", telephone)
        messages.success(request, f"Le contact [{copie.nom}] a été créé.")
    else:
        service.modifier(id, nom, telephone)
        messages.success(request, f"Le contact [{nom}] a été modifié.")
    return redirect("contacts")


# deletion; the anti-CSRF token has already been verified by CsrfViewMiddleware
def supprimer(request, id):
    contact = contact_ou_404(service.supprimer(id))
    messages.success(request, f"Le contact [{contact.nom}] a été supprimé.")
    return redirect("contacts")
  • lines 13–16: a utility function—a nonexistent contact returns a 404 response to terminate the view;
  • lines 20–22: the GET view of the list, which does not modify anything;
  • lines 27–48: a contact’s record. In GET, it displays the form, populated with the contact’s information; in POST, it processes the form; in DELETE, it deletes the contact. The same URL and [/contacts/2] are thus used to view, save, and delete. The decorator [require_http_methods] is checked when the view is called, i.e., after [process_view]: it does indeed see the method DELETE;
  • lines 35–37: an invalid form is redisplayed;
  • lines 42–47: A form can have multiple submit buttons. When the form is submitted, the browser sends, in addition to the fields, the name (attribute [name]) of the clicked button, and only that button’s name. [in] checks for the presence of a key in a dictionary: ["dupliquer" in request.POST] is true if the form was submitted via the [dupliquer] button. Depending on the button, the view either duplicates or saves the contact;
  • line 48: in both cases, the PRG flow (example 20), with a flash message;
  • lines 52–55: deletion. It does not need to verify the anti-CSRF token: [CsrfViewMiddleware] did so beforehand. A missing or invalid token would have stopped the request with a 403 error.

docs.title: 4.9.6. The confirmation window
docs.text:
The browser can display a confirmation box (function [JavaScript] [confirm]), but it is not very attractive, and its appearance depends on the browser. Here we use a modal window from [Bootstrap], displayed by a few lines of [JavaScript]. The window is a fragment, included in the parent template, and is therefore present—though hidden—on all pages:

{# a single window for the entire page, hidden (d-none) by default #}
<div id="modale-confirmation" class="d-none">
  <div class="modal-backdrop fade show"></div>
  <div class="modal fade show d-block" tabindex="-1" role="alertdialog" aria-modal="true">
    <div class="modal-dialog modal-dialog-centered">
      <div class="modal-content">
        <div class="modal-header">
          <h5 class="modal-title">Confirmation</h5>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-body">
          <p class="mb-0" id="modale-confirmation-message"></p>
        </div>
        <div class="modal-footer">
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-secondary" data-action="non">Non, revenir</button>
          <button type="button" class="btn btn-danger" data-action="oui">Oui, confirmer</button>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
  • line 2: the [d-none] class from [Bootstrap] hides the element;
  • lines 3–4: the gray background, followed by the window, are drawn by the classes of [Bootstrap];
  • line 11: the message's position;
  • lines 14–15: the two buttons, of type [button] (not [submit]: they do not submit any form), distinguished by their [data-action] attribute.

  • Lines 12–14: Flash messages (example 20);
  • line 20: the window, included on all pages;
  • line 22: the script, placed at the bottom of the page: when it runs, the elements it searches for already exist. It is a static file, stored in the [static/js] folder.

The [static/js/app.js] script:

// Confirmation for forms with the data-confirmation="..." attribute
// Without JavaScript, these forms are simply submitted without confirmation.
(() => {
  const modale = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation');
  const message = document.getElementById('modale-confirmation-message');
  let enAttente = null; // The form to submit if confirmation is given

   // 1. We intercept the submission of forms requiring confirmation
  document.querySelectorAll('form[data-confirmation]').forEach((formulaire) => {
    formulaire.addEventListener('submit', (evenement) => {
      evenement.preventDefault(); // The submission is suspended
      enAttente = formulaire;
      message.textContent = formulaire.dataset.confirmation;
      modale.classList.remove('d-none'); // the window appears
    });
  });

   // 2. The two buttons in the window
  modale.addEventListener('click', (evenement) => {
    const action = evenement.target.dataset.action;
    if (action === 'oui') {
      enAttente.submit(); // Submit, SANS Trigger the 'submit' event again
    } else if (action === 'non') {
      modale.classList.add('d-none');
      enAttente = null;
    }
  });
})();
  • line 3: the code is enclosed in an anonymous function that is executed immediately; its variables do not interfere with those of the other scripts on the page;
  • lines 4–6: the window, the message location, and the form awaiting confirmation;
  • Lines 9–16: For each form that has the [data-confirmation] attribute, the [submit] event—triggered when the form is submitted—is intercepted. [preventDefault()] suspends the submission; the form is put on hold, and its message ([dataset.confirmation], the value of the [data-confirmation] attribute) is displayed in the window that appears;
  • lines 19–27: a single handler for clicks in the window: [evenement.target] is the element clicked; its attribute [data-action] specifies which button it is. “Yes” submits the pending form using the [submit()] method, which—unlike clicking a button—does not trigger the [submit] event (otherwise, the window would reappear); “No” hides the window.

Without [JavaScript], the form is simply submitted without confirmation: the page remains usable. This is progressive enhancement: [JavaScript] adds convenience, but the application does not depend on it.

docs.title: 7. The Lifecycle of a Request
docs.text:
Between the arrival of a request and the dispatch of its response, [Django] goes through several steps, and the application can intervene at each one. We have already encountered several of these intervention points: the middleware components and their method [__call__] (examples 03, 12, 16, 23), their [process_exception] methods (examples 08 and 12) and [process_view] methods (example 21), and route converters (example 12). This chapter combines them into a single example, which displays a message in the console at each step so that the order can be observed:

    1. the [request_started] signal: the request has just arrived. A signal is a notification, emitted by [Django] at a specific moment, that application functions—the receivers—can receive. They cannot act on the request: they are simply notified;
    1. The [__call__] method of the middleware components, before the call to [get_response]: the middleware components are processed in the order specified by the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration. Routing has not yet taken place: a middleware component does not yet know which view will handle the request. It may also respond on its own, without invoking the rest of the chain: in that case, neither the subsequent middleware components nor the view are called;
    1. Routing: Once all middleware components have been processed, [Django] searches for the route that matches the requested path (example 02); the route parameter converters (example 12) are called at this point. If no route matches, a [Http404] (404) exception is thrown;
  • 3 and 4. The [process_view] method of the middleware components, in the order specified: the view has been selected but not yet called. A middleware component then knows the view and its parameters; it can let the process continue (return [None]), respond on behalf of the view, or throw an exception;
    1. the view, and the template it generates;
  • x. The [process_exception] middleware method, if the view has thrown an exception, in the reverse order of the configuration. The first one to provide a response stops the search. If none provides one, [Django] generates the error response itself: its detailed page in debug mode, or the application’s error page, provided by the views [handler400], [handler403], [handler404], and [handler500] (see below). An exception thrown elsewhere (in the [__call__] or [process_view] of a middleware component, or in routing) does not pass through [process_exception]: [Django] converts it into an error response upon exiting the relevant middleware;
  • 6 and 7. The [__call__] method of the middleware components, following the call to [get_response], in the reverse order of the configuration: the response is ready, and each middleware component can modify it (add a header, a cookie);
    1. The [request_finished] signal, sent after the response is sent to the browser. Receivers can no longer modify the response: they are used for processing tasks that can wait (such as closing database connections, which is what [Django] itself does), without making the user wait.

This is equivalent to the filters of [Java] and the interceptors of [Spring MVC], the action filters of [ASP.NET Core MVC], and the functions [before_request] / [after_request] and [Flask] functions, the middleware in [Laravel], and the event listeners in [Symfony]. Compared to these, the difference lies in the structure: a middleware component encapsulates the rest of the processing (it calls [get_response], and thus sees the request before and the response after, within the same code, like the Russian nesting dolls in Example 03), whereas an event listener reacts to an event, and you must listen for two events—one before and one after the action—to take action. The order of the middleware components, meanwhile, follows the list in the [MIDDLEWARE] configuration, rather than a numerical sequence: this is easier to read, but you must be familiar with the ordering constraints for the middleware components in [Django] (the session before authentication, for example; as specified in the [Django] documentation).

# calcul/journal.py: a message in the development server console

import sys


def log(message):
     # stderr: error output, displayed by the console just like Django messages
    print(message, file=sys.stderr)

docs.title: 7.1.2. Before and after everything else: the signals
docs.text:
# calcul/signaux.py: two Django signals, emitted at the beginning and end of each request

from django.core.signals import request_finished, request_started
from django.dispatch import receiver

from . import chrono
from .journal import log


# @receiver: the function is called each time the request_started signal is emitted,
# before all middleware
@receiver(request_started)
def debut(sender, environ, **kwargs):
    log(f"--- {environ['REQUEST_METHOD']} {environ['PATH_INFO']}")
    log("0. signal request_started")


# request_finished: at the very end, APRÈS before sending the response to the browser; we
# the response can no longer be changed
@receiver(request_finished)
def fin(sender, **kwargs):
    duree = chrono.arreter()
     # the measurement has not started if the view has not been reached
    if duree is not None:
        log(f"8. signal request_finished (fin, {duree} ms)")
  • line 3: the two signals from [Django] that frame each request;
  • lines 12–15: the [@receiver] decorator hooks the [debut] function onto the [request_started] signal: it will be called every time the signal is emitted. A receiver receives the signal emitter ([sender]), followed by named parameters specific to each signal; [**kwargs] collects those it does not name, as required by the documentation for [Django] (a signal may receive new parameters in a future version). [request_started] provides [environ], the WSGI dictionary for the query (example 01): the [HttpRequest] object does not yet exist. The receiver displays the method and the path, followed by message #0;
  • lines 20–25: message No. 8, when everything is finished, with the duration measured by the timer (see below), if the measurement has started.

[Django] sends other signals: before and after saving a template from ORM ([pre_save], [post_save]), when a user logs in ([user_logged_in])... and the application can define its own. A receiver must be registered when the application starts, before the first request. The designated location for this is the application configuration:

# calculation/apps.py: the application’s CONFIGURATION calculation

from django.apps import AppConfig


class CalculConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "calcul"

     # ready: Django calls it once, at startup, when all applications
     # are loaded. Signal receivers are attached here
    def ready(self):
        from . import signaux  # noqa: F401 (l'importation suffit à les brancher)
  • lines 6–7: An application’s configuration is a class that inherits from [AppConfig], conventionally located in the application’s [apps.py] module, and which [Django] locates on its own. [name] is the name of the application package. This is also where you would give the application a human-readable name ([verbose_name]);
  • lines 11–12: [Django] calls the method [ready] once, at startup, when all applications are loaded. Importing the [signaux] module there is sufficient: its [@receiver] decorators attach the receivers when they execute. The import is done within the method, rather than at the top of the file, because a module that uses the ORM templates cannot be imported until the applications have been loaded. The comment [# noqa: F401] instructs code-checking tools not to flag an “unused” import.

docs.title: 7.1.3. Before and After the View: The Journal Middleware
docs.text:
# calcul/middleware.py: the middleware from Example 24, in the order specified by the configuration MIDDLEWARE

from django.core.exceptions import BadRequest, PermissionDenied
from django.http import Http404
from django.shortcuts import render

from . import chrono
from .erreurs import ErreurDomaine
from .journal import log


# the PREMIER middleware: it processes each request before the others (and before
# routing), and the response APRÈS all the others
class Journal:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        log("1. Journal, avant (avant le routage)")
        response = self.get_response(request)
        log(f"7. Journal, après (code {response.status_code})")
        return response


# process_view: APRÈS routing: the middleware knows the chosen route
class Bloquer:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
         # resolver_match: the result of the routing (the view, the route name...)
        log(f"3. Bloquer, process_view (route : {request.resolver_match.url_name})")
        if "bloquer" in request.GET:
             # an exception: the subsequent code (Chrono, the view) is not executed
            raise PermissionDenied("accès bloqué")
        return None


# middleware that only acts on views marked by the @chronometre decorator:
# AVANT the view (process_view), APRÈS it; the end of the measurement is handled by the signal
# request_finished (see calculation/signaux.py)
class Chrono:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        response = self.get_response(request)
        if getattr(request, "chronometre", False):
            log(f"6. Chrono, après la vue (code {response.status_code})")
        return response

    def process_view(self, request, view_func, view_args, view_kwargs):
         # getattr(object, name, default): the object’s attribute, or the default value if it does not exist
        if getattr(view_func, "chronometre", False):
            log("4. Chrono, process_view (avant la vue)")
            request.chronometre = True
            chrono.demarrer()
        return None


# process_exception: an exception was thrown; this middleware handles it
# with our error page
class PageErreur:
    CODES = {BadRequest: 400, PermissionDenied: 403, Http404: 404}

    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        return self.get_response(request)

    def process_exception(self, request, exception):
        for classe, code in self.CODES.items():
            if isinstance(exception, classe):
                log(f"x. PageErreur, process_exception (HTTP {code})")
                break
        else:
             # the `else` clause of a `for` loop: executed if the loop was not terminated by a `break`
            if not isinstance(exception, ErreurDomaine):
                return None    # all others: the Django error page
            log(f"x. PageErreur, process_exception (ErreurDomaine : {exception})")
            code = 500
         # the response replaces the exception; it then passes through the middleware again
         # (Chrono, then Log), just like a regular response
        return render(request, "erreur.html", {"code": code}, status=code)
  • Lines 14–22: the first middleware in the configuration: it processes the request before all others (message #1) and the response after all others (message #7), along with its code ([status_code]). It does not know the route, since routing has not yet taken place. It is used for processing that applies to all requests: logging, handling a proxy (the case study mentions this in relation to the clients’ address IP)...

docs.title: 7.1.4. Routing: calculation/convertisseurs.py
docs.text:
# calculation/convertisseurs.py: a path converter (see Example 12): the segment
# converted to an integer, or to None if it is not an integer (in which case the
# view that determines this)

from .journal import log


class EntierConverter:
     # any segment, without a slash
    regex = r"[^/]+"

    def to_python(self, value):
        log(f'2. EntierConverter, le routage (valeur reçue : "{value}")')
        try:
            return int(value)
        except ValueError:
            return None

    def to_url(self, value):
        return str(value)

A route converter (example 12), which writes message No. 2. It accepts any segment (the expression [[^/]+]: one or more characters that are not slashes) and converts it to a whole number, or to [None] if it is not one: unlike the [int] converter (example 02), which would return a 404 page for [/carre/abc]; here, the view will determine the outcome. The file [config/urls.py] saves it as [entier]:

# config/urls.py: the main routing table

from django.urls import path, register_converter

from calcul import erreurs, views
from calcul.convertisseurs import EntierConverter

# the "integer" converter (see calcul/convertisseurs.py)
register_converter(EntierConverter, "entier")

urlpatterns = [
    path("carre/<entier:n>", views.carre, name="carre"),
]

# the application’s error page views: Django uses them for errors
# 400, 403, 404, and 500 (except, in debug mode, for 400, 404, and 500, which it replaces
# with its detailed pages)
handler400 = erreurs.page_400
handler403 = erreurs.page_403
handler404 = erreurs.page_404
handler500 = erreurs.page_500
  • Lines 18–21: the error page views, described later.

docs.title: 7.1.5. After routing: the "Block" middleware
docs.text:
Let’s return to the [calcul/middleware.py] file:

  • Lines 26–39: The second middleware only acts within its method ***[process\_view], after routing. [request.resolver_match] describes the result of the routing (Example 16): the route name ([url_name]***), the view, and its parameters. Message No. 3;
  • Lines 36–38: The parameter [?bloquer] of URL causes a 403 error (Forbidden, access denied): The exception [PermissionDenied] interrupts processing; the subsequent [process_view]s and the view are not called.

docs.title: 7.1.6. Before the view: the Chrono middleware and the @chronometre decorator
docs.text:
We want to time only certain views—those that request it. All we need to do is mark them with a decorator of our own design:

# calcul/chrono.py: one timer per thread, and the @chronometre decorator

import threading
import time

# threading.local: an object whose attributes are PROPRES for each thread
# (thread); the server processes each request in its own thread
_local = threading.local()


def demarrer():
     # perf_counter_ns: a precise timer, in nanoseconds
    _local.debut = time.perf_counter_ns()


# the elapsed time in milliseconds, or None if the timer has not started
def arreter():
    debut = getattr(_local, "debut", None)
    _local.debut = None
    if debut is None:
        return None
    return round((time.perf_counter_ns() - debut) / 1e6)


# a DÉCORATEUR that does not change the view: it MARQUE it, via an attribute that the
# Chrono middleware can read
def chronometre(vue):
    vue.chronometre = True
    return vue
  • lines 27–29: a decorator that does not replace the view; it adds an attribute, [chronometre], and returns it. In [Python], a function is an object to which attributes can be added. This is how [Django] itself marks certain views: [@csrf_exempt] (Example 18) adds the attribute [csrf_exempt], which [CsrfViewMiddleware] reads in its method [process_view];
  • Line 8: The timestamp must be passed from [process_view] to the signal [request_finished]. However, the server processes multiple requests simultaneously: a regular module variable would be shared by all of them. A [threading.local] object has attributes specific to each thread: each request, processed in its own thread, has its own start time;
  • lines 11–22: starting and stopping the timer. [time.perf_counter_ns()] is a precise clock, in nanoseconds, designed to measure durations. [getattr(objet, nom, défaut)] returns an object’s attribute, or the default value if it does not exist: the timer may not have started in this thread. The duration is returned in milliseconds.

The middleware that reads the mark, in the file [calcul/middleware.py]:

  • lines 55–61: in [process_view], if the view contains the mark, message #4 is sent, and the timer starts. The mark is also stored in the request for later use. The decorator [@require_GET], applied on top of [@chronometre] (file [calcul/views.py]), does not clear the mark: [functools.wraps] (example 08) copies the attributes of the function it wraps;
  • lines 49–53: in [__call__], after the view, message #6, with the response code, if the view was timed.

docs.title: 7.1.7. The view: calculation/views.py
docs.text:
# calculation/views.py: a timed view

from django.core.exceptions import BadRequest
from django.shortcuts import render
from django.views.decorators.http import require_GET

from .chrono import chronometre
from .erreurs import ErreurDomaine
from .journal import log


# n: the route parameter, provided by our converter EntierConverter;
# @chronometer: the Chrono middleware measures the duration of this view
@require_GET
@chronometre
def carre(request, n):
    log(f"5. vue carre({n})")
    if n is None:
        raise BadRequest("pas un entier")    # Error 400: see PageErreur
    if n == 13:
        raise ErreurDomaine("13 porte malheur")    # an “unexpected” error
    return render(request, "calcul/resultat.html", {"n": n, "carre": n * n})
  • line 15: the view is marked with our decorator [@chronometre];
  • line 16: the parameter [n] is provided by our converter;
  • lines 18–19: a parameter that is not an integer: error 400 (Bad Request), caused by the exception [BadRequest] (example 07);
  • lines 20–21: the number 13 causes an “unexpected” error, a [ErreurDomaine] exception from the application;
  • line 22: the normal case. The [calcul/resultat.html] template simply displays the result.

docs.title: 7.1.8. Error handling: the PageErreur middleware and error views
docs.text:
The last middleware in the [calcul/middleware.py] file replaces the error pages from [Django] with our own, for exceptions that escape the view:

  • line 67: a dictionary whose keys are exception classes and whose values are the corresponding HTTP codes;
  • lines 76–79: [isinstance] (example 03) checks whether the exception is of one of these classes (or a child class). If so, display message No. x, along with the code, and [break] terminates the loop;
  • Lines 80–85: The [else] of a [for] loop is executed if the loop has completed without a [break]: none of the three classes is suitable. A [ErreurDomaine] exception is an “unexpected” error, converted into a “custom” error page with status code 500 (Internal Server Error). The exception message is displayed in the console but not on the page: it may contain internal details that are not relevant to the user. Other exceptions are handled by [Django] ([return None]);
  • line 88: the response, which replaces the exception. It then passes through the preceding middleware components ([Chrono], then [Journal]), just like a regular response.

This middleware only handles exceptions thrown by the view. For other cases (the [PermissionDenied] exception from the [Bloquer] middleware, the 404 error from a URL middleware with no route), [Django] uses the application’s error views, declared in the [config/urls.py] file by the variables [handler400], [handler403], [handler404], and [handler500] (lines 18–21), and written to the file [calcul/erreurs.py]:

# calculation/erreurs.py: an application exception, and the error page views

from django.shortcuts import render

from .journal import log


# an application exception: an “unexpected” error of a specific type
class ErreurDomaine(Exception):
    pass


# error page views (see config/urls.py): exception is the exception that
# caused the error
def page_400(request, exception):
    return page(request, 400)


def page_403(request, exception):
    return page(request, 403)


def page_404(request, exception):
    return page(request, 404)


# The 500 page does not receive the exception
def page_500(request):
    return page(request, 500)


def page(request, code):
    log(f"x. vue de la page d'erreur {code}")
    return render(request, "erreur.html", {"code": code}, status=code)
  • lines 9–10: the application exception: a class that inherits from [Exception], without adding anything to it ([pass] is the statement that does nothing: a block cannot be empty);
  • lines 15–29: The error views receive the request and the exception (except for view 500, which receives only the request);
  • lines 32–34: the same error page for all of them, with the error code (message #x).

There is one subtlety: in debug mode, [Django] retains its detailed pages for errors 400, 404, and 500, and uses these views only for error 403. This is intentional: during development, the detailed page is more useful. Outside of debug mode, all four views are used. Without these views, [Django] would use, outside of debug mode, its plain pages (example 03), or application templates named [400.html], [403.html], [404.html], and [500.html] if they exist: this is another, even simpler way to replace the error pages. The application’s error page:

{% extends "layout.html" %}

{# the error page; its template: the error code #}
{% block contenu %}
  <div class="alert alert-danger">
    <h1 class="h4">Erreur {{ code }}</h1>
    <p class="mb-0">
      {% if code == 400 %}Requête incorrecte.{% elif code == 403 %}Accès refusé.{% elif code == 404 %}Page introuvable.{% else %}Erreur interne du serveur.{% endif %}
    </p>
  </div>
{% endblock %}
